rationale: A is better — a larger area under the curve means better discrimination across all cutoffs, with 1.0 perfect and 0.5 no better than chance (the diagonal). The optimal cutoff sits at the upper-left corner, closest to 100% sensitivity with 0% false positives. Note the AUC comparison is independent of prevalence, which is why the last option fails — unlike PPV, discrimination is a property of the test itself.

stem: Which measure can be calculated directly from a case-control study, and why not the other?
options: Relative risk, because exposure is known first
Odds ratio, because the investigator fixed the number of cases and controls
Attributable risk, because incidence is measurable
Cumulative incidence, because participants are followed forward in time from exposure
Both equally, since the 2×2 table is the same
rationale: The odds ratio. In a case-control study the investigator chooses how many cases and controls to enrol, so the proportion who are diseased is an artefact of the sampling — and you cannot compute a risk when you invented the denominator. Relative risk needs incidence, which requires following people forward from exposure, i.e. a cohort. The saving grace: for a rare disease the OR approximates the RR.

stem: A cohort of 500 smokers and 1,500 non-smokers is followed; 75 in each group develop disease. The relative risk is:
options: 3.0 — smoking triples the risk
1.0 — smoking shows no association here
0.33 — smoking appears protective
2.0 — smoking doubles the risk
Cannot be calculated from a cohort
rationale: RR = 3.0. Risk in smokers = 75/500 = 0.15; in non-smokers = 75/1,500 = 0.05; RR = 0.15 / 0.05 = 3. The trap is the equal case counts — 75 and 75 look like no association until you notice the denominators differ threefold. Always divide by the group size before comparing. An RR of 1.0 would mean no association, and below 1.0 would suggest protection.

stem: Coffee drinking is associated with lung cancer. After stratifying by smoking, the association disappears. Smoking is a confounder here because it meets which criteria?
options: It is associated with coffee, is an independent risk factor for lung cancer, and is not on the causal pathway
It is associated with coffee and lies directly on the causal pathway between coffee and cancer, so adjusting for it removes the true effect
It is measured with error, producing information bias
It affects who agreed to enter the study, producing selection bias
It modifies the effect of coffee differently in each stratum
rationale: A confounder must satisfy all three: associated with the exposure (smokers drink more coffee), an independent risk factor for the outcome (smoking causes lung cancer on its own), and not on the causal pathway between them (coffee does not cause smoking). Being on the pathway would make it a mediator, and adjusting for a mediator wrongly erases a real effect. The give-away in this stem is that the association vanished on stratification — effect modification would instead give different effects in each stratum, not none.

stem: Cases with a disease recall past exposures more thoroughly than controls do. This is:
options: Selection bias caused by differential enrollment
Recall bias, a form of information bias
Confounding caused by unequal exposure prevalence
Lead-time bias caused by earlier diagnosis
Observer bias caused by unequal outcome assessment
rationale: Recall bias — a type of information (measurement) bias, and a classic weakness of case-control designs, where exposure is ascertained after the outcome is known. Being ill motivates people to search their memory for a cause. Contrast: selection bias is about who ends up in the study; confounding is a third variable explaining the association; random error is noise, not a systematic distortion. Bias distorts in a direction; chance does not.

stem: A study identifies people by their exposure status from old employment records and follows their outcomes forward to today. This design is:
options: Cross-sectional
Retrospective cohort
Case-control
Randomised controlled trial
Prospective cohort
rationale: A retrospective cohort. The defining feature of any cohort is that groups are assembled by exposure and followed toward the outcome; ‘retrospective’ only says the exposure was recorded in the past, so the follow-up has already happened. It is still a cohort, and it still yields incidence and relative risk. A case-control would start from people who already have the disease; a cross-sectional study measures exposure and outcome at the same moment and so cannot establish which came first.

stem: A test with 99% sensitivity is negative. What does that let you do, and what is the mnemonic?
options: Confidently rule the disease IN — SpPIn
Confidently rule the disease OUT — SnNOut
Confidently rule the disease OUT — SpPOut
Nothing without knowing specificity
Confidently rule the disease IN — SnNIn
rationale:
SnNOut: a highly SeNsitive test, when Negative, rules OUT. High sensitivity means few false negatives, so a negative result is trustworthy. The partner rule is SpPIn: a highly SPecific test, when Positive, rules IN.

⚠ Her Epi 4 handout misstates this. It reads “the specificity was very high (Specificity = 60%) to rule out a DVT” — which is self-contradictory twice over: ruling out is a sensitivity argument, and 60% is not high. Use SnNOut/SpPIn and answer the concept.

stem: From a 2×2 table, which two measures are read DOWN the columns rather than across the rows?
options: PPV and NPV
Sensitivity and specificity
Sensitivity and PPV
Specificity and NPV
Prevalence and incidence
rationale: Sensitivity and specificity read down the columns — down the disease-positive column and the disease-negative column, because each is conditioned on true disease status. PPV and NPV read across the rows, conditioned on the test result. That single orientation rule prevents the commonest arithmetic error on these questions, and it also explains why only the row-wise measures move with prevalence.

stem: A disease has incidence 10 per 1,000 per year and average duration 5 years. Estimated prevalence is about:
rationale: About 50 per 1,000. Prevalence ≈ incidence × duration = 10/1,000/year × 5 years = 50/1,000. The relationship is the engine behind several exam favourites: a disease that is rapidly fatal or rapidly cured has low prevalence despite high incidence, while a chronic incurable one accumulates prevalence. It only holds in a steady state and when prevalence is low.

stem: A screening programme detects disease earlier but does not change the date of death. Five-year survival nevertheless improves. This is:
options: A genuine treatment benefit
Lead-time bias
Confounding by indication
Recall bias
Regression to the mean
rationale: Lead-time bias. Diagnosing earlier starts the survival clock sooner without postponing death, so measured survival lengthens while nothing about the patient's life has changed. It is the reason screening programmes must be judged on mortality rates in the population, not on survival from diagnosis. Its companion is length-time bias, where screening preferentially catches slow-growing disease and so looks better than it is.

stem: A study reports a relative risk of 1.8 with a 95% confidence interval of 0.9 to 3.4. The correct interpretation is:
options: A significant 80% increase in risk
Not statistically significant, because the interval includes 1
Not statistically significant, because the interval includes 0
Significant, because the point estimate exceeds 1
Invalid, because the interval is too wide to interpret
rationale: Not significant, because the interval includes 1. For a ratio measure — RR, OR, HR — the null value is 1, not 0: a ratio of 1 means the two risks are equal. Zero is the null only for a difference (risk difference, mean difference). Mixing the two up is one of the most common misreadings of a results table, and the point estimate of 1.8 does not rescue it: the data are compatible with a modest protective effect.

stem: Which pairing of macromolecule class to its activated precursor is correct?
options: Protein — acyl CoA
Carbohydrate — UDP-glucose
Lipid — amino acyl tRNA
Nucleic acid — glucose 6-phosphate
Carbohydrate — acetyl CoA
rationale: Carbohydrate → UDP-glucose. The full set she wants: protein → amino acyl tRNA, lipid → acyl CoA, nucleic acid → nucleoside triphosphates. The principle underneath is worth more than the list: biosynthesis never uses the plain building block — it uses an energy-charged, carrier-attached version, because attaching the carrier is where the thermodynamic cost is paid. That is also why anabolism needs a separate NADPH pool.

stem: A patient has a defect in SGLT1 in the intestinal brush border. Which sugar's absorption is most impaired, and why?
options: Fructose, because it uses GLUT5
Glucose, because it enters against its gradient using the Na⁺ gradient
Galactose only, because it has a dedicated transporter
All three equally, since SGLT1 handles every monosaccharide
None, because absorption is entirely by passive diffusion down gradients
rationale: Glucose (and galactose) via SGLT1, which is secondary active transport: it drags the sugar against its concentration gradient by riding the Na⁺ gradient that the basolateral Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase maintains. The ATP is spent by that pump, not by SGLT1 itself — hence secondary. Fructose is the exception: it crosses by facilitated diffusion through GLUT5, needs no Na⁺, and is therefore unaffected. Exit to blood is by GLUT2 for all of them.

stem: A report gives the case-fatality rate for a new infection as 2%. This figure describes:
options: The proportion of the population who will die of it
The proportion of people with the disease who die from it
The number of new cases per 1,000 person-years
The proportion of all deaths attributable to the disease
The frequency of illness in a defined population
rationale: Case-fatality rate is deaths ÷ people with the disease — a measure of how lethal the illness is once you have it, not how common it is. Keep the family straight: morbidity = frequency of illness; mortality rate = deaths in the whole population; proportionate mortality = share of all deaths from that cause. The denominator is what distinguishes them, and reading a case-fatality rate as a population risk overstates the danger enormously.

stem: Dietary fructose is phosphorylated in the liver by fructokinase. Why does this bypass the main regulated step of glycolysis, and what follows clinically?
options: It produces fructose 6-phosphate, which enters above PFK-1
It produces fructose 1-phosphate, entering below PFK-1 and escaping regulation
It produces glucose 6-phosphate, which inhibits hexokinase
It produces glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate directly
It requires no ATP, so flux is unregulated
rationale: Fructokinase makes fructose 1-phosphate, and aldolase B then cleaves it to DHAP + glyceraldehyde — both of which enter glycolysis below PFK-1. Since PFK-1 is the committed, regulated step, fructose pours into the pathway unregulated. That is precisely why a high-fructose diet drives hepatic lipogenesis: the carbon arrives past the gate that would otherwise slow it down. Note the contrast with hexokinase, which phosphorylates fructose to fructose 6-P in muscle — a minor route.

stem: A child is found to have fructose in the urine on routine testing but is entirely well, with normal growth and no liver disease. The defective enzyme is:
options: Aldolase B
Fructokinase
Glucokinase
Galactokinase
Aldose reductase
rationale:
Fructokinase deficiency = essential fructosuria, and it is benign. Block the first step and nothing phosphorylated can accumulate — the unphosphorylated fructose simply spills into the urine and the patient is fine.

This is the key discriminator with hereditary fructose intolerance: the dangerous defect is always the one downstream of a phosphorylation, because that is where a trapped phosphorylated intermediate builds up. Same logic recurs in galactose.

stem: An infant becomes hypoglycaemic and vomits whenever fruit or sucrose is introduced, and develops liver dysfunction. The mechanism of the hypoglycaemia is:
options: Fructose directly inhibits glucokinase
Fructose 1-phosphate accumulates, trapping inorganic phosphate and depleting ATP, which blocks glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis
Fructokinase deficiency prevents any fructose from being phosphorylated
Excess fructose 6-phosphate drives glycolysis uncontrollably
Galactose 1-phosphate competes for the same transporter
rationale:
Hereditary fructose intolerance — aldolase B deficiency. Fructokinase keeps phosphorylating fructose, but aldolase B cannot cleave the product, so fructose 1-phosphate accumulates. It sequesters the cell's inorganic phosphate, ATP cannot be regenerated, and both glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis stall — hence hypoglycaemia that does not respond to glucagon.

The onset on weaning is the clinical giveaway: symptoms begin exactly when fruit, sucrose or honey enters the diet.

stem: Place the galactose pathway in order, from dietary galactose to a glycolytic intermediate.
options: Galactokinase → 4-epimerase → GALT → phosphoglucomutase
Galactokinase → GALT → 4-epimerase → phosphoglucomutase
GALT → galactokinase → phosphoglucomutase → 4-epimerase
Phosphoglucomutase → galactokinase → GALT → 4-epimerase
4-epimerase → galactokinase → GALT → phosphoglucomutase
rationale:
Galactokinase → GALT → 4-epimerase → phosphoglucomutase. Galactokinase phosphorylates galactose to galactose 1-phosphate. GALT (galactose 1-P uridyltransferase) swaps UMP off UDP-glucose onto it, giving UDP-galactose + glucose 1-phosphate. The 4-epimerase regenerates UDP-glucose so the cycle can run again, and phosphoglucomutase converts glucose 1-P to glucose 6-P, which enters glycolysis.

Notice the design: UDP-glucose is recycled, not consumed — which is why the epimerase matters.

context: A neonate is brought in on day 3 of life with jaundice, vomiting after feeds and hepatomegaly. Urine contains a reducing sugar, but the glucose-specific dipstick is negative. AST and ALT are elevated; haemoglobin is normal.
stem: What is the most likely diagnosis, and which single laboratory finding in the stem points at it most specifically?
options: Hereditary fructose intolerance — the vomiting whenever feeds contain fruit or sucrose
Classic galactosemia — a reducing sugar in urine with a negative glucose dipstick
Essential fructosuria — the reducing sugar in urine
Biliary atresia — the jaundice and hepatomegaly
Glycogen storage disease — the hepatomegaly
rationale:
Classic galactosemia (GALT deficiency). The decisive finding is a reducing sugar in the urine with a negative glucose-specific dipstick: the dipstick detects glucose only, so a positive reducing-substance test with a negative dipstick means a reducing sugar that is not glucose — here galactose.

Timing supports it: a neonate presenting on day 3, i.e. once lactose feeding is established. Lactose is glucose + galactose. Hereditary fructose intolerance presents later, when fruit or sucrose is introduced at weaning, not on milk.

context: A neonate is brought in on day 3 of life with jaundice, vomiting after feeds and hepatomegaly. Urine contains a reducing sugar, but the glucose-specific dipstick is negative. AST and ALT are elevated; haemoglobin is normal.
stem: Her handout asks what the biochemical effects are. Which sequence is correct?
options: Galactose 1-P accumulates first; free galactose then also accumulates as less is converted
Free galactose accumulates first, and galactose 1-phosphate never rises at any stage of the disease
UDP-galactose accumulates, causing the liver damage
Glucose 1-P accumulates and inhibits glycolysis
Galactitol accumulates in liver, causing hepatomegaly
rationale:
Her own answer: galactose 1-phosphate accumulates in the tissues first, and because less galactose is then being converted onward, free galactose also builds up in tissue and blood. As both rise, cells are damaged — in this case chiefly the liver.

Keep galactitol separate: it is made by aldose reductase from excess galactose and its damage is to the lens, causing cataracts, not the hepatomegaly.

context: A neonate is brought in on day 3 of life with jaundice, vomiting after feeds and hepatomegaly. Urine contains a reducing sugar, but the glucose-specific dipstick is negative. AST and ALT are elevated; haemoglobin is normal.
stem: The infant is put on a strictly galactose-free diet. Can tissues still obtain the galactose they need for glycolipids and glycoproteins?
options: No — dietary galactose is the only source
Yes — glucose → glucose 1-P → UDP-glucose, then the 4-epimerase makes UDP-galactose
Yes — GALT works in reverse when galactose is absent
No — but the requirement disappears after infancy
Yes — galactose is synthesised de novo from acetyl-CoA
rationale:
Yes, from glucose. Glucose → glucose 1-phosphate → UDP-glucose, and the C4 epimerase converts that to UDP-galactose. So a galactose-free diet does not starve the brain of gangliosides or the body of glycoproteins.

This is her second case question, and it is reassuring in a way worth carrying into counselling: the diet removes the toxin without creating a deficiency.

context: A neonate is brought in on day 3 of life with jaundice, vomiting after feeds and hepatomegaly. Urine contains a reducing sugar, but the glucose-specific dipstick is negative. AST and ALT are elevated; haemoglobin is normal.
stem: AST 61 and ALT 40 are elevated, bilirubin is high, and haemoglobin is normal. The correct interpretation of the raised bilirubin is:
options: Haemolysis, since bilirubin is raised
Liver cell damage
Biliary obstruction, given the conjugated fraction
Physiological jaundice of the newborn
Gilbert syndrome unmasked by illness
rationale:
Her reasoning, verbatim in structure: the raised aminotransferases indicate liver cell damage, and because haemoglobin is not low, excessive haemolysis is unlikely. The likelier explanation is that the damaged liver cannot conjugate a normal bilirubin load.

The exam skill here is not the diagnosis — it is using a normal haemoglobin to rule OUT haemolysis. A finding that is normal can be as informative as one that is abnormal.

stem: A child has bilateral cataracts but no liver disease, no vomiting and normal growth. The deficient enzyme and the mechanism of the cataracts are:
options: GALT; galactose 1-phosphate accumulates in the lens and damages the fibre cells
Galactokinase; excess galactose is reduced by aldose reductase to galactitol, which accumulates in the lens
Aldolase B; fructose 1-phosphate accumulates in the lens
4-epimerase; UDP-galactose accumulates in the lens
Aldose reductase; galactose itself accumulates in the lens
rationale:
Galactokinase deficiency. Block the first step and galactose itself accumulates — no phosphorylated intermediate builds up, so the liver is spared. The excess galactose is instead reduced by aldose reductase to galactitol, which is osmotically active, is trapped in the lens, and causes cataracts.

Same chemistry as glucose → sorbitol in diabetic cataract. Cataracts alone = galactokinase; cataracts plus liver failure and vomiting = GALT.

stem: Compare the two galactose defects on long-term dietary strictness. Which is correct, and why?
options: GALT deficiency needs the stricter lifelong diet
Galactokinase deficiency needs the stricter lifelong diet, because GALT-deficient children gain an alternate route that requires galactose 1-phosphate
Both need identical lifelong restriction
Neither needs restriction after infancy
GALT deficiency resolves spontaneously once the liver matures
rationale:
Counter-intuitive but correct: galactokinase deficiency needs the more restrictive diet for life. GALT-deficient children can eventually tolerate some galactose because an alternate childhood enzyme lets galactose 1-phosphate react with UTP to form UDP-galactose, bypassing GALT. That rescue requires gal-1-P — which a galactokinase-deficient patient cannot make at all, having no way to phosphorylate galactose.

So the enzyme with the milder acute presentation carries the stricter long-term restriction. Severity at presentation does not predict severity of management.

stem: Sugar nucleotides such as UDP-glucose exist because:
options: They store energy more densely than ATP
Attaching the sugar to a nucleotide activates it for transfer reactions and biosynthesis
They allow sugars to cross the plasma membrane without needing any dedicated transporter protein
They protect sugars from oxidation
They are the only form a kinase can phosphorylate
rationale:
A sugar nucleotide is an activated sugar. Coupling the sugar to UDP raises its transfer potential, so it can be handed onto a growing glycogen chain, a glycolipid, or — as here — onto galactose 1-phosphate by GALT.

This is the same principle as activated precursors generally: biosynthesis never uses the plain building block, it uses a carrier-attached, energy-charged version. UDP-glucose is the activated precursor for carbohydrate.

stem: Which pairing of enzyme block to the accumulating compound is correct?
options: Aldolase B → fructose; galactokinase → galactose 1-phosphate; fructokinase → fructose 6-phosphate
Fructokinase → fructose; aldolase B → fructose 1-phosphate; galactokinase → galactose; GALT → galactose 1-phosphate
Fructokinase → fructose 1-phosphate; GALT → galactose
Aldolase B → glyceraldehyde; GALT → UDP-galactose
All four blocks cause accumulation of the parent sugar only
rationale:
The whole reading in one line. Block the first enzyme of either pathway and the unphosphorylated sugar accumulates — benign, it leaves in the urine (essential fructosuria) or is diverted to a polyol (galactokinase deficiency → galactitol → cataracts). Block the second and a phosphorylated intermediate is trapped inside the cell — dangerous, because it sequesters phosphate and damages the organ (hereditary fructose intolerance, classic galactosemia).

First enzyme blocked = mild. Second enzyme blocked = severe. The pattern is worth more than the four names.

stem: A retrovirus copies its RNA genome into DNA using reverse transcriptase. Ritchie states the central dogma as Rule #1 and immediately adds Rule #2. What does the retrovirus actually demonstrate?
options: That the central dogma is simply wrong, and that information normally flows RNA → DNA rather than DNA → RNA in the majority of organisms
That information transfer has exceptions to the usual DNA → RNA → protein direction, without protein ever acting as a template
That protein can serve as a template for RNA in some organisms
That replication and transcription are the same process
That RNA viruses do not use the genetic code
rationale:
Rule #2 is “there are exceptions to every rule” — retroviruses run RNA → DNA. What survives untouched is the one-way step at the end: nothing ever reads protein back into nucleic acid. So the exception is real but bounded.

Notice she uses the same logic for telomerase later in the lecture — Tert has reverse transcriptase activity, so telomerase is the human example of the same exception.

The trap: “information normally flows RNA → DNA” overshoots. Reverse transcription is the exception, not the norm — and calling the dogma “wrong” is exactly the overcorrection a distractor is built to catch.

stem: Match each process to what it copies. Which line is correct?
options: Replication copies only the genes a cell currently needs, while transcription copies the entire genome once during every single cell cycle
Replication copies the entire genome so each daughter cell gets a complete set; transcription copies only what is needed at that moment
Both replication and transcription copy the entire genome, differing only in product
Translation copies DNA into protein directly
Transcription copies the entire genome; translation selects which parts to use
rationale:
Her framing: replication is all-or-nothing — every daughter cell must receive a complete copy of the genome. Transcription is selective — only some of the information is needed in a given cell at a given time.

That asymmetry is the whole reason gene regulation exists as a topic: a cell has no choice about replication, but enormous choice about transcription.

The trap: the option that has transcription copying the entire genome sounds plausible if you are thinking about how much DNA is present. Presence is not the same as being transcribed.

stem: Her practice question asks what it means to say the genetic code is unambiguous. Choose the statement that captures it.
options: Any amino acid is specified by a single codon
Any given codon always encodes the same amino acid
Some amino acids are specified by several different codons
No nucleotides are shared by adjacent codons
All organisms use the same genetic code
rationale:
Unambiguous = one codon → one amino acid, always. UUU is Phe every time; CAG is Gln every time.

Her own answer note is worth memorising because it names each foil: “any amino acid is specified by a single codon” and “some amino acids are specified by several codons” both describe degeneracy; “all organisms use the same code” describes universality; “no nucleotides are shared” describes non-overlapping.

The trap: four of the five options are true statements about the code. Only one answers this property. When every option is true, the question is asking which label fits — read the property name in the stem, not the biology.

stem: 64 codons encode 20 amino acids plus 3 stop signals. Which pair of consequences follows directly from that arithmetic?
options: The code is degenerate, and most amino acids have more than one codon
The code is unambiguous, and each codon has exactly one meaning
The code is universal, and all organisms share it
The code is non-overlapping, so codons do not share nucleotides
The code is co-linear, so the protein sequence follows the nucleotide order
rationale:
61 sense codons distributed over 20 amino acids must mean redundancy — that is degeneracy, and it is a counting argument, not a biological observation. Phe has 2 codons, Arg has 6.

Every other property listed is a genuine attribute of the code but none of them is forced by the numbers. Unambiguity in particular is logically independent: a code could be degenerate and ambiguous; ours is degenerate and unambiguous.

The trap: unambiguity is the neighbouring concept and the one students pair with degeneracy, so it is the natural second-guess. The stem says directly from that arithmetic — only redundancy is forced by 61 > 20.

stem: The coding sequence of a gene region is 5'-TTT-GTC-ATG-TGA-GGG-3'. What is the corresponding amino acid sequence?
options: Phe-Val-Met-Stop
Lys-Gln-Tyr-Thr-Pro
Gly-Ser-Val-Leu-Phe
Pro-Ser-His-Asp-Phe
Phe-Val-Met-Stop-Gly
rationale:
Transcribe first: the coding strand reads the same as the mRNA with T→U, giving 5'-UUU-GUC-AUG-UGA-GGG-3'. Then UUU = Phe, GUC = Val, AUG = Met, UGA = stop.

Translation ends at the stop codon. GGG is still in the mRNA, but no glycine is added — the ribosome releases.

The trap: the option ending …Stop-Gly is the one that catches people who translate mechanically to the end of the sequence. A stop codon is not a residue and nothing follows it. This is her keyed question 10.

stem: For the same gene region 5'-TTT-GTC-ATG-TGA-GGG-3', what is the complementary DNA sequence?
options: 5'-AAA-CAG-TAC-ACT-CCC-3'
5'-CCC-TCA-CAT-GAC-AAA-3'
5'-GGG-AGT-GTA-CTG-TTT-3'
5'-AAA-CAG-UAC-ACU-CCC-3'
5'-GGG-AGU-GUA-CUG-UUU-3'
rationale:
Two rules combine here. (1) The complement is antiparallel, so pairing T-T-T at the given 5' end produces A-A-A at the complement's 3' end. (2) By convention every sequence is written 5'→3', so you must then flip it. Pair, then reverse: 5'-CCC-TCA-CAT-GAC-AAA-3'.

The trap: the option reading AAA-CAG-TAC-ACT-CCC is the correct base-by-base complement written in the wrong direction — it is what you get if you pair and forget to reverse, and it is the single most common error on this question type. Two other options contain U, which makes them RNA, not a complementary DNA strand.

stem: Which statement about the structure of DNA is true?
options: The two strands align in parallel directions
The two strands are held together only by hydrogen bonds
Base pairs comprise either two purines or two pyrimidines
Purine nucleotides sit on one strand and pyrimidines on the other
There are 12 nucleotide pairs per helical turn
rationale:
Her keyed answer. The two strands are joined only by hydrogen bonds between the paired bases — which is exactly why a helicase can separate them without breaking any covalent bond, and why an AT-rich origin (2 H-bonds per pair rather than 3) melts first.

The other statements fail in order: strands are antiparallel, not parallel; every base pair is one purine with one pyrimidine, which is what keeps the helix a constant width; purines and pyrimidines are therefore distributed on both strands; and there are ~10 base pairs per turn.

The trap: the “two purines or two pyrimidines” option is the one that feels chemically reasonable until you remember the width constraint — a purine-purine pair is too fat, pyrimidine-pyrimidine too thin.

stem: A single strand of DNA is drawn vertically, with a free phosphate at the top and a free hydroxyl at the bottom, reading A, C, G, T from top to bottom. How is this strand written?
options: 5'-ACGT-3'
3'-ACGT-5'
5'-TGCA-3'
3'-TGCA-5'
5'-GCAT-3'
rationale:
The free phosphate marks the 5' end and the free hydroxyl marks the 3' end. So the top is 5', the bottom is 3', and reading top to bottom gives 5'-ACGT-3'. Her keyed answer, question 11.

Fix the landmark and this whole family of questions becomes mechanical: phosphate = 5', OH = 3'. It is the same landmark that explains why polymerase can only extend a 3' end.

The trap: 3'-ACGT-5' has the right bases in the right order and is not even a wrong description of the molecule — but sequences are written 5'→3' by convention, so it is the wrong answer. Correct chemistry, wrong convention, is a classic distractor build.

stem: All of the following are present in the nucleosome core except:
options: H1
H2A
H2B
H3
H4
rationale:
The nucleosome core is a histone octamer: two each of H2A, H2B, H3 and H4. H1 is the linker — it sits between adjacent nucleosomes on the DNA outside the bead, not inside the core.

Her image is worth keeping: DNA wound around the core like thread around a spool, negatively charged DNA looping twice around a positively charged octamer. The electrostatics are the point — that is why histone acetylation, which removes positive charge, loosens the grip.

The trap: H1 is unquestionably a histone and unquestionably part of chromatin, so it reads as belonging. The question turns on the word core.

stem: Arrange these in order of increasing structural complexity: chromatid · solenoid (30 nm fiber) · double-stranded DNA · beads on a string (11 nm fiber) · histone proteins · chromosome.
options: Histone proteins → dsDNA → beads on a string → solenoid → chromatid → chromosome
dsDNA → histone proteins → beads on a string → solenoid → chromatid → chromosome
dsDNA → beads on a string → histone proteins → solenoid → chromosome → chromatid
Histone proteins → beads on a string → dsDNA → solenoid → chromatid → chromosome
dsDNA → solenoid → beads on a string → chromatid → histone proteins → chromosome
rationale:
Her keyed order runs from the two components upward: histone proteins and double-stranded DNA are the raw materials; together they form the 11 nm beads-on-a-string; that coils into the 30 nm solenoid; which is packed into a chromatid; and after S phase two chromatids make the chromosome as seen in mitosis.

Anchor the two numbers — 11 nm nucleosome fiber, 30 nm solenoid — and the middle of the sequence is never in doubt.

The trap: the option starting dsDNA → histone proteins orders the two components against each other, but they are peers, not successive levels. Both are inputs to the same first structure.

stem: The inactive X chromosome in a female somatic cell is facultative heterochromatin. Which feature of the definition does it illustrate?
options: It contains highly repetitive DNA that is never transcribed in any cell of the body at any time
It is chromatin that could be genetically active but has been switched off during development
It is lightly packed and rich in genes being actively transcribed
It is chromatin that changes structure with every cell cycle at random
It is a region with no genes, so transcription is impossible
rationale:
Facultative heterochromatin is the conditional kind: DNA that can be euchromatic and transcribed, but has been turned off during some part of development. The late-replicating inactive X is her own named example.

Contrast constitutive heterochromatin — never transcribed in any cell, highly repetitive, e.g. centromeric DNA. The one-word test: could this be on in some other cell? Yes → facultative. No → constitutive.

The trap: the “highly repetitive, never transcribed” option is a correct definition — of constitutive heterochromatin. Two adjacent, both-true definitions with one label in the stem is precisely the format that punishes reading the stem quickly.

stem: A tissue sample shows a strikingly high proportion of euchromatin in its nuclei compared with another tissue from the same person. The most reasonable inference is:
options: That tissue has a different genome sequence
That tissue is transcriptionally more active, since euchromatin is loosely packed and gene-rich
That tissue is in mitosis while the other is in interphase, so all of its chromatin is condensed
That tissue has lost its histone proteins
That tissue is aneuploid
rationale:
Same genome, different chromatin structure. Her point about tissue-specific chromatin alterations is exactly this: the differences are stably inherited through cell division and reflect the functions the tissue carries out. Euchromatin = loosely packed, gene-rich, actively transcribed.

This is the conceptual bridge into the gene regulation lectures — differentiation is not a change in sequence, it is a change in what is readable.

The trap: “different genome sequence” is the answer if you forget that every somatic cell in one person carries the same DNA. Structure, not sequence, is what differs between tissues.

stem: Fill the blanks in order: “______ are sequences of DNA that occupy a specific ______ on a chromosome and are present in different ______ within the population.”
options: Genes … locus … alleles
Alleles … locus … genes
Loci … allele … genes
Genes … allele … loci
Alleles … gene … loci
rationale:
Genes … locus … alleles. Her keyed question 4, and the three words are constantly swapped.

Fix them with her cookbook metaphor: the gene is the recipe; the locus is the page it is printed on, the same page in everyone's copy; the alleles are the variant versions of that recipe circulating in the population — Mom's beef tamales, Dad's pork tamales.

The trap: Alleles … locus … genes gets the middle word right and swaps the outer two, so it survives a quick skim. Check the third blank first — “different ___ within the population” can only be alleles — and the whole option collapses.

stem: After S phase, a duplicated chromosome consists of two sister chromatids. How do sister chromatids differ from homologs?
options: Sister chromatids are identical copies made in S phase; homologs are the maternal and paternal versions of the same chromosome and carry different alleles
Sister chromatids come one from each parent and carry different alleles; homologs are identical copies made during S phase of the same cycle
Sister chromatids carry different alleles; homologs are identical
Sister chromatids are found only in gametes; homologs only in somatic cells
They are two names for the same structure at different stages
rationale:
Sister chromatids are identical — one was copied from the other in S phase, so barring a replication error they carry the same alleles. Homologs are not identical: one came from the egg, one from the sperm, and at any locus they may carry different alleles.

Her third term is worth having ready: the chromatids on the two dyads from a homologous pair are non-sister chromatids — related but not identical. That is the pair that crossing over acts on.

The trap: the option that swaps the two definitions is the whole question. Anchor on the word sister — sisters here means copies, not siblings from different parents.

stem: A human somatic cell has 46 chromosomes. Which statement about ploidy is correct?
options: Somatic cells are haploid (46) and gametes diploid (23)
Somatic cells are diploid with two copies of each chromosome; gametes are haploid with one member of each pair, 23 chromosomes
Somatic cells are diploid with 23 chromosomes; gametes are haploid with 46
Both somatic cells and gametes are diploid, differing only in size
Ploidy refers to the number of chromatids present, so a somatic cell after S phase is correctly described as tetraploid rather than diploid
rationale:
Diploid = two copies of each chromosome — in humans 46, being 22 pairs of autosomes plus XX or XY. Haploid = one member of each pair — a gamete with 23.

Her cookbook version: two full sets of 23 themed cookbooks, one set from Mom's family and one from Dad's.

The trap: the tetraploid option is the interesting one. After S phase the cell has twice the DNA, but the two sister chromatids are still one chromosome held at a single centromere — so the cell remains diploid. Ploidy counts centromeres, not chromatids.

stem: A chromosome is described as acrocentric. Where is the centromere, and what does the term tell you?
options: Centrally placed, giving two arms of roughly equal length
Near one end, so the p arm is very short
Exactly at the tip, so there is no p arm at all
At a position intermediate between central and terminal
It varies between cell divisions
rationale:
Using the centromere as the landmark: metacentric = central, arms roughly equal; submetacentric = intermediate; acrocentric = near one end, leaving a very short p (short) arm and a long q arm.

Worth carrying forward: the acrocentric chromosomes are the ones bearing stalks and satellites, and they are the ones that fuse in a Robertsonian translocation — which is where this reappears in the very next lecture.

The trap: “exactly at the tip, no p arm at all” describes telocentric, which is a real chromosome shape but is not among the human forms she asks for. A distractor that names a real thing from outside the required set is harder to reject than an invented one.

stem: Working outward from a chromosome tip, what is the correct order of the telomeric region, and why does gene density matter here?
options: Telomere → subtelomeric repeats → unique chromosome-specific DNA, with very high gene density near the telomeres
Unique chromosome-specific DNA → telomere → subtelomeric repeats, with very low gene density throughout the region
Subtelomeric repeats → telomere → unique DNA, with no genes anywhere in the region
Telomere → unique DNA → subtelomeric repeats, with gene density irrelevant
Centromere → telomere → satellite, with genes only at the centromere
rationale:
From the tip inward: the telomere itself (3–20 kb of TTAGGG repeat, common to every human chromosome end), then subtelomeric repeats (100–300 kb, shared among subsets of chromosomes), then unique chromosome-specific sequence carrying the most distal genes.

The gene density point is the clinically useful part: there is a very high density of genes near the telomeres, which is why subtelomeric rearrangements are a recognised cause of unexplained intellectual disability.

The trap: the option with “no genes anywhere in the region” leans on the intuition that repeats mean junk. The repeats have no genes; the region as a whole is gene-rich.

stem: What is the function of the telomere, as she defines it?
options: To anchor spindle microtubules during mitosis
To maintain the discreteness of chromosomes, keeping them from joining or sticking to one another
To serve as the origin of replication for each chromosome, the point from which both forks set out
To hold sister chromatids together after duplication
To silence the genes nearest the chromosome ends
rationale:
Her wording: telomeres maintain the discreteness of chromosomes, preventing them from joining with other chromosomes or sticking together. A capped end is read as an end; an uncapped end is read as a double-strand break and gets fused, which is how end-to-end fusions and the resulting instability arise.

The trap: two options describe the centromere — anchoring spindle microtubules via the kinetochore, and tethering sister chromatids. Centromere and telomere are the two chromosome landmarks introduced on the same page, so mixing their jobs is the intended error. Centromere = holds together and gets pulled. Telomere = caps and keeps apart.

stem: All of the following statements about DNA replication are true except:
options: Replication requires a template strand to copy from
Replication requires a primer
Replication is generally unidirectional from the origin
Replication is semi-conservative
DNA chains are always synthesised in the 5' → 3' direction
rationale:
Replication is bidirectional: two replication forks leave the origin in opposite directions, forming a replication bubble that grows at both ends. Her keyed question 14.

The other four are the load-bearing facts of the whole lecture — template, primer, semi-conservative, 5'→3' — and are worth being able to recite as a set.

The trap: in an EXCEPT question, four true statements make the reading feel like agreement all the way down, and it is easy to select the last thing that sounded slightly odd. Decide explicitly, per option, true or false, before choosing.

stem: Why is one new strand made continuously and the other in Okazaki fragments?
options: Because the two parental strands have different base compositions
Because polymerase can only extend a free 3'-OH, so on the strand whose template runs the wrong way relative to fork movement, synthesis must restart repeatedly
Because primase can only prime one strand
Because the lagging strand is copied only after the leading strand has finished the whole molecule
Because helicase unwinds only one strand at a time
rationale:
This is a derivation, not a fact to memorise. Two constraints: the strands are antiparallel, and polymerase adds only to a free 3'-OH, i.e. it always moves 5'→3'. One template is therefore oriented so synthesis runs toward the advancing fork — continuous, the leading strand. The other is oriented so synthesis runs away from the fork, so every time the fork opens more template, polymerase must go back and start again — discontinuous Okazaki fragments on the lagging strand.

Both are still made 5'→3'. Nothing is ever built backwards.

The trap: “the lagging strand is copied after the leading strand has finished” sounds like what lagging means. Both strands are copied at the same time at the same fork; the name refers to the restarting, not to a delay.

stem: In her diagram of a replication bubble, two Okazaki fragments on the same lagging strand are labelled A (nearer the origin) and B (further away). Which was synthesised first, and why?
options: B, because the lagging strand is built from the outside in
A, because template nearer the origin is exposed first and each new fragment uses template that has just become available
They are made simultaneously by two polymerases
B, because polymerase moves in the same direction as the fork and therefore lays down the outermost fragment first of all
It cannot be determined without knowing which strand is leading
rationale:
A. The fork opens outward from the origin, so template is exposed origin-first. Each new Okazaki fragment is laid on the stretch that has just become single-stranded, so the fragment closest to the origin was made first. Her keyed question 20.

Hold both facts at once and it is consistent: each individual fragment is synthesised 5'→3', i.e. back toward the origin, while the series of fragments marches outward with the fork. That double motion is the part that trips people.

The trap: “polymerase moves in the same direction as the fork” is true of the leading strand and false here — importing the leading-strand picture is the standard error.

stem: A bacterial culture is grown so that both DNA strands are heavy-labelled, then shifted to light medium for exactly one round of replication. What do the daughter molecules look like, and what does that demonstrate?
options: One fully heavy molecule and one fully light molecule — conservative replication
Two molecules each with one heavy parental strand and one light new strand — semi-conservative replication
Two molecules each with heavy and light patches scattered along both of their strands — dispersive replication
Two fully light molecules — the parental strands are degraded
One hybrid molecule and one heavy molecule — asymmetric replication
rationale:
Semi-conservative: the parental duplex separates and each strand serves as a template, so every daughter molecule is half old, half new. After one round, all molecules are hybrids.

Worth carrying the next round too, because that is where the alternatives finally separate: after a second round you get two hybrids plus two fully light molecules. Conservative replication would have given one all-heavy and one all-light from the very first round; dispersive would never give a clean hybrid band.

The trap: the dispersive option describes patchwork strands, which superficially also sounds like “half old, half new”. The distinction is where the old material sits — an intact strand, not scattered stretches.

stem: Ciprofloxacin kills bacteria by inhibiting DNA gyrase. Which activity is lost, and what happens at the fork?
options: Strand separation is lost, so the helix never opens
The relief of overwinding ahead of the fork is lost, so torsional strain builds and the fork stalls
RNA priming is lost, so polymerase has no free 3'-OH anywhere on either strand to extend from at the fork
Re-annealing of separated strands is no longer prevented
Okazaki fragments can no longer be joined
rationale:
Gyrase is a topoisomerase that works ahead of the fork, introducing negative supercoils to relieve the overwinding that helicase unwinding necessarily creates downstream. Block it and the DNA cannot keep unwinding — the fork stalls. Bacterial gyrase differs enough from the human enzyme to be a genuine drug target, which is exactly why she flags it.

The trap: each wrong option is a real job done by a real protein at the same fork — helicase separates strands, primase lays the RNA primer, SSB prevents re-annealing, ligase seals nicks. When four options are all true statements about something, the question is testing which protein, so read the enzyme name in the stem first and answer from it.

stem: Match the fork protein to its job. Which line is entirely correct?
options: Helicase separates the parental strands; SSB coats the single strands to prevent re-annealing and protect them from nucleases
SSB separates the parental strands; helicase then coats the single strands to prevent them from re-annealing behind it at the fork
Primase separates the strands; gyrase lays down the RNA primer
Ligase separates the strands; topoisomerase seals the nicks
DnaA unwinds the whole chromosome; SSB proofreads the new strand
rationale:
Helicase binds ssDNA near the fork and moves into neighbouring double-stranded regions, unwinding. SSB (single-stranded DNA-binding protein) then does three things her handout lists explicitly: binds ssDNA, prevents re-annealing, and protects it from nucleases.

Upstream of both, DnaA binds the DnaA boxes in oriC and melts the AT-rich DNA unwinding element — it opens the origin, it does not unwind the chromosome.

The trap: the first two options use the same two proteins with the jobs swapped. Whenever a matching question reuses one option's nouns in a different order, check the pairing rather than recognising the words.

stem: In E. coli, which activity of DNA polymerase I removes the RNA primers, and how does it differ from the proofreading activity?
options: The 3' → 5' exonuclease removes primers, chewing forward like a snowplough
The 5' → 3' exonuclease removes primers, chewing forward like a snowplough; the 3' → 5' exonuclease proofreads by backing up over a just-added wrong base
An endonuclease removes primers; there is no proofreading activity
DNA polymerase III removes the primers; polymerase I proofreads
RNase H removes the primers in E. coli, as it does in eukaryotes
rationale:
Polymerase I is three enzymes in one protein: 5'→3' polymerase, 3'→5' exonuclease (proofreading), and 5'→3' exonuclease (primer removal, her “snowplough”).

The directions are not arbitrary. Proofreading must act on the 3'-OH end you just extended, so it runs backwards, 3'→5'. Primer removal must chew forward from the primer's 5'-phosphate end while the polymerase fills in behind it — so 5'→3'. Get the direction from the end each job has to reach and you never need to memorise the pair.

The trap: the option swapping the two exonucleases is the whole question, and the option naming RNase H is right for eukaryotes — where RNase H and FEN1 remove primers, not the polymerase. Correct fact, wrong organism.

stem: Which statement about E. coli DNA replication is false?
options: Replication begins with proteins binding the origin and helicase unwinding the DNA
Primase makes an RNA primer
DNA polymerase III synthesises the new leading strand 5' → 3'
The new lagging strand is synthesised as one continuous strand
DNA ligase closes the phosphate backbone between fragments
rationale:
The lagging strand is by definition discontinuous — separate Okazaki fragments, later joined by ligase. Her keyed question 13.

Everything else is the correct sequence: pre-priming at oriC, priming by primase, elongation by pol III (5'→3' synthesis plus 3'→5' proofreading), and sealing by ligase.

The trap: the ligase option is the subtle one. If the lagging strand really were continuous there would be nothing for ligase to seal — so the option you are asked to reject and the option that disproves it are both on the page. Two options that cannot both be true is a fast way to find the false one.

stem: A eukaryotic cell line carries a mutation that abolishes the 3' → 5' exonuclease activity of DNA polymerase ε and δ, leaving synthesis intact. What is the predicted consequence?
options: Replication stops entirely, since the polymerases cannot elongate
The mutation rate rises sharply
RNA primers are never removed, so the strands stay nicked
Only the lagging strand is affected, since ε works on the leading strand
Telomeres shorten faster with each division
rationale:
The 3'→5' exonuclease is the proofreading function: it removes a nucleotide that was just misincorporated at the free 3'-OH of the newly synthesised strand. Take it away and synthesis proceeds normally but fidelity collapses — a hypermutator phenotype. Real medicine: POLE and POLD1 proofreading-domain mutations cause ultramutated colorectal and endometrial cancers.

Both major replicative polymerases have it — ε on the leading strand, δ on the lagging — so both strands are affected.

The trap: “only the lagging strand is affected” rewards knowing that ε and δ split the strands and then punishes not noticing the stem knocked out both. Also note polymerase α has no proofreading, which is why it only lays a short stretch before handing off.

stem: Which sequence correctly describes the eukaryotic polymerase hand-off at a replication fork?
options: Polymerase α primes and lays a short DNA stretch, then ε takes the leading strand and δ elongates the Okazaki fragments
Polymerase δ primes, then α and ε elongate both strands
Polymerase ε primes and elongates both strands alone
Polymerase α elongates both strands throughout the fork, with δ and ε acting only as proofreading subunits behind it at all times
Polymerase III primes and polymerase I elongates, as in bacteria
rationale:
α is the initiator: it carries primase activity (laying the RNA primer on the leading strand and on every Okazaki fragment) plus a short burst of DNA synthesis. It hands off quickly because it has no proofreading — you do not let a low-fidelity enzyme copy a chromosome.

Then the two highly processive replicative enzymes take over: ε on the leading strand, δ elongating the lagging-strand fragments, both with 3'→5' proofreading.

The trap: the option keeping α on both strands throughout is what you would predict if you only remembered that α starts things. The reason it cannot is the fidelity argument, which is also why the hand-off exists at all.

stem: Which statement best describes telomerase?
options: It is a DNA-dependent RNA polymerase
It carries its own RNA template with it
It prevents the ends of eukaryotic chromosomes from growing too long
Its inactivation contributes to the extended lifespan of cancer cells
It repairs double-strand breaks at chromosome ends
rationale:
Telomerase carries a portable RNA template (Terc) plus a protein (Tert) with reverse transcriptase activity. Her keyed question 15. RNA template → DNA synthesis, which is the second time this lecture contradicts the plain central dogma.

Each wrong option is inverted rather than merely wrong: telomerase is an RNA-dependent DNA polymerase, not the reverse; it makes ends longer, not shorter; and cancer cells reactivate telomerase to become immortal — inactivation is what limits normal somatic lifespan.

The trap: “DNA-dependent RNA polymerase” contains all the right words in the wrong order, and that is enough to look right at speed. Read enzyme names as template-dependent, product-producing: telomerase reads RNA and writes DNA.

stem: Why does the very end of a linear chromosome's lagging strand fail to be replicated, and what exactly does telomerase do about it?
options: Polymerase simply falls off at the end of the template and cannot rebind
The final primer's position leaves no upstream 3'-OH to fill the gap after it is removed; telomerase extends the 3' end of the PARENT strand so a primer can be placed further out
The ends are heterochromatic and inaccessible; telomerase decondenses them
Ligase cannot seal the terminal nick; telomerase seals it instead
Helicase cannot unwind the last turn; telomerase unwinds it
rationale:
Her wording: “the last bit of DNA at the 3' end of the template cannot be primed because there is no free 3'-OH.” Remove that terminal RNA primer and there is nothing upstream for a polymerase to extend from, so a gap is left and the chromosome shortens each division.

The fix is indirect and that is the examinable part: telomerase extends the 3' end of the parent strand, adding TTAGGG repeats so that a primer can be laid further out and the gap now falls in expendable repeat sequence. Note her caveat — the very ends still are not replicated, but it no longer matters, because what is lost is repeat, not gene.

The trap: “extends the daughter strand” is the intuitive answer and the wrong one. Telomerase acts on the parent template.

stem: Cytarabine (araC), didanosine (ddI) and zidovudine (AZT) are all nucleoside analogs. What structural feature makes them work, and why must they be given as nucleosides?
options: They are modified on the base so that they mispair with the template strand
They are modified on the sugar so that chain elongation cannot continue; they are given as nucleosides because cellular kinases must phosphorylate them to the active nucleotide
They inhibit helicase directly; the nucleoside form crosses membranes better but is otherwise identical
They intercalate between base pairs; phosphorylation would prevent intercalation
They block primase; the nucleoside form is the active drug
rationale:
All three are modified on the sugar. ddI and AZT lack or replace the 3'-OH, so once incorporated there is no hydroxyl for the next nucleotide — chain termination. araC swaps deoxyribose for arabinose, which likewise blocks continued replication.

They are supplied as nucleosides because they must be phosphorylated by cellular kinases to the triphosphate before a polymerase will accept them. That activation requirement is also a selectivity mechanism — and the therapeutic logic is the same in both settings: hit whatever is replicating fastest, a tumour or a virus.

The trap: “modified on the base, so they mispair” describes a different drug class entirely. The stem gives you three drugs whose shared feature is a sugar modification.

stem: A child has severe pre- and postnatal growth deficiency with normal body proportions, a narrow face, a sun-sensitive facial rash, normal intellect, low immunoglobulins with recurrent otitis and sinusitis, and cytogenetics showing a ten-fold increase in sister-chromatid exchanges. What is the diagnosis and the defective protein class?
options: Xeroderma pigmentosum — a nucleotide excision repair endonuclease
Bloom syndrome — a RecQ DNA helicase encoded by BLM
Ataxia telangiectasia — a DNA damage checkpoint kinase
Fanconi anaemia — an interstrand crosslink repair protein
Cockayne syndrome — a transcription-coupled repair factor
rationale:
Bloom syndrome, autosomal recessive, BLM at 15q26.1, encoding a RecQ DNA helicase that works in replication and repair. Lose it and parental strand separation is deregulated, replication errors accumulate, and you get chromosomal rearrangements and breakage.

The single decisive clue is the ten-fold increase in sister-chromatid exchanges — her handout calls this diagnostic. Growth deficiency with normal proportions and normal intellect, photosensitivity, mild immunodeficiency and early cancer risk complete the picture.

The trap: every option is a genuine chromosome-instability syndrome, and photosensitivity alone points just as well at xeroderma pigmentosum. Anchor on the lab finding, not the rash — the SCE number is the one feature that belongs to only one of these.

stem: Bloom syndrome and the nucleoside analogs both illustrate a single principle about replication. Which is it?
options: Replication errors are always silent because proofreading corrects everything
Anything that disrupts replication hits the fastest-dividing cells hardest
Replication defects cause disease only in gametes
Only enzymes that synthesise DNA matter clinically; accessory proteins do not
Chromosome instability is unrelated to cancer risk
rationale:
Two ends of one idea. In Bloom syndrome a defective helicase makes replication error-prone in every dividing cell, so the price is genomic instability and high, early cancer risk. With nucleoside analogs the same vulnerability is exploited on purpose — you poison replication and the cells that suffer are the ones replicating most, which is what makes them anticancer and antiviral drugs, and equally what produces marrow suppression and mucositis as side effects.

The trap: “only enzymes that synthesise DNA matter clinically” is refuted by Bloom syndrome itself — BLM is a helicase, it never adds a nucleotide, and losing it still causes cancer predisposition. Accessory proteins at the fork are drug targets and disease genes in their own right; gyrase and ciprofloxacin are the other example in this same lecture.

stem: A cytogeneticist photographs a patient's metaphase chromosomes, arranges the homologous pairs by size, centromere position and banding, and then writes 47,XY,+21. Which term applies to which product?
options: The arranged picture is the karyotype; the written description is the karyogram; the idealised reference drawing is the idiogram
The arranged picture is the karyogram; the written description is the karyotype; the idealised reference drawing is the idiogram
The arranged picture is the idiogram; the written description is the karyogram; the reference drawing is the karyotype
All three terms describe the written description at different resolutions
The karyogram and idiogram are the same thing; the karyotype is the stain used
rationale:
Karyogram = the picture (a systematic visual display of the actual chromosomes, arranged by size, centromere location and banding pattern). Karyotype = the written description in standard ISCN notation. Idiogram = the stylised ideal drawing — a chromosome map you compare against, not a patient's chromosomes at all.

A memory hook that holds: -gram is the thing you look at, -type is the thing you type.

The trap: karyogram and karyotype are used loosely and interchangeably in ordinary speech, which is exactly why she made it Learning Objective 1 and why the swapped option is the popular wrong answer.

stem: On a G-banded chromosome, what do the dark (G+) and light (G−) bands correspond to, and why does that matter?
options: Dark bands are euchromatin with actively transcribed genes
Dark bands are heterochromatin and mostly not transcribed; light bands are euchromatin and gene-rich
Dark bands are regions of DNA damage; light bands are intact DNA
Dark bands mark centromeres only; light bands mark telomeres only
The colours are arbitrary and carry no information about chromatin
rationale:
Giemsa banding reflects a real difference in chromatin. G+ dark = heterochromatin, mostly not transcribed. G− light = euchromatin, mostly transcribed genes.

Tie it back to the previous lecture and it stops being a stain fact: euchromatin was defined there as loosely packed and gene-rich, heterochromatin as tightly packed and gene-poor. The stain is simply making that visible.

The trap: “dark = dense = more stuff = more genes” is an intuitive chain and it is backwards. Dense packing is what silences a region.

stem: Standard cytogenetic analysis uses metaphase cells and detects rearrangements larger than about 5 Mb. High-resolution banding detects down to about 2–3 Mb. What is done differently to achieve that?
options: The microscope magnification is increased beyond 1000×
Compounds are used that interfere with chromosome condensation, so prophase cells give longer chromosomes and more bands
More cells are counted — 40 instead of 20
A fluorescent probe is hybridised to the region of interest
The chromosomes are digested with a restriction enzyme before staining
rationale:
Resolution here is a function of chromosome length, not optics. Metaphase chromosomes are maximally condensed, so bands merge. Treat cells with agents that interfere with condensation and catch them in prophase, and the chromosomes are longer, the bands separate, and smaller rearrangements become visible.

Her numbers are worth carrying: standard analysis counts 20 cells, analyses 10, karyotypes 2, at 1000× light microscopy.

The trap: the fluorescent-probe option describes FISH — a genuinely higher-resolution technique, and the right answer to a different question. The stem says high-resolution banding, which is still karyotyping.

stem: Decode the address 9q21.3 completely.
options: Chromosome 9, short arm, region 2, band 1, sub-band 3
Chromosome 9, long arm, region 2, band 1, sub-band 3
Chromosome 9, long arm, region 21, band 3
Chromosome 21, long arm of chromosome 9, band 3
Chromosome 9, long arm, region 1, band 2, sub-band 3
rationale:
Read it strictly left to right: 9 = chromosome · q = long arm · 2 = region · 1 = band · .3 = sub-band. Her own worked example.

Two conventions make this readable every time: regions are numbered outward from the centromere (region 1 is closest), and the decimal point introduces sub-bands. Also worth having: cen is band p10/q10, pter and qter are the arm telomeres, st stalk, sa satellite.

The trap: reading “21” as a two-digit region is the standard error — and it is the one that also makes people misread q10 in a Robertsonian karyotype. Every digit before the decimal is a separate level.

stem: A miscarriage specimen is triploid, 69,XXY. Which term set describes it, and what does the placenta look like if the extra set is paternal?
options: Aneuploid; the placenta is small and underdeveloped
Euploid and polyploid; the placenta is large with hydatidiform change
Euploid and polyploid; the placenta is small, underdeveloped and fibrotic
Aneuploid and monosomic; the placenta is normal
Diploid with a structural rearrangement; the placenta is large
rationale:
Sort the vocabulary first. Euploid = an exact multiple of the haploid number — 69 is 3 × 23, so triploidy is euploid, and polyploid because it is more than two sets. Aneuploid means not a multiple of 23, which is why a trisomy (47) is aneuploid and a triploidy (69) is not.

Her empirical rule, and it is a classic exam discriminator: extra PATERNAL set → large placenta with hydatidiform change (disorganised, proliferating, pre-malignant); extra MATERNAL set → small placenta. Commonest cause overall is dispermy.

The trap: most people file “abnormal chromosome number” under aneuploidy reflexively. 69 is abnormal and euploid at the same time.

stem: A gamete is formed containing both homologs of chromosome 21 — one of maternal-grandmother origin and one of maternal-grandfather origin. Where did non-disjunction occur, and is this the more or less common event?
options: Meiosis II, and it is the more common site
Meiosis I, and it is the more common site
Meiosis II, and it is the less common site
Mitosis, which is the only way this can happen
Meiosis I, and it is the less common site
rationale:
The two grandparental origins are the giveaway. Meiosis I separates homologs, so a failure there delivers both homologs — genetically distinguishable chromosomes — into one gamete. Meiosis II separates sister chromatids, so a failure there delivers two copies of the same homolog.

And her frequency point: non-disjunction is more common in meiosis I, more common in oocytes, and rises with maternal age — most plausibly because primary oocytes sit arrested in prophase I for decades. Note that the arrest is in meiosis I, which is consistent with meiosis I being the vulnerable division.

The trap: meiosis I and meiosis II are one word apart and the whole answer turns on homologs vs sister chromatids. Read what the gamete contains, then name the division.

stem: Which set gives the only three autosomal trisomies compatible with postnatal survival, and what general principle explains why others are not?
options: Trisomy 13, 18 and 21 — surviving trisomies involve small, gene-poor chromosomes, whereas trisomy of a large chromosome adds too much material
Trisomy 1, 2 and 3 — surviving trisomies involve the largest chromosomes
Trisomy 13, 18 and 21 — surviving trisomies always involve the largest metacentric chromosomes, which happen to carry the fewest genes of any in the karyotype
Trisomy 16, 21 and X — these are the only chromosomes that can be trisomic at all
Trisomy 8, 9 and 21 — survival depends on the parental origin of the extra chromosome
rationale:
47,+21 · 47,+18 · 47,+13 are the three she names. All three are small chromosomes, and 13 · 21 (with 14, 15, 22) are the acrocentrics, whose short arms carry redundant rRNA genes.

Her dosage principle covers both directions: trisomies of large metacentric chromosomes do not survive because the extra dose is too large, and on the loss side, missing more than about 2% of the genome is lethal — which is why losing part of chromosome 2 is worse than losing part of 22. She also states the asymmetry directly: too little is worse than too much, which is why monosomies are rarer than trisomies among liveborns.

The trap: one option gives the right three chromosomes with a reason that contradicts itself — 13, 18 and 21 are not large metacentrics. A right answer attached to wrong reasoning is still wrong, and this lecture is full of that build.

stem: A phenotypically normal woman has karyotype 46,XX,t(5;13)(q11;q12). Her first child by a chromosomally normal man had multiple malformations and died at 13 days, with karyotype 46,XY,del(5)(q11;qter),dup(13)(q12;qter). What happened?
options: The mother's translocation became unbalanced by a new mutation in the child
The mother is a balanced carrier; at meiosis the quadrivalent segregated so the child inherited a derivative chromosome without its counterpart, producing a deletion plus a duplication
The child's abnormality is unrelated to the mother's translocation
The father must also carry a cryptic translocation
The mother's karyotype was misread, because a phenotypically normal balanced carrier cannot have a chromosomally abnormal child, and the finding here must therefore be a laboratory error
rationale:
This is her Big Ticket Item. The mother has the normal amount of chromosome material, merely rearranged — hence balanced, hence normal phenotype. At meiosis the translocated and normal chromosomes attempt to pair, forming a quadrivalent, and the segregation modes that follow are not all balanced. Inherit one derivative without its partner and you get too much of one segment and too little of another — the child's del + dup.

Her two practical corollaries are the examinable payoff: couples with recurrent unexplained miscarriage should have both partners karyotyped, and a child with a duplication or deletion should prompt karyotyping of the parents.

The trap: the option asserting a balanced carrier cannot have an affected child inverts the entire lesson — being balanced protects the carrier, not the offspring.

stem: In the Philadelphia chromosome the breakpoint on chromosome 9 is at q34.1 and on chromosome 22 at q11.2, in a male. Write the karyotype.
rationale:
46,XY,t(9;22)(q34.1;q11.2). Three conventions do all the work: the total chromosome count comes first and a reciprocal translocation does not change it (still 46 centromeres); the lower-numbered chromosome is listed first, with sex chromosomes ahead of autosomes; and the breakpoints are listed in the same order as the chromosomes.

Biology worth keeping: the ABL tyrosine kinase from 9 is moved next to BCR on 22 and switched on constitutively, causing chronic myelogenous leukemia. So a balanced translocation with no net gain or loss can still cause disease, by altering gene expression at the breakpoint.

The trap: the option listing 22 before 9 keeps every breakpoint correctly paired and still fails the ordering convention. And the count options test whether you know a reciprocal exchange leaves the number at 46.

stem: What is a derivative chromosome, and how is it named?
options: Any chromosome carrying a de novo mutation that was not present in either parent
A structurally rearranged chromosome produced by a change between two or more chromosomes; named for the chromosome that retains an intact centromere
A chromosome with two centromeres; named for whichever centromere is active
A chromosome lacking a centromere; named for the arm that survives
A chromosome derived from the father; named for its parental origin
rationale:
Named by its centromere. A derivative chromosome is the rearranged product of a structural change involving two or more chromosomes, and it takes the identity of the chromosome whose centromere is intact.

The rule is not arbitrary — the centromere is what lets a chromosome be segregated at all, so it is the functional identity of the piece. This is also why the alternatives she describes matter: an acentric fragment has no centromere and is lost, and a dicentric chromosome has two and gets pulled apart. Both end in miscarriage, which is exactly the paracentric-inversion outcome later in the lecture.

The trap: the acentric and dicentric options are real structures from this same lecture, placed here to be confused with der.

stem: Which statement about a Robertsonian translocation is correct?
options: It is a fusion of any two chromosomes at their telomeres, and the chromosome count stays at 46 because nothing at all is lost during the fusion event
It is a fusion of two acrocentric chromosomes at the centromere; the count falls to 45, and the carrier is usually normal because the lost short-arm material is redundant rRNA genes
It is a fusion of two metacentric chromosomes, and the carrier is always abnormal
It involves chromosomes 13, 14, 15, 21 and 22 but does not change the chromosome count
It is always balanced in the strict sense, since nothing at all is lost
rationale:
A Robertsonian translocation fuses two acrocentric chromosomes — 13, 14, 15, 21, 22 — at the centromere. Two centromeres become one, so the count drops by one to 45: e.g. 45,XX,rob(13;14)(q10;q10). (Note q10 = the q side of the centromere, region 1, band 0.)

Her careful phrasing is the examinable nuance: material is lost from the short arms, so strictly speaking it is unbalanced — practically speaking it behaves as balanced, because the lost material is redundant rRNA gene clusters also present on the other acrocentrics. Hence a normal carrier.

The trap: the option asserting nothing at all is lost is the tempting simplification, and it is the half of her sentence she deliberately spends a line on.

stem: A woman with 45,XX,rob(21;21)(q10;q10) has a child by a 46,XY man. The child's karyotype is 46,XY,+21,rob(21;21)(q10;q10)mat. Mother and child both “have a Robertsonian 21” — so why is only the child affected?
options: The child inherited the translocation from the mother
Counting copies of chromosome 21 material shows the mother has two and the child has three
The child's translocation arose de novo and is therefore more severe
The mother is mosaic and the child is not
The chromosome counts differ, 45 versus 46, and the count alone determines the phenotype
rationale:
Her explicit warning, and the reason she built the example: analyse each individual by COUNTING — chromosomes, and copies of the relevant segment — rather than word-associating from “Robertsonian translocation.”

The mother has 45 chromosomes but two copies of 21 material, both fused into one structure — normal dose, normal phenotype. The child has 46 chromosomes and three copies of 21 material: one normal 21 from the father, plus the mother's fused pair. That is trisomy 21, which is why the +21 appears in the karyotype.

The trap: the option keying on 45 vs 46 gets the right pair of numbers and the wrong reasoning — the count is a symptom here, the dose of chromosome 21 is the cause. A 45,XX,rob(13;14) carrier is also 45 and entirely normal.

stem: Compare 46,XX,del(4)(p16.3) with 46,XY,del(7)(q11.23;q21.2). What structural difference does the notation reveal?
options: The first is interstitial with two breakpoints, losing the segment between them; the second is terminal with one breakpoint
The first is terminal — one breakpoint, with everything distal to it lost; the second is interstitial — two breakpoints, with the segment between them lost
Both are terminal; the second simply lists the band more precisely
The first is a duplication and the second a deletion
The first involves the long arm and the second the short arm
rationale:
Count the breakpoints. One breakpoint means everything from there to the telomere is gone — a terminal deletion (Wolf-Hirschhorn, 4p16.3). Two breakpoints mean the piece between them is excised and the ends rejoin — an interstitial deletion (Williams syndrome, del 7q11).

They also differ in detectability, which is the clinically useful half: Wolf-Hirschhorn deletions are typically large enough for routine karyotyping (a macrodeletion), while Williams is a microdeletion — too small to see on a routine karyogram and found by FISH or microarray.

The trap: the swapped option is the obvious one; the “more precise band” option is subtler and is worth rejecting explicitly. A semicolon between two bands is a second breakpoint, not extra precision.

stem: A duplication is described as producing partial trisomy for a region. How does it typically arise, and how does its severity compare with a deletion of the same region?
options: From unequal crossing over during meiosis; generally less severe than losing the same material
From unequal crossing over during meiosis; generally more severe than losing the same material
From non-disjunction in meiosis II; severity is identical to a deletion
From a Robertsonian fusion; always lethal
From telomere fusion; severity depends only on the parental origin
rationale:
A duplication commonly arises by unequal crossing over — during recombination a segment moves onto its homolog's place while the homolog keeps its own, so one product gains and the other loses. Three copies of that region is a partial trisomy.

Her dosage rule, stated in this lecture and again in the aneuploidy section: missing material is worse than extra material. Consequences still depend on the size and location of the segment, but for the same region a duplication is generally the milder lesion.

The trap: “more severe” feels right if you reason that extra gene product is actively harmful. Her framing is the reverse and it is consistent across the whole lecture — including why monosomies are rarer among liveborns than trisomies.

stem: The karyotype 46,XX,ins(20;4)(q13.1;q12q27) is reported. Which reading is correct?
options: A segment of chromosome 20 was inserted into chromosome 4
A segment of chromosome 4 was inserted into chromosome 20 — the recipient is listed first — and it is not a reciprocal exchange, so reproductive risk is high
Chromosomes 20 and 4 exchanged material reciprocally, so the carrier's offspring are at no increased risk
Chromosome 20 was deleted and chromosome 4 duplicated
Two segments of chromosome 4 were inserted into each other
rationale:
Convention: for ins, the recipient chromosome is listed first. So a piece of 4 (spanning q12→q27) has landed in 20 at q13.1.

Two consequences she flags. It is not reciprocal — nothing came back from 20 — so it is a one-way move. And the reproductive risk is high, for a mechanical reason worth understanding rather than memorising: at meiosis chromosome 4 still wants to pair with its homolog, but part of it is now sitting on 20 and pulling the pairing there, so segregation frequently produces unbalanced gametes.

The trap: reading an insertion as a reciprocal exchange makes it look like a balanced translocation and therefore low-risk. The ordering convention is the only thing in the notation that tells you which direction the material moved.

stem: Sort these four by whether a routine karyogram (~550 bands) can see them: Wolf-Hirschhorn (4p−) · Cri-du-chat (5p−) · Williams (del 7q11) · Shprintzen (del 22q11).
options: All four are visible on routine karyotyping
Wolf-Hirschhorn and Cri-du-chat are macrodeletions visible on routine karyotyping; Williams and Shprintzen are microdeletions needing FISH or microarray
Williams and Shprintzen are macrodeletions visible on routine karyotyping; Wolf-Hirschhorn and Cri-du-chat are microdeletions requiring FISH or a microarray to detect
None are visible on routine karyotyping; all four require FISH
Only the deletions on the short arm can be seen, regardless of size
rationale:
Her two worked pairs. Macrodeletions — Wolf-Hirschhorn (4p−) and Cri-du-chat (5p−) — are large enough to see on a routine karyogram. Microdeletions — Williams (del 7q11) and Shprintzen/22q11 — are not, and need FISH or chromosome microarray.

The unifying term is copy number variation (CNV): a quantitative difference in the amount of DNA from a deletion or duplication. Critically, a CNV may be pathogenic or entirely benign depending on its size and location — finding one is not the same as finding a diagnosis.

The trap: the option keying on short arm offers a rule that is true of three of the four examples and has nothing to do with the actual variable, which is size. A pattern that fits most of the data is the most dangerous kind of wrong rule.
