stem: Two carriers are compared: one with 46,XX,inv(9)(p12;q13) and one with 46,XY,inv(10)(q11.23;q26.3). Classify each and give the reproductive consequence.
options: Both are pericentric, with breakpoints straddling the centromere, so both can produce offspring carrying a deletion plus a duplication

The inv(9) is pericentric — the breakpoints straddle the centromere — so offspring may have a deletion plus duplication; the inv(10) is paracentric, both breaks on the long arm, so abnormal conceptions are acentric or dicentric and miscarry
The inv(9) is paracentric and the inv(10) pericentric, with the risks reversed
Both paracentric; neither carries any reproductive risk
Classification depends on the sex of the carrier, not the breakpoints
rationale:
Read the arms in the breakpoint list. inv(9)(p12;q13) has one break on p and one on q, so the inverted segment contains the centromere — pericentric. inv(10)(q11.23;q26.3) has both breaks on q, so the centromere is outside — paracentric.

The outcomes differ because of what recombination inside the loop produces. Pericentric → recombinant chromosomes that each keep a centromere but carry a deletion plus a duplication — viable, abnormal offspring, the same Big Ticket Item as the balanced translocation. Paracentric → acentric fragments and dicentric chromosomes, which do not survive, so the outcome is miscarriage rather than an affected liveborn.

The trap: both inversions are balanced and both carriers are phenotypically normal, so the two look interchangeable until you check which arms the breakpoints sit on. Peri- = around the centromere; para- = alongside it.

stem: A cytogeneticist reports that one X chromosome has two long arms and no short arm. What is this called, how did it form, and is it balanced?
options: A ring chromosome, formed by fusion of the two arm tips after terminal deletions at both ends; balanced
An isochromosome, i(Xq), formed by a horizontal split of the centromere instead of a vertical one — one arm duplicated and the other deleted, so it is unbalanced
A pericentric inversion of the X; balanced
A Robertsonian translocation of X with itself; practically balanced
A derivative X from a reciprocal translocation; balanced
rationale:
Isochromosome, written i(Xq) — a mirror-image chromosome carrying two copies of one arm. It arises when the centromere divides in the wrong plane: a “horizontal” split of the two sister chromatids rather than the normal vertical one.

It is unbalanced by construction — one arm duplicated, the other deleted. That is also why she notes it is not viable for most autosomes but can be tolerated on a sex chromosome, X-inactivation and the small gene content of Yp giving some latitude. i(Xq) is a recognised Turner syndrome karyotype.

The trap: every wrong option here is balanced. The phrase “two long arms and no short arm” is itself the statement that material has been lost — if you can name the missing arm, it cannot be balanced.

stem: Which set of statements about ring chromosomes is correct?
options: Formed by terminal deletions at both ends followed by fusion; unbalanced; unstable in division, so often lost and producing mosaics; 99% sporadic
Formed by fusion of two acrocentric chromosomes at the centromere; balanced; stable through division; usually inherited from a carrier parent rather than arising de novo
Formed by a single interstitial deletion; balanced; stable; always inherited from the mother
Formed by inversion of a whole arm; unbalanced; stable; visible only on FISH
Formed by centromere duplication; balanced; unstable; never detectable on karyotype
rationale:
A ring forms when both ends of a chromosome are lost to small terminal deletions and the raw ends fuse to each other. Since material was deleted from both arms, it is unbalanced, and most cause an abnormal phenotype.

The distinctive behaviour is the instability: a ring segregates badly and is often lost in mitosis, so ring carriers are frequently mosaic. She adds that 99% are sporadic, and that a ring is visible on a karyogram — so unlike a microdeletion, this is one you can see.

The trap: “the ends joined up, so nothing is missing” is the intuition to kill. The fusion is only possible because the tips were deleted first — a capped telomere does not stick to anything, which is precisely what telomeres are for.

stem: A couple has had four unexplained first-trimester miscarriages. Both partners are healthy with normal development. What is among the first tests, and what is the reasoning?
options: Karyotype both partners, because one may be a phenotypically normal carrier of a balanced rearrangement that yields unbalanced conceptions
Karyotype the woman only, since chromosome errors arise almost entirely in oocytes
Karyotype neither — a normal phenotype in both partners rules out a chromosomal cause
Test only for numeric abnormalities, since balanced structural rearrangements do not cause recurrent miscarriage in either partner of a couple
Test the products of conception only; parental karyotypes add nothing
rationale:
Her Practical Big Ticket Item, stated in exactly this scenario: when a couple has multiple miscarriages of unknown cause, chromosome analysis of both partners should be one of the first tests.

The logic runs through the whole lecture. A balanced reciprocal translocation, Robertsonian translocation or pericentric inversion leaves a carrier with a completely normal phenotype, and it is only at meiosis that the rearrangement causes trouble — producing conceptions with duplications and deletions, many of which miscarry. Context for scale: almost half of spontaneous miscarriages carry a chromosome abnormality.

The trap: “both partners are healthy, so it is not chromosomal” is the reasoning this entire lecture exists to break — and testing only the woman misses that either partner can be the balanced carrier.

stem: A pedigree shows vertical transmission, both sexes affected in roughly equal numbers, male-to-female transmission and male-to-male transmission. Which mode does this describe, and which single feature is decisive?
options: X-linked dominant; the vertical transmission is decisive
Autosomal dominant; the male-to-male transmission is decisive because it rules out X-linked and mitochondrial modes
Autosomal recessive; the equal sex ratio is decisive
Mitochondrial; the vertical transmission is decisive
X-linked recessive; the male-to-male transmission is decisive here because fathers pass an X only to daughters, never to sons
rationale:
Autosomal dominant. Vertical transmission — affected in every generation — says dominant. Equal sex ratio says autosomal. But the feature that closes the case is male-to-male transmission.

Her “rule it out” logic: a father gives his son a Y, never his X, so father→son transmission excludes any X-linked mode. And mitochondria come only from the mother, so it excludes mitochondrial inheritance too. One observation kills three of the five options at once.

The trap: vertical transmission alone is shared by AD, XLD and mitochondrial disease, so keying on it leaves you choosing between three live options. Look for the feature that eliminates, not the feature that suggests.

stem: A pedigree is vertical, affects both sexes, but shows no transmission from any affected male, while every child of an affected female is affected. Which mode is this?
options: X-linked dominant
Mitochondrial
Autosomal dominant
X-linked recessive
Autosomal recessive
rationale:
Mitochondrial (homoplasmic). Two features have to co-occur: affected men transmit to nobody, and affected women transmit to all their children, sons and daughters alike. Mitochondria are inherited from the oocyte's cytoplasm only.

The trap: X-linked dominant is the near neighbour and shares “no male-to-male transmission”. The two separate cleanly on two checks: an affected XLD father transmits to all his DAUGHTERS (a mitochondrial father transmits to no one at all), and an affected XLD mother transmits to HALF her children (a mitochondrial mother to all of them). All-or-none from the mother, nothing from the father = mitochondrial.

stem: A pedigree has only male patients, the disease skips generations, and there is no male-to-male transmission. Which mode fits best?
options: Autosomal recessive
X-linked recessive
X-linked dominant
Autosomal dominant
Mitochondrial
rationale:
X-linked recessive. Her three-feature signature: skipping generations says recessive; a bias toward affected males says X-linked (a male is hemizygous, so one mutant allele is enough); and no male-to-male transmission is consistent with, though not proof of, an X-linked mode.

The trap: autosomal recessive also skips generations, so the tempting move is to stop at “skipping = recessive”. The discriminator is the sex ratio — her rule is that a sex bias makes autosomal inheritance, particularly autosomal dominant, less likely. Note her hedge: a sex bias makes autosomal less likely but does not rule it out, which is why the question asks for the most likely mode rather than the certain one.

stem: A pedigree shows a female sex bias of about 2:1 among the affected, no male-to-male transmission, the affected male transmits to all his daughters, and affected females transmit to half their children. Which mode is this, and why is the ratio about 2:1?
options: X-linked recessive; the ratio reflects skewed X-inactivation
X-linked dominant; females have two X chromosomes and so two chances to receive the mutant allele, making affected females roughly twice as common
Autosomal dominant with sex-limited expression; the female excess is coincidental and would disappear in a larger pedigree, since autosomes are unaffected by sex
Mitochondrial; females transmit more efficiently
Autosomal recessive; carrier frequency is higher in females
rationale:
X-linked dominant. The transmission arithmetic is the fingerprint: an affected father passes his single X to every daughter and to no son, so all daughters are affected and no sons are; an affected heterozygous mother passes the mutant X to half her children regardless of sex.

The 2:1 female excess falls straight out of having two X chromosomes and therefore twice the chance of receiving an affected one.

The trap: XLD and XLR both lack male-to-male transmission and both show a sex bias — in opposite directions. Male excess → recessive. Female excess → dominant. Check which sex is over-represented before anything else.

stem: A 1-year-old girl has failure to thrive, cognitive impairment and poor motor function. Her parents and one brother and one sister are normal; a second brother died of a similar condition at 18 months. On this information alone, the most likely mode is:
options: Autosomal dominant
Autosomal recessive
X-linked recessive inheritance
X-linked dominant
Mitochondrial
rationale:
Autosomal recessive. Her reasoning, worth copying wholesale: the condition is absent in one generation and present in the next — classic recessive; it affects a girl and a boy — classic autosomal; and it is fatal in infancy, so affected individuals never reproduce and the trait can only appear from unaffected carrier parents.

She also argues explicitly against X-linked dominant: it would require the mother to be a carrier showing skewed X-inactivation or mosaic for the mutation, and it does not explain two similarly affected children of different sexes. Autosomal recessive is the simpler explanation.

The trap: a dead male infant pulls hard toward X-linked recessive. It cannot be, because an affected female is also present — that would need a carrier mother and an affected father, which the stem excludes. Note her caution: with more relatives another mode might fit better, and the question is answerable only on what is given.

stem: Two unaffected parents have a child with sickle cell anaemia (autosomal recessive) and a second child who is healthy. What is the probability that the healthy child is homozygous normal?
options: 1 in 2
1 in 3
2 in 3
3 in 4
1 in 4
rationale:
Both parents must be carriers (Aa × Aa), since they produced an aa child — they are obligate carriers. The Punnett square gives 1 AA : 2 Aa : 1 aa.

Now use the information in the stem: this child is healthy, so aa is impossible and must be removed from the denominator. Three equally likely genotypes remain, of which one is AA — so 1 in 3 homozygous normal, and correspondingly 2 in 3 a carrier.

The trap: 1 in 4 is the unconditional Punnett answer and is the single most common error on this question type — it answers “what is the chance a child is AA?” rather than “given this child is healthy, what is the chance they are AA?” Whenever a stem calls someone unaffected, delete the affected box before you count.

stem: Marsha is unaffected. Both of her parents are unaffected carriers of an autosomal recessive disease. What is the probability that Marsha is a carrier?
rationale:
2/3 — her worked answer. Marsha's parents are Aa × Aa, giving AA, Aa, aA, aa. She is unaffected, so omit the aa genotype. Of the three remaining possibilities, two carry the mutant allele.

This 2/3 rule is worth committing as a reflex, because it is the building block for every multi-generation problem: an unaffected sib of an affected child, from two carrier parents, is 2/3 likely to be a carrier. Chain it with the product rule and you can do almost any pedigree question in this lecture.

The trap: 1/2 is what you get by thinking “one allele from each parent, 50/50” and forgetting the conditioning. She flags this explicitly: when assessing an unaffected individual with two known carrier parents, you must remove the affected genotype from the equation.

stem: A man is affected with a rare autosomal recessive disease. He has two healthy daughters, each of whom has one healthy son. All spouses are homozygous normal. What is the probability that both grandsons are carriers?
rationale:
Work forward one generation at a time. The affected man is aa, so every child receives a mutant allele from him; with homozygous normal mothers, both daughters are obligate carriers (Aa) with probability 1. Each daughter then transmits the mutant allele to a given child with probability 1/2.

The two grandsons are independent, so apply the product rule: 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4.

The trap: 1/9 is the answer if you mistakenly treat each daughter as only 2/3 likely to be a carrier and then square (2/3 × 1/2)². The 2/3 rule applies to the unaffected child of two carriers — here the father is affected, not a carrier, so his daughters' carrier status is certain, not probable. Ask whether the parent is affected or a carrier before you reach for 2/3.

stem: When do you multiply probabilities and when do you add them?
options: Multiply for mutually exclusive outcomes; add for independent events that occur together in the same pregnancy or sibship
Multiply when independent events must BOTH occur; add when mutually exclusive outcomes would EITHER satisfy the question
Always multiply in autosomal problems and add in X-linked problems
Add whenever more than one child is involved; multiply for a single child
Multiply for dominant conditions and add for recessive ones
rationale:
Product rule = AND. Independent events that must all happen: both twins affected, and the child is a girl. Multiply.

Sum rule = OR. Mutually exclusive ways of satisfying the same question: an affected child could be either a boy or a girl. Add.

A worked example that uses both: the chance an autosomal dominant couple's next child is an affected female is 1/2 affected AND 1/2 female = 1/4.

The trap: the first option is the two rules with their conditions swapped, and it reads perfectly well at speed. Anchor on the English word in the question — “both” or “and” → multiply; “either” or “or” → add.

stem: A man with haemophilia B, an X-linked recessive disorder, asks his chance of having a similarly affected son. Assuming his partner is not a carrier, the best answer is:
rationale:
0%. Her reasoning is one sentence and it settles the whole family of questions: a man contributes either his X or his Y to a child. To have a son he must contribute the Y — so the mutant X cannot reach a son. He gives that X to every daughter, all of whom become obligate carriers.

The corollary is the classic exam line: X-linked recessive disease skips from an affected grandfather to a grandson through an unaffected carrier daughter, which is exactly why these pedigrees look like they skip generations.

The trap: 50% is the reflex answer, imported from the shape of every other genetics problem. Nothing here is 50/50: father→son transmission of an X-linked allele is impossible, not unlikely.

stem: A woman is a known carrier of an X-linked recessive condition and her partner is unaffected. She is carrying a male fetus. What is the probability that this fetus is affected — and how would the answer change if the sex were unknown?
options: 1/2 if male; 1/4 if the sex is unknown
1/4 if male; 1/2 if the sex is unknown
1/2 in both cases
1/4 in both cases
2/3 if male; 1/3 if the sex is unknown
rationale:
A carrier mother is XAXa and passes one X at random, so a son has a 1/2 chance of being affected — being hemizygous, one mutant X is enough.

With the sex unknown you need male AND affected, which by the product rule is 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4.

The trap: the two numbers are both correct — for different questions — and the whole item turns on whether the stem has already told you the sex. Information given in the stem is information you must condition on. This is the same discipline as deleting the aa box for an unaffected person.

stem: Two sisters are both affected with an X-linked dominant condition and both are pregnant by unaffected men. What is the chance that both sisters will have an affected child?
rationale:
Each affected sister is heterozygous XAX, so she transmits the mutant X to half her children, sons and daughters alike — 1/2 for each pregnancy. The two pregnancies are independent, so by the product rule: 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4.

Keep the XLD transmission pair straight, because they are asymmetric: affected mother → 1/2 of all children; affected father → all daughters, no sons. Which parent is affected changes the arithmetic completely.

The trap: 1/2 is the per-sister answer, and it is what you select if you read “chance a sister has an affected child” instead of “chance both sisters do”. The word both is the entire question.

stem: A woman has MELAS, a mitochondrial disorder. Which relative is not at risk of inheriting it from her?
options: Her daughter
Her son
Her daughter's son
Her daughter's daughter
Her son's daughter
rationale:
Mitochondria are inherited from the oocyte's cytoplasm only. So all of an affected woman's children are at risk — sons included — but the line stops at every son. Her son's children get their mitochondria from his partner, so her son's daughter is not at risk.

The pattern to carry: an affected woman transmits to every child; an affected man transmits to none. That is what makes a mitochondrial pedigree look matrilineal even though both sexes are affected.

The trap: “her son” is the tempting answer — sons are the dead end for transmission, so it is easy to file them as safe. A son is at risk himself; he simply cannot pass it on. Being unable to transmit and being unaffected are different things.

stem: In an autosomal recessive pedigree, who can be labelled an obligate carrier with certainty?
options: Any unaffected sibling of an affected individual
Both parents of an affected individual, since each must have contributed a mutant allele
Any unaffected individual who has an affected grandparent on either side of the pedigree
Only the mother, since she contributes the cytoplasm
Any individual who has married into the family
rationale:
An affected person is aa and received one mutant allele from each parent. If neither parent is affected, each must be Aa — that is a certainty, not a probability, which is what obligate means. In her worked case the obligate carriers are precisely the parents of the affected individuals.

The trap: an unaffected sibling is the near miss, and the distinction is the point of the term. A sibling is 2/3 likely to be a carrier — probable, not obligate. Certainty comes from being a parent of an affected child, never from being a sib of one.

stem: First cousins Frank and Jenny have a daughter affected by a rare autosomal recessive disease, and she carries two identical copies of the same mutant allele. What does this let you infer about earlier generations?
options: Nothing beyond Frank and Jenny both being carriers
Both allele copies trace to a shared ancestor, so Frank's parent and Jenny's parent are both obligate carriers, and exactly one of their own parents in generation I carries the allele
Both of Frank's grandparents must be carriers
The allele must have arisen de novo in the affected child, since neither Frank nor Jenny is affected
Frank and Jenny must each be affected themselves
rationale:
Two identical copies of a rare allele in a child of consanguineous parents means both copies descend from one common ancestor — this is identity by descent. Frank and Jenny are first cousins, so the allele must have been present in their shared grandparents' generation and travelled down through both of their parents. Therefore Frank's parent and Jenny's parent are both obligate carriers.

Her final refinement, which rests on rare diseases being rare: in generation I, one of the two grandparents is a carrier and the other is homozygous normal — you cannot tell which without testing, but you can be confident it is not both. She adds that even without knowing the two alleles are identical, consanguinity alone would make you assume the common ancestors are carriers unless told otherwise.

The trap: “both grandparents must be carriers” over-reads the evidence — only one allele needs to be in circulation, and a rare disease makes two independent carriers in one couple very unlikely.

stem: A couple, both unaffected, are expecting a child. Their first child has an autosomal recessive condition. What is the chance the new baby is an affected girl, and which rules did you use?
options: 1/4 — the product rule alone
1/8 — the product rule, applied to affected (1/4) and female (1/2)
1/2 — the sum rule
1/16 — the product rule applied three times over, once for each event
1/6 — the sum rule then the product rule
rationale:
Two independent conditions must both hold, so this is the product rule. The parents are obligate carriers, so P(affected) = 1/4; P(female) = 1/2; together 1/4 × 1/2 = 1/8.

Note what is not conditioned here. The stem does not tell you the baby is unaffected, so the aa box stays in and the answer is the plain 1/4 — unlike the 2/3 questions, where being told someone is healthy removes a box.

The trap: 1/4 is the answer to “affected” with the word girl ignored, and it is the most-chosen wrong option on this pattern. Also note the past child changes nothing — each conception is independent; having one affected child does not use up the risk.

stem: Why can you overdose on vitamin A but rarely on vitamin C, and what does that imply about which kind of vitamin needs constant resupply?
options: Vitamin A is water soluble and therefore accumulates in the tissues; vitamin C is fat soluble and is stored in fat, so vitamin C is the one that causes toxicity at high intakes taken over a long time
Vitamin A is fat soluble, hydrophobic and stored in tissues rather than excreted, so toxicity is possible; vitamin C is water soluble and readily cleared, so deficiency is the practical risk
Both are fat soluble; the difference is the dose used
Vitamin A has no upper limit; vitamin C is toxic above the RDA
Neither can cause toxicity; only minerals can
rationale:
Her framing is a single trade-off. Fat-soluble (A, D, E, K) are hydrophobic, not readily excreted, and stored in tissue — so the failure mode is overdose. Water-soluble (the eight Bs and C) are easily cleared, so the failure mode is deficiency, and they need continual resupply.

Also worth carrying: deficiency bites hardest in rapidly growing or metabolising tissue — skin, mucosa, red cells, neural tissue, and in developing embryos. That single sentence predicts why almost every deficiency syndrome in this lecture is dermatitis, anaemia, a neurological picture, or a birth defect.

The trap: the first option is the correct physiology with the two vitamins swapped, which is the fastest way to lose a mark you actually knew.

stem: The RDA is defined as the amount of a nutrient needed to meet the requirements of:
options: The average healthy adult, i.e. 50% of the population
Nearly all of the healthy population, 97–98%, with values specific for age and sex including pregnancy and lactation
Every person without exception, including those with malabsorption or unusually increased metabolic requirements of any sort
Hospitalised patients under metabolic stress
The minimum needed to prevent the classic deficiency syndrome
rationale:
97–98% of the healthy population — a generous figure by design, not an average. It is set for age and sex separately, with distinct values for pregnant and lactating women (folate, for example, goes from 400 µg to 600 µg).

The naming is worth knowing because labels use all three: RDA, RDI (Reference Daily Intake — currently on nutrition labels), and DRI (Dietary Reference Intake — the most current, likely to replace the others). All are set by the Food and Nutrition Board and updated as evidence changes.

The trap: “the minimum to prevent the deficiency syndrome” is how people intuitively read an RDA, and it is much lower than the actual definition. She also states you will not be tested on the individual DRI values — know the definition, not the numbers.

stem: Match the fat-soluble vitamin to its function and deficiency. Which line is correct?
options: Vitamin A — bone metabolism; deficiency causes rickets in children
Vitamin K — blood clotting; deficiency causes hypoprothrombinaemia and haemorrhagic disease
Vitamin E — visual cascade as part of rhodopsin
Vitamin D — antioxidant; deficiency causes hyporeflexia and ataxia
Vitamin K — antioxidant; deficiency causes night blindness
rationale:
Her four, each with one function and one deficiency:
A (retinol) — visual cascade, part of rhodopsin → night blindness.
D (cholecalciferol) — bone metabolism → rickets in children.
E (α-tocopherol) — antioxidant → hyporeflexia and ataxia.
K (phylloquinone) — clotting cascade → hypoprothrombinaemia and haemorrhagic disease.

Note that vitamin K is the one whose deficiency is routinely anticipated rather than discovered — newborns get an injection at birth.

The trap: every wrong option is built by rotating correct facts onto the wrong letter. Learning them as four pairs rather than four lists is what makes rotation obvious.

stem: Her classification sorts the water-soluble vitamins by what their coenzymes carry. Which grouping is correct?
options: Hydrogen/hydride: riboflavin, niacin, ascorbate · Carbon chains: thiamine, pantothenate · One-carbon: biotin, folate, cobalamin · Nitrogen: pyridoxal
Hydrogen/hydride: thiamine, pantothenate · Carbon chains: riboflavin, niacin · One-carbon: pyridoxal · Nitrogen: biotin, folate, cobalamin
Hydrogen/hydride: biotin, folate · Carbon chains: ascorbate, niacin · One-carbon: thiamine · Nitrogen: riboflavin
All nine carry one-carbon groups, and they differ only in the oxidation state of the carbon they carry, not in the identity of the group itself at all
Hydrogen/hydride: niacin only · Carbon chains: all the rest
rationale:
Her four groups, and the organising idea of the whole lecture:
Hydrogen or hydride carriers — riboflavin (FAD/FMN), niacin (NAD⁺), ascorbate.
Carbon-chain carriers — thiamine (TPP), pantothenate (CoA).
One-carbon carriers — biotin (CO₂), folate (THF), cobalamin (methyl).
Nitrogen carrier — pyridoxal (PLP).

Her own problem set asks exactly this: which coenzymes carry hydrogen? Answer — NAD⁺, FMN and ascorbate. With her emphatic note that they carry hydrogen atoms, not protons — the electrons go too, and that is why they have reducing power.

The trap: nine vitamins invite rote listing, and a rote list has no error-check. Carrying the four groups means a misplaced vitamin looks wrong immediately.

stem: A dehydrogenase oxidises an alkane to an alkene. Which coenzyme is used, which vitamin does it come from, and name two enzymes that do this.
options: NAD⁺ from niacin; glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate dehydrogenase and lactate dehydrogenase in glycolysis and fermentation
FAD from riboflavin; succinate dehydrogenase in the TCA cycle and acyl-CoA dehydrogenase in fatty acid oxidation
TPP from thiamine; pyruvate dehydrogenase and α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase
CoA from pantothenate; acetyl-CoA carboxylase and pyruvate carboxylase
PLP from pyridoxal; ALT and AST
rationale:
Her rule, and it is worth holding as a rule rather than as examples: a dehydrogenase that oxidises an alkane to an alkene always reduces FAD to FADH₂. The named cases are succinate dehydrogenase (TCA) and acyl-CoA dehydrogenase (β-oxidation) — and both are the first oxidation of a C–C single bond in their pathways.

The companion rule from the oxidation-states lecture: FAD for C=C, NAD⁺ for C=O. Two of the electrons' worth of chemistry, one letter apart.

Also flagged: FADH₂ is a substrate of the electron transport chain, and cytochrome P450s use both FAD and FMN — heme monooxygenases named for their 450 nm absorbance, important in detoxifying xenobiotics such as in acetaminophen overdose.

The trap: NAD⁺ is the reflex answer for any enzyme called a dehydrogenase. The substrate's bond decides the cofactor, not the enzyme's name.

stem: NAD⁺/NADH sits at roughly 1000/1 while NADP⁺/NADPH sits at roughly 1/10 to 1/100. What does each ratio commit its coenzyme to?
options: NAD⁺ favours reduction and biosynthesis, so NADPH is the one that feeds the electron transport chain; NADPH favours oxidation and ATP production instead, which is why the two ratios are set in opposite directions by the cell

The high NAD⁺/NADH ratio favours oxidising metabolites to make ATP, so NADH feeds the electron transport chain; the low NADP⁺/NADPH ratio favours reducing metabolites, so NADPH is the reducing power for biosynthesis
The two ratios are equivalent and the coenzymes are freely interchangeable
Both ratios favour oxidation; they differ only in which tissues use them
NADPH is the main substrate of the electron transport chain
rationale:
This is a mass-action argument, not a memorised fact. Keep the oxidised form 1000-fold in excess and the cell is poised to oxidise — so NAD⁺ runs catabolism (GAPDH in glycolysis is her example) and the NADH produced is a substrate of the ETC. Keep the reduced form 10–100-fold in excess and the cell is poised to reduce — so NADPH is the reducing power for reductive biosynthesis, e.g. the reductases of fatty acid synthesis.

Her explicit warning: NAD⁺/NADH and NADP⁺/NADPH are NOT metabolically interchangeable, even though they differ by a single phosphate.

The trap: her problem set asks which reducing equivalents the ETC uses; the answer is FADH₂ and NADH only. NADPH is reducing power but the ETC does not use it — that is the most-missed distinction in the set.

context: A 64-year-old woman with a long history of alcohol use has recently had a strangulated hernia repaired with bowel resection. She becomes weak, with diarrhoea and marked weight loss. She has a rash over her face, neck and the dorsum of both hands. She is irritable with altered mental status. Since the resection her diet has been predominantly corn-based.
stem: What is the diagnosis, and what single dietary supplement would you recommend?
options: Beriberi; oral thiamine
Pellagra; oral nicotinamide
Scurvy; high-dose vitamin C
Multiple carboxylase deficiency; oral biotin
Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome; parenteral thiamine
rationale:
Pellagra — niacin deficiency — treated with oral nicotinamide. Her keyed case. The four Ds are Dermatitis, Diarrhoea, Dementia and Death; this patient has three of them, and the rash in a sun-exposed distribution (face, neck, dorsum of hands) is the classic pattern.

Two risk factors point the same way and both are hers. A corn-based staple diet causes pellagra because the nicotinate in corn is bound and must be released by alkali extraction before the gut can absorb it — which is exactly what traditional nixtamalisation does and what a modern corn diet omits. And chronic alcohol use causes deficiency through absorption problems.

The trap: alcohol use plus altered mental status pulls hard toward thiamine and Wernicke-Korsakoff — and both options are on the page. The discriminators are the rash and the diarrhoea, which belong to pellagra, against the ocular signs and ataxia of Wernicke, which are absent here.

stem: A previously well 14-year-old presents with vomiting, abdominal pain, palpitations, hepatotoxicity, metabolic acidosis and hypoglycaemia progressing to hyperglycaemia. He had taken eleven 500-mg timed-release niacin tablets over 36 hours, hoping to defeat a urine drug screen. Which of her teaching points does this case illustrate?
options: Water-soluble vitamins are cleared so readily by the kidney that megadoses of any of them are harmless at any intake, which is why no upper limit is ever set for them
Vitamins present new clinical problems driven by behaviour and by advances in medicine, so a toxic dose of a water-soluble vitamin is possible and must be asked about
Niacin toxicity is identical in presentation to pellagra
The symptoms are due to marijuana, not niacin
Timed-release preparations cannot be absorbed in toxic amounts
rationale:
Her Measurable Outcome E — using niacin and thiamine as examples, explain how vitamins represent new challenges to physicians. The behaviour here (megadose niacin to beat a drug screen) is not something a textbook deficiency list would prepare you for, and 5.5 g over 36 hours produced real hepatotoxicity, acidosis and glucose derangement.

The thiamine half of the same outcome is her other example: bariatric surgery creates thiamine deficiency in patients who would never otherwise have been at risk — a deficiency generated by an advance in medicine.

The trap: “water-soluble means you cannot overdose” is the rule from the first page of the lecture and it is a generalisation, not a guarantee. The general rule and its clinical exception are both examinable, and this case exists to make sure you hold them together.

stem: Vitamin C is unique among the nine water-soluble vitamins in one structural respect. What is it, and what is its main enzymatic role?
options: It is the only one with no coenzyme derivative — the ingested form is the active form — and it acts as a reducing agent for prolyl and lysyl hydroxylases acting on collagen
It is the only one that is a nucleotide, and it works in the electron transport chain as a carrier of hydride
It is the only one covalently attached to its enzyme, and it works in carboxylation
It is the only one containing a metal ion, and it works in methyl transfer
It is the only one that carries nitrogen, and it works in transamination
rationale:
Every other water-soluble vitamin is converted into a coenzyme derivative — riboflavin into FAD/FMN, niacin into NAD⁺, thiamine into TPP, and so on. Ascorbate is the exception: the dietary form is the active form. Her table records the coenzyme derivative for vitamin C as a dash.

Functionally it is an antioxidant / reducing agent, and its named enzymes are prolyl and lysyl hydroxylases, which hydroxylate proline and lysine residues in collagen.

The trap: “contains a metal ion” is true of cobalamin (cobalt) and “covalently attached to its enzyme” is true of biotin — each option is another vitamin's unique feature. When a stem says unique, the distractors will be the other vitamins' unique features.

stem: A patient with a long-standing poor diet has bleeding gums with gum regression, easy bruising and joint pain. Explain the mechanism linking the vitamin to all three findings.
options: Impaired haem synthesis, so all three findings are anaemic in origin and would resolve with iron, and the gum changes reflect mucosal pallor rather than any defect in connective tissue
Without ascorbate, prolyl and lysyl hydroxylases cannot hydroxylate collagen, so collagen-containing tissues — blood vessels, connective tissue and bone — are structurally weak
Impaired clotting factor synthesis, identical to vitamin K deficiency
Impaired platelet production from marrow failure
Impaired calcium absorption, weakening bone and vessel walls
rationale:
Scurvy. One mechanism explains the whole presentation: vitamin C is required for the hydroxylation of proline and lysine in collagen, and hydroxylated residues are what let collagen cross-link into a strong triple helix. Without them the collagen is defective and every collagen-containing tissue fails — blood vessels (bruising, gum bleeding), connective tissue (gum regression), bone (joint pain).

Her fun fact is a good retrieval hook: most mammals synthesise ascorbate from glucose; humans, other primates, guinea pigs and bats lost the terminal enzymes — the gene is still there, mutated to silence roughly a million years ago.

The trap: bleeding in a malnourished patient reads as a clotting problem, and vitamin K is sitting right there in the same lecture. Scurvy bleeds because the vessel wall is weak, not because the clotting cascade has failed.

stem: Which set of enzymes requires the coenzyme form of thiamine?
options: Pyruvate carboxylase and acetyl-CoA carboxylase
Pyruvate dehydrogenase complex, α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase complex, and transketolase
Prolyl and lysyl hydroxylases
Succinate dehydrogenase, acyl-CoA dehydrogenase
All aminotransferases
rationale:
Thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP) serves the PDH complex, the α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase complex, and transketolase of the pentose phosphate pathway. Her keyed question 7.

There is a pattern rather than a list here: the first two are oxidative decarboxylations of an α-keto acid, and transketolase moves a two-carbon unit. All three are carbon-chain transfers, which is precisely the group she filed thiamine under.

The trap: every distractor is a genuine and correctly-grouped enzyme set for a different vitamin — the carboxylases belong to biotin, the hydroxylases to vitamin C, the alkane-to-alkene dehydrogenases and P450s to riboflavin, and the aminotransferases to B6. Getting this question right is really a test of the whole summary table.

context: A 47-year-old man is admitted three months after gastric bypass surgery with confusion, horizontal nystagmus and a broad-based unsteady gait. Serum lactate is elevated.
stem: What is the deficiency, why is the lactate high, and what is the risk if it goes untreated?
options: Niacin; lactate rises from impaired glycolysis; untreated it causes pellagra

Thiamine; PDH cannot function, so pyruvate accumulates and is shunted to lactate; untreated, Wernicke encephalopathy progresses to Korsakoff syndrome with irreversible memory impairment and confabulation
Cobalamin; lactate rises from methylmalonic acid accumulation; untreated it causes pernicious anaemia and subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord over months to years
Biotin; lactate rises because pyruvate carboxylase fails; untreated it causes dermatitis and hair loss
Pyridoxal; lactate rises from failed transamination; untreated it causes seizures
rationale:
Thiamine deficiency — Wernicke encephalopathy, and the triad in the stem is hers: mental status change, ocular abnormality (nystagmus), gait ataxia — the “drunken sailor” walk.

The lactate follows from the biochemistry. TPP is required by the PDH complex, so without it pyruvate cannot enter the TCA cycle; pyruvate accumulates and is reduced to lactate, giving lactic acidosis. Her mechanism for the brain injury: thiamine deficiency impairs cerebral energy use, injuring the brain regions with the highest metabolic demand.

Untreated, it progresses to Korsakoff syndrome — persistent memory impairment with confabulation, false information given with no intent to deceive. Her at-risk list: malnourished patients, alcoholics, post-surgical patients and particularly gastric bypass.

The trap: the biotin option is genuinely tempting — pyruvate carboxylase does require biotin, and blocking it would also affect pyruvate. But the clinical picture here is ocular and cerebellar, not dermatitis, and the classic bariatric-surgery deficiency is thiamine.

stem: Pantothenic acid gets its name from the Greek for “from everywhere”. What does its coenzyme do, and why is that name reassuring?
options: It becomes NAD⁺ and carries hydride; the name reflects its role in every redox reaction the cell performs, from glycolysis through to the electron transport chain, and it is required in far larger amounts than any other water-soluble vitamin as a result, which is why deficiency is so rapidly apparent

It becomes coenzyme A and part of the acyl carrier protein of fatty acid synthase, carrying acyl groups as thiol esters on an –SH group; since CoA is needed to metabolise all fat, protein and carbohydrate through the TCA cycle, one is unlikely to survive a true deficiency
It becomes THF and carries one-carbon groups; the name reflects its presence in leafy greens
It becomes TPP and carries carbon chains; the name reflects its wide tissue distribution
It is covalently attached to carboxylases; the name reflects its role in all carboxylations
rationale:
Pantothenate → coenzyme A, and it also forms part of the acyl carrier protein (ACP) of the fatty acid synthase complex. The business end is a thiol (–SH) group that carries acyl groups as activated thiol esters — acetyl-CoA, succinyl-CoA, fatty acyl-CoA.

Her point about the name is a real argument: pantothenate is ubiquitous in natural foods, and that is fortunate, because CoA is required to metabolise all fat, protein and carbohydrate via the TCA cycle. No true deficiency has been characterised — the few reported cases were reversible, and opinions on its DRI vary widely.

The trap: the summary table lists pantothenate's deficiency as “None”, which reads like an unimportant vitamin. The reasoning is the opposite: it is so central that a true deficiency is not survivable, and so widely available that it does not arise.

stem: Biotin is the coenzyme for which class of enzyme, and which two reactions does she name as gateways into major pathways?
options: All dehydrogenases; glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate dehydrogenase entering glycolysis and lactate dehydrogenase entering fermentation
All carboxylases; pyruvate carboxylase entering gluconeogenesis and acetyl-CoA carboxylase entering fatty acid synthesis
All aminotransferases; ALT and AST
All hydroxylases; prolyl and lysyl hydroxylase
All kinases; hexokinase and phosphofructokinase-1
rationale:
Biotin serves all carboxylases, carrying a one-carbon group specifically as CO₂, and it is unusual in being covalently attached to its enzyme rather than floating free.

Her two gateways are worth holding as a pair because each is the committed entry to a pathway: pyruvate carboxylase (pyruvate → oxaloacetate, the first step of gluconeogenesis) and acetyl-CoA carboxylase (acetyl-CoA → malonyl-CoA, the committed step of fatty acid synthesis).

The trap: carboxylase and decarboxylase are one syllable apart and this is where thiamine and biotin get swapped. Biotin ADDS CO₂ (carboxylase); TPP is involved when CO₂ comes OFF (oxidative decarboxylation).

stem: Two patients have functional biotin deficiency. One eats large quantities of raw eggs; the other has a defect in holocarboxylase synthetase and normal biotin intake. Explain each.
options: Both have inadequate dietary biotin

Raw egg white contains avidin, which binds biotin tightly and blocks its absorption — cooking denatures avidin and releases the biotin; holocarboxylase synthetase attaches biotin to a lysine residue on carboxylases, so losing it produces an apparent deficiency even when biotin is plentiful

Raw eggs destroy biotin by oxidation, and holocarboxylase synthetase deficiency degrades the vitamin before it can be attached to its enzymes, so both patients lose biotin by the same final route, which is why both respond to the same dose of supplementary biotin given by mouth over several weeks
Both are caused by intestinal bacteria consuming the vitamin
Raw eggs induce urinary loss; holocarboxylase synthetase blocks absorption
rationale:
Two different failure points for the same end result. Avidin, a protein in raw egg white, binds biotin so tightly that it prevents absorption — the binding is strong enough to be exploited as a laboratory tool. Cooking denatures avidin and the problem disappears.

Holocarboxylase synthetase (HLCS) attaches biotin to a lysine residue on the carboxylases. Lose that enzyme and biotin is present but cannot be installed where it works — a deficiency of function, not of supply. That is why the syndrome is called multiple carboxylase deficiency: every carboxylase fails at once.

Her other at-risk group: pregnant women, with subclinical deficiency demonstrated in over half in several studies, presumably from high fetal demand. Deficiency shows as hair loss, dermatitis and neurological symptoms — hence biotin's other name, vitamin H, from the German for hair and skin.

The trap: “both have inadequate intake” misses the entire point — neither patient is short of dietary biotin.

stem: Folate's coenzyme THF can carry a one-carbon unit at several oxidation states — methyl, methylene, methenyl and formyl. Which processes depend on this, and what is the headline deficiency consequence?
options: Fatty acid oxidation and ketogenesis; deficiency causes hypoglycaemia and a metabolic acidosis with raised ketone bodies in both blood and urine on testing
Nucleotide synthesis (purines and thymidine) and amino acid synthesis such as methionine; deficiency causes neural tube defects and increases miscarriage
The electron transport chain; deficiency causes lactic acidosis
Collagen hydroxylation; deficiency causes scurvy
Transamination; deficiency causes hyperammonaemia
rationale:
THF's versatility is the point — carrying one-carbon units at several oxidation states lets one coenzyme serve chemistry that would otherwise need several. Its jobs are purine synthesis, thymidine synthesis, and one-carbon transfers in amino acid synthesis such as methionine.

Follow that to the clinic and the deficiency picture is predictable: cells that cannot make nucleotides cannot divide, so the tissues that suffer are the fastest-dividing ones. Folate is absolutely critical to neural tube development, and deficiency raises the rate of neural tube defects and spontaneous miscarriage — which is why the DRI rises from 400 µg to 600 µg in pregnancy, and why supplementation must begin before conception, since the neural tube closes in the fourth week.

The trap: the summary table lists megaloblastic anaemia under folate as well as under B12, so the two blur. Both cause it — for the same reason, failed DNA synthesis — but neural tube defects are folate's alone.

stem: Cobalamin is the only reason cobalt is required in the diet. Which two enzymes does she name as requiring it, and what is the deficiency called?
options: Pyruvate carboxylase and acetyl-CoA carboxylase, the two gateway carboxylases; deficiency presents as scurvy with bleeding gums, poor wound healing and perifollicular haemorrhage in a patient with a long-standing poor diet

Homocysteine methyltransferase, which remethylates homocysteine to methionine, and methylmalonyl-CoA mutase, in the catabolism of odd-chain fatty acids and some amino acids; deficiency causes pernicious anaemia
Transketolase and PDH; beriberi
ALT and AST; pellagra
Prolyl and lysyl hydroxylase; rickets
rationale:
Her two: homocysteine methyltransferase (homocysteine + methyl → methionine) and methylmalonyl-CoA mutase (catabolism of odd-numbered-carbon fatty acids and some amino acids). B12 carries a methyl group — its one-carbon cargo — and the cobalt in cobalamin is the only reason cobalt is a required trace mineral.

Deficiency causes pernicious anaemia, a megaloblastic anaemia: B12 is needed to make red blood cells, and the marrow is another fast-dividing tissue.

The two enzymes also explain the two lab findings that separate B12 from folate in practice: blocking the methyltransferase raises homocysteine (folate deficiency does too), while blocking the mutase raises methylmalonic acid — which only B12 deficiency does.

The trap: B12 and folate share the anaemia and share a raised homocysteine, so they are easy to merge. Methylmalonic acid is B12's alone.

stem: A patient started on isoniazid for tuberculosis develops a peripheral neuropathy. Which vitamin is depleted, what does its coenzyme carry, and which enzymes are affected?
options: Thiamine; carbon chains; PDH and transketolase
Pyridoxal (B6); nitrogen, as the amine group in transamination; all aminotransferases, including ALT and AST
Niacin; hydride; GAPDH and lactate dehydrogenase
Riboflavin; hydrogen; succinate dehydrogenase and the cytochrome P450 enzymes of the liver, plus acyl-CoA dehydrogenase
Biotin; CO₂; pyruvate carboxylase
rationale:
Pyridoxal → pyridoxal phosphate (PLP), the lecture's only nitrogen carrier. It shuttles the amine group in transamination, interconverting α-amino acids and their corresponding α-keto acids, and is required by all aminotransferases — ALT and AST being the two you will order as liver enzymes for the rest of your career.

Her deficiency note: B6 deficiency is fairly rare except when drug-induced, and isoniazid for TB is the named cause — she is explicit that the mechanism is not clear. Practically, patients on isoniazid are co-prescribed B6.

The trap: a neuropathy in a lecture full of vitamins fits several answers — thiamine, B12 and B6 all produce neurological pictures. The decisive clue is the drug, not the symptom.

stem: Which single vitamin would you most expect to be deficient in each of: a strict vegan · someone on a corn-based staple diet · someone three months after bariatric surgery?
options: Cobalamin · niacin · thiamine
Niacin · cobalamin · thiamine
Thiamine · niacin · cobalamin
Folate · thiamine · niacin
Ascorbate · cobalamin · folate
rationale:
Vegan → cobalamin (B12). Her food-source table lists B12 only in dairy, eggs, fortified cereals, meat, poultry and seafood — it is the one vitamin in the table with no unfortified plant source, which is exactly why she added the table and told you to use it when advising patients who cannot or choose not to eat certain foods.

Corn-based staple → niacin, because the nicotinate in corn needs alkali extraction before it can be absorbed → pellagra.

Bariatric surgery → thiamine, her named example of a deficiency created by an advance in medicine → Wernicke-Korsakoff.

The trap: the options are the same three vitamins in different orders, so recognition is worthless and only the pairing scores. Match each risk factor to its mechanism — no plant source · needs alkali release · surgically shortened absorption — rather than trying to recall the list.

stem: Which statement about the coenzyme derivatives of the water-soluble vitamins is correct?
options: All nine of the vitamins must be converted into a coenzyme derivative before they become active, and that includes vitamin C
The active coenzyme forms are derivatives of the dietary vitamin in every case except vitamin C, where the ingested form is already active
The coenzymes are synthesised de novo by the body and the dietary vitamin is optional
Only the B vitamins that carry carbon require conversion
Coenzyme derivatives are interchangeable, so one B vitamin can substitute for another
rationale:
Her exact statement: the “active” coenzyme forms of the water-soluble vitamins are derivatives of the vitamin forms obtained in the diet, except for vitamin C.

Two consequences worth carrying. First, a defect in the conversion step produces a deficiency even when intake is normal — biotin and HLCS is the worked example in this lecture. Second, vitamins are by definition not synthesised by the body for practical purposes and must come from the diet, so the conversion is downstream of an obligatory dietary supply.

The trap: “all nine” is right for eight of nine, and a rule that holds 89% of the time is the kind that survives until it is examined. Her summary table makes the exception visible in one glance: vitamin C's coenzyme column is a dash.

stem: A gene sits on chromosome 17, short arm, region 1, band 1, sub-band 2. Write its band address.
rationale:
17p11.2 — chromosome, then arm, then region, band and sub-band with the decimal point introducing the sub-band. (This is the Smith-Magenis / Charcot-Marie-Tooth region, if you want a hook for it.)

Build it in the same order every time and the notation writes itself: number → arm letter → region → band → .sub-band.

The trap: 17q11.2 differs by one letter and puts the gene on the wrong arm — arm errors are the most common and the least noticed. Check p vs q before anything else.

stem: Why does consanguinity raise the risk specifically of autosomal recessive disease and not of autosomal dominant disease?
options: Related parents generate new recessive mutations more frequently during gametogenesis
Related parents are more likely to carry the same rare allele inherited from a shared ancestor
Related parents carry more recessive alleles overall than unrelated parents
Dominant alleles become recessive when inherited from two related parents
Consanguinity selectively increases meiotic nondisjunction of autosomes
rationale:
A dominant condition needs one mutant allele, so it appears whether or not the parents are related — consanguinity adds nothing. A recessive condition needs two copies of the same allele, and for a rare allele the chance that two unrelated people both carry it is very small. Relatives share a recent common ancestor, so they are far more likely to carry the same allele identical by descent.

That is precisely the reasoning in her Frank-and-Jenny case: two identical copies in the child point back to one ancestral allele, making both cousins' parents obligate carriers.

The trap: “more mutations overall” is a real-sounding but false mechanism — consanguinity does not create mutations, it concentrates existing ones into homozygotes.

stem: A karyotype reads 46,XY,der(14)t(14;21)(q10;q10). What does the der(14) tell you?
options: Chromosome 14 was deleted
The rearranged chromosome is identified as 14 because the intact centromere it retains is chromosome 14's
There are two copies of chromosome 14
Chromosome 14 was inverted
The rearrangement was inherited from the father rather than arising de novo in the patient
rationale:
der = derivative chromosome, and the number after it names the chromosome whose centromere is intact in the rearranged product. So der(14) is a single chromosome built from 14 and 21 material, carrying chromosome 14's centromere.

The q10;q10 breakpoints tell you this is centromeric fusion of two acrocentrics — a Robertsonian translocation, which is why rob and der are used interchangeably for these.

The trap: “inherited from the father” is what pat would say, and mat marks maternal origin — a real suffix from her nomenclature table, placed here to be confused with der.

stem: A newborn has a karyotype showing trisomy 21 in some cells and a normal complement in others — a mosaic. Which error most likely produced this, and how does it differ from the usual cause of trisomy 21?
options: Meiotic non-disjunction in the oocyte, exactly the same mechanism as classic full trisomy 21
Mitotic non-disjunction after fertilisation, which produces two cell lines, whereas classic trisomy 21 arises from meiotic non-disjunction and affects every cell
A Robertsonian translocation, which always produces mosaicism
A ring chromosome 21, which is always meiotic in origin
Failure of X-inactivation in the early embryo
rationale:
An error in meiosis is present in the gamete, so the zygote and every cell descended from it carries it. Mosaicism requires an error after fertilisation — mitotic non-disjunction, failure of sister chromatids to separate in a somatic division — producing an abnormal line alongside the normal one. She notes this directly: most aneuploidy is meiotic, though some mosaic aneuploidy is due to mitotic errors.

Recall the meiotic detail for contrast: meiosis I fails to separate homologs; meiosis II (and mitosis) fails to separate sister chromatids, with meiosis I the more common site, more common in oocytes, and rising with maternal age.

The trap: the ring-chromosome option quietly reverses a real fact — rings are unstable and often lost in division, so they are a classic CAUSE of mosaicism, not something that excludes it.

stem: Two balanced inversion carriers each want to know their reproductive risk. Which produces the higher chance of a liveborn child with an abnormal phenotype, and why?
options: Paracentric, because its acentric and dicentric recombinant products are viable and can be carried to term without any early pregnancy loss occurring at all in practice
Pericentric, because its recombinant chromosomes each retain a single centromere and so can be carried to term while carrying a duplication and a deletion
They are identical in risk, since both are balanced in the parent
Paracentric, because it involves the centromere
Neither carries any reproductive risk
rationale:
Both carriers are phenotypically normal; the difference is in what recombination inside the inversion loop produces.

Pericentric — the inverted segment contains the centromere, so recombinant chromosomes each end up with one centromere. They segregate normally and are viable, but carry a duplication and a deletion — hence a liveborn child with an abnormal phenotype.

Paracentric — the centromere is outside the loop, so recombination yields an acentric fragment (no centromere, lost) and a dicentric chromosome (two centromeres, torn apart). Neither survives, so the outcome is miscarriage rather than an affected liveborn.

The trap: “paracentric involves the centromere” inverts the prefixes. Peri- = around/including; para- = beside/excluding.

stem: What is an idiogram used for, and how does it differ from what you get from a patient sample?
options: It is the patient's own chromosomes photographed and then arranged in numbered pairs, which is exactly what the laboratory reports back to the clinician
It is a stylised ideal drawing of the banding pattern of each chromosome — a reference map the patient's karyogram is compared against, band for band
It is the written ISCN description of the patient's chromosomes
It is the stain used to reveal the bands
It is a fluorescent probe map used only in FISH
rationale:
An idiogram is a reference drawing, not a patient's chromosomes at all — a stylised, idealised banding map showing the relationship between short and long arms, centromeres, stalks and satellites.

Its purpose is comparison. The cytogeneticist arranges the patient's real chromosomes into a karyogram and compares each chromosome band for band with its homolog and against the idiogram to find structural change. That comparison is what makes the karyotype — the written description — possible.

The trap: she flags the spelling herself — idiogram, not ideogram. And the option describing the patient's photographed chromosomes is the karyogram, the term it is most often confused with.

stem: An adult reports difficulty seeing at night, with normal vision in daylight. Which vitamin, and what is its molecular role?
options: Vitamin D; it regulates calcium in the retina
Vitamin A (retinol); it forms part of rhodopsin in the visual cascade
Vitamin E; it protects retinal membranes as an antioxidant
Vitamin K; it maintains retinal vessel integrity through clotting factors
Vitamin C; it maintains corneal collagen
rationale:
Vitamin A (retinol) functions in the visual cascade as part of rhodopsin, the pigment of the rod cells, and rods are what you see with in low light. Deficiency in adults therefore presents as night blindness with daylight (cone) vision preserved.

Keep the fat-soluble four as function-and-deficiency pairs: A rhodopsin → night blindness · D bone → rickets · E antioxidant → hyporeflexia and ataxia · K clotting → haemorrhagic disease.

The trap: the vitamin E option supplies a true fact — it is an antioxidant and membranes are protected — attached to the wrong syndrome. A true statement about a vitamin is not the same as the right vitamin for the symptom.

stem: The RDA for folate is 400 µg for most adults and 600 µg for pregnant and lactating women. What principle does that difference illustrate?
options: RDAs are averages, so about half of all pregnant women will need more than the 600 µg figure quoted here, and the rest will need rather less than it in practice
RDAs are set separately for age and sex, including distinct values for pregnancy and lactation, because requirements change with physiological state
The higher value is a toxic threshold, not a requirement
Pregnancy values are extrapolated from children's requirements
Only fat-soluble vitamins have pregnancy-specific values
rationale:
An RDA is not one number for humanity. It is set to cover 97–98% of the healthy population and is specific for age and sex, with separate values for pregnant and lactating women — because requirement follows physiological demand.

Folate is the clearest case: demand rises with fetal tissue growth, and the consequence of falling short is neural tube defects, so the target moves up rather than the population being expected to average out.

The trap: “RDAs are averages” is the intuitive reading and it is wrong in a way that matters — an average would leave half the population short. The definition is deliberately set near the top of the requirement distribution.

stem: A patient has scaly dermatitis, a smooth purplish tongue, and cracking at the corners of the mouth. Which deficiency, and what is notable about it?
options: Niacin; it is the classic four-D syndrome of dermatitis, diarrhoea
Riboflavin; it is not associated with any major human disease, showing instead as this mucocutaneous triad
Ascorbate; it reflects failed collagen hydroxylation
Biotin; it reflects avidin binding
Cobalamin; it reflects megaloblastic change in mucosa
rationale:
Riboflavin (B2) deficiency: scaly dermatitis, glossitis (the tongue appearing smooth and purplish), and cheilosis (breaking and chapping of the skin around the mouth).

What she flags is the absence of a named syndrome — riboflavin deficiency is not associated with any major human disease, unlike niacin (pellagra), thiamine (Wernicke-Korsakoff) or vitamin C (scurvy). It presents as a mucocutaneous picture and stops there. That is a fair exam target precisely because there is no disease name to recall.

The trap: pellagra also causes dermatitis, so the two overlap on the skin. The discriminator is what else is present: pellagra brings diarrhoea and dementia; riboflavin deficiency stays confined to skin and mucosa.

stem: Coenzyme A carries acyl groups as activated thiol esters on its –SH group. Which set are all examples of that cargo?
options: NADH, FADH₂ and NADPH
Acetyl-CoA, succinyl-CoA and fatty acyl-CoA
TPP, PLP and THF
Glucose 6-phosphate, fructose 6-phosphate and G3P
Pyruvate, lactate and oxaloacetate
rationale:
Acetyl-CoA, succinyl-CoA and fatty acyl-CoA — her three examples. Each is an acyl group held on CoA's thiol (–SH) as a thiol ester, and a thiol ester is a high-energy, activated linkage, which is what makes the acyl group transferable.

That is the same principle as UDP-glucose in carbohydrate metabolism: biosynthesis never uses the plain building block, it uses a carrier-attached, energy-charged version. CoA is the carrier for acyl groups.

The trap: the reducing-equivalent option is the pull, because CoA and NAD share “coenzyme” and both are central to metabolism. CoA carries carbon chains; NAD and FAD carry hydrogen. Different groups in her classification.

stem: Which type of reaction interconverts α-amino acids and their corresponding α-keto acids, and which coenzyme is required?
options: Oxidation-reduction; NAD⁺
Aminotransferase (transamination) reaction; pyridoxal phosphate
Hydration-dehydration; no coenzyme
Isomerase reaction; thiamine pyrophosphate acting as the coenzyme
Acid-base reaction; biotin
rationale:
A transamination, catalysed by an aminotransferase and requiring pyridoxal phosphate (PLP). Her keyed problem-set answer. The amine group is lifted off the amino acid onto PLP (making PMP) and handed to a keto acid — PLP is the nitrogen carrier, the only one in her classification.

Worth noticing what does not happen: the carbon skeleton is unchanged and no net oxidation or reduction occurs. The amino acid becomes a keto acid purely by swapping –NH₂ for =O.

The trap: converting an amine to a ketone looks like an oxidation, which makes the redox option genuinely tempting. It is a group transfer, and that is why it needs a carrier rather than NAD⁺.

stem: A patient with chronic alcohol use gives detailed, confident but demonstrably false accounts of recent events, with no apparent intent to deceive, and cannot form new memories. Ocular signs and ataxia have resolved. Which stage is this, and what does it imply?
options: Wernicke encephalopathy, which is fully reversible with thiamine
Korsakoff syndrome
Pellagra dementia, which is reversible with nicotinamide
Hepatic encephalopathy from cirrhosis
B12 deficiency causing subacute combined degeneration
rationale:
Korsakoff syndrome — her definition: a persistent state of mental dysfunction, with memory impairment associated with confabulation, giving blatantly false information but with no real intent to deceive.

Hold the two stages apart. Wernicke encephalopathy is the acute, potentially reversible phase — mental status change, ocular abnormality such as nystagmus, and gait ataxia. Korsakoff is what remains once the acute signs settle and is largely irreversible, which is why thiamine is given urgently rather than after investigation.

The trap: the pellagra option offers dementia, one of the four Ds, in a patient with alcohol use — and chronic alcohol use genuinely causes both deficiencies. The discriminator is confabulation with preserved older memory, which is Korsakoff's signature, not a global dementia.

context: A 19-year-old eats a carbohydrate-rich meal. Pancreatic β cells release insulin, which binds receptors on skeletal muscle, activating intracellular signalling proteins and moving GLUT4 transporters to the plasma membrane so glucose enters the cell.
stem: Which event is the reception step?
options: Release of insulin from pancreatic β cells
Binding of insulin to its receptor
Activation of intracellular signalling proteins
Movement of GLUT4 to the plasma membrane
Removal of phosphate groups from signalling proteins
rationale:
Reception is the ligand binding its receptor — here insulin binding the insulin receptor. Her four steps, in order: reception → transduction → response → termination.

Map the rest of the stem onto them and the whole lecture is one worked example: insulin release supplies the signal; activation of intracellular proteins is transduction; GLUT4 moving to the membrane is the response; dephosphorylation is termination.

The trap: β-cell release feels like the beginning and therefore like reception. It is the production of the signal — reception happens in the target cell, not the sending one.

context: A 19-year-old eats a carbohydrate-rich meal. Pancreatic β cells release insulin, which binds receptors on skeletal muscle, activating intracellular signalling proteins and moving GLUT4 transporters to the plasma membrane so glucose enters the cell.
stem: Which event is the cellular response?
options: Binding of insulin to its receptor
Activation of the insulin receptor
Movement of GLUT4 transporters to the plasma membrane
Binding of intracellular signalling proteins to the activated receptor
Release of insulin from pancreatic β cells
rationale:
GLUT4 translocation is the response — the point at which the cell actually changes what it does, taking up glucose and lowering blood glucose.

Note where the boundary sits: receptor activation and the recruitment of intracellular proteins are still transduction, the passing of the message from protein to protein. The response is the behaviour change at the end of that chain, and glucose entering the cell is downstream of it.

The trap: “binding of intracellular signalling proteins to the activated receptor” happens inside the cell, so it reads as the intracellular answer. Being intracellular is not the test — changed cell behaviour is.

stem: A 22-year-old has persistent hyperglycaemia despite normal insulin production. Insulin binds its receptor normally, but activation of intracellular signalling proteins is markedly impaired. Which component is defective?
options: Ligand production
Receptor recognition
Signal transduction
Signal termination
Hormone degradation
rationale:
Signal transduction — the conversion of an extracellular signal into intracellular responses. The stem hands you the localisation: insulin is made (so not ligand production) and binds normally (so not receptor recognition), yet the downstream proteins fail. The break is between the receptor and the response.

This is the mechanism of type 2 diabetes as she frames it: normal insulin, normal binding, defective signalling → hyperglycaemia.

The trap: both termination options are the wrong direction. A failure of termination would prolong signalling and lower glucose, not raise it. When a distractor names the right pathway, check which way its failure would push the number.

stem: A signalling protein is switched on when a phosphate is added and off when it is removed. Which enzyme adds the activating modification, and what else can phosphorylation do?
options: A phosphatase; it can only activate or inhibit proteins
A kinase; phosphorylation may activate a protein, inhibit it, alter its location, or change its interactions
A G protein; phosphorylation only changes protein location
The receptor itself; phosphorylation only changes which proteins it interacts with, and nothing else about it
A second messenger; phosphorylation only inhibits proteins
rationale:
Kinases add phosphate; phosphatases remove it. Protein phosphorylation is what she calls the central theme of cell signalling, and the four possible consequences are worth holding as a set: activate · inhibit · alter location · change interactions.

That breadth is the point. Phosphorylation is not a synonym for “turn on” — the same modification switches one protein on and another off, which is why a single kinase cascade can produce a coordinated, multi-directional response.

The trap: G proteins and second messengers are genuine relay machinery she names in the same paragraph, but neither is the enzyme that performs the phosphorylation.

stem: An experimental signalling molecule readily diffuses across the plasma membrane, and within hours the expression of several genes changes. Where is its receptor?
options: The extracellular matrix
The plasma membrane exclusively
The cytoplasm or the nucleus
The Golgi lumen
The lysosomal membrane
rationale:
Her rule pairs the chemistry of the ligand with the location of the receptor. Hydrophobic signals cross the membrane and use intracellular receptors in the cytoplasm or nucleus, whose response is the direct regulation of gene transcription. Hydrophilic signals cannot cross and must use cell-surface receptors.

Two clues in the stem both point the same way: it diffuses across the membrane, and the outcome is a change in gene expression over hours rather than seconds. Steroid hormones are the archetype.

The trap: “plasma membrane exclusively” is the default assumption about receptors and is contradicted by the first six words of the stem. Read the ligand's solubility — it determines the receptor's address.

stem: Which set are all mechanisms of signal termination?
options: Neurotransmitter reuptake · receptor internalisation · dephosphorylation by protein phosphatases
Ligand binding · receptor dimerisation · kinase activation
Second messenger production · G protein activation · gene transcription initiation in the nucleus itself
Hormone secretion · receptor synthesis · protein phosphorylation
Chromatin remodelling · transcription factor binding · translation
rationale:
Her three termination mechanisms, one at each level of the pathway:
Ligand removal — hormone degradation, neurotransmitter reuptake.
Receptor inactivation — desensitisation, internalisation.
Dephosphorylation — protein phosphatases reversing the kinases.

The organising idea is that every activating step has a matching off-switch, which is why she insists signals must stop appropriately. A signal that cannot be terminated is as pathological as one that cannot start — constitutively active growth signalling is her definition of the cancer mechanism.

The trap: every other option lists real signalling events, but they are all activating. Sort each item by direction before choosing.

stem: EGFR and RAS mutations cause cancer through a shared signalling mechanism. What is it, and how does it differ from the mechanism in diabetes?
options: Both cause loss of signalling; diabetes causes excess signalling

Growth signalling becomes constitutively active — permanently on without a ligand — driving uncontrolled proliferation; diabetes is the opposite failure, defective insulin signalling causing hyperglycaemia
Both are failures of ligand production
Both are failures of receptor synthesis
Cancer is a termination defect and diabetes is a reception defect, so the two conditions are entirely unrelated to one another
rationale:
Her two disease examples are deliberately opposite failures of the same machinery. Cancer — too much signal: mutations in EGFR (the receptor) or RAS (the transducer) leave growth signalling constitutively active, firing without a ligand, so proliferation never stops. Diabetes — too little signal: insulin signalling is defective, so glucose uptake fails and blood glucose rises.

The useful generalisation is that a pathway can fail in either direction, and where in the pathway the mutation sits predicts the phenotype: a receptor stuck on and a receptor that cannot transduce are opposite diseases from adjacent proteins.

The trap: the first option gets both diseases exactly backwards, and reads perfectly well if you are pattern-matching on the words rather than the direction.

stem: Her roadmap lists four modes of receptor-effector coupling. Which pairing is correct?
options: Receptor as a transcription factor — the nicotinic acetylcholine receptor of the neuromuscular junction
Receptor that is itself an ion channel — the nicotinic cholinergic acetylcholine receptor
Receptor that is itself an enzyme — the estrogen receptor
Receptor coupled to an enzyme — the insulin receptor
Receptor as a transcription factor — the β-adrenergic receptor
rationale:
Her four modes with her own examples:
1. Receptor as a transcription factor — the estrogen receptor (covered in L011, Gene Regulation 1).
2. Receptor that IS an ion channel — the nicotinic cholinergic acetylcholine receptor (L023, Schwartz).
3. Receptor that IS an enzyme — tyrosine kinase (insulin, IGF) or guanylate cyclase (ANF, nitric oxide) (L024, He).
4. Receptor COUPLED to an enzyme — adenylate cyclase (glucagon, β-adrenergic), phospholipase C (α1-adrenergic), or kinases such as JAK on the EPO receptor and the serine/threonine kinase TGF-β receptor (L025, He).

The trap: modes 3 and 4 are one word apart. The insulin receptor IS the enzyme — its own cytoplasmic domain is the tyrosine kinase — so it belongs to mode 3, not mode 4. “Coupled to” means a separate effector enzyme.

stem: A drug activates a receptor whose own cytoplasmic domain is a guanylate cyclase. Which coupling mode is this, and which natural ligands use it?
options: Receptor coupled to adenylate cyclase; glucagon and the β-adrenergic receptor agonists
Receptor that is itself an enzyme; atrial natriuretic peptide and nitric oxide
Receptor as a transcription factor; estrogen
Receptor that is an ion channel; acetylcholine
Receptor coupled to phospholipase C; α1-adrenergic agonists
rationale:
If the catalytic domain is part of the receptor protein itself, the mode is receptor-as-enzyme. Her two examples of this class are the tyrosine kinase receptors (insulin, IGF) and the guanylate cyclase receptors for atrial natriuretic peptide (ANF) and nitric oxide.

Worth carrying forward: this is why nitrates work in angina — NO drives guanylate cyclase, cGMP rises, and vascular smooth muscle relaxes.

The trap: adenylate cyclase and guanylate cyclase differ by one syllable and sit in different modes — adenylate cyclase is a separate effector the receptor is coupled to (glucagon, β-adrenergic), while guanylate cyclase is part of the receptor. Read which enzyme, then ask whether it is inside the receptor or beside it.

stem: Why does a multicellular organism need signalling at all? Her opening example is a carbohydrate-rich meal.
options: Because each cell must independently sense blood glucose and act alone
Because liver, muscle and adipose must respond in a coordinated way to one event, and insulin signalling is what coordinates multiple tissues at once
Because cells cannot store energy without a signal
Because glucose cannot cross membranes without a hormone in any tissue
Because signalling is required only during embryonic development
rationale:
Her three opening questions all have one answer: how does the liver know to stop making glucose, how do muscle cells know to take it up, how does adipose know to store energy? Insulin signalling coordinates the response of multiple tissues to a single event.

The general statement she builds on it: to function, cells must continuously sense their environment, communicate with neighbours, and coordinate activity across tissues and organs. Without that, development, homeostasis and immune responses all fail.

The trap: the option restricting signalling to development is a real misconception worth killing — signalling is what maintains moment-to-moment homeostasis in an adult, which is exactly why its failure produces diabetes and cancer.

stem: About 98% of the human genome does not code for protein. What does she say follows from that?
options: Most of the genome is never transcribed at all and is therefore functionally inert junk DNA
Most of the genome IS transcribed into RNA, and in general the more complex the organism the greater the non-coding proportion
The non-coding portion consists entirely of introns
Only the 2% that codes for protein is transcribed
Non-coding DNA is transcribed only in disease states
rationale:
Her two claims, and the second is the surprising one: non-coding does not mean non-transcribed. Although only ~2% encodes protein, most of the genome is transcribed into RNA, and the whole set of transcripts in a cell is the transcriptome.

She also notes the trend across organisms — the more complex the organism, the greater the fraction of its genome that is non-coding, which argues that regulatory RNA is part of what complexity is made of. She adds that the coding/non-coding split is itself an oversimplification.

The trap: equating “doesn't make protein” with “junk” is the older view this lecture exists to replace — miRNA, siRNA, snRNA and rRNA are all non-coding and all essential.
