stem: Which statement about mRNA abundance and structure in a human cell is correct?
options: mRNA is ~85% of total cellular RNA and each species is highly abundant
mRNA is only 3–5% of total RNA, and since each species encodes one protein the abundance of any given mRNA is extremely low, with 10³–10⁴ different mRNAs in a cell
All human mRNAs are polycistronic, carrying several open reading frames on a single transcript as bacterial messages do, so one mRNA yields several different proteins
mRNA is heavily chemically modified, unlike DNA
All mRNAs are the same length, around 1000 nucleotides
rationale:
mRNA is only 3–5% of total RNA — the bulk is rRNA. And because each mRNA species encodes one particular protein, with 1,000 to 10,000 different mRNAs present, any single mRNA is extremely rare.

Her other features: size is highly variable (200 to ~10,000 nt, like the genes that encode them), and the base composition is A, C, G, U with very little modification — in contrast to tRNA, which is heavily modified.

The trap: polycistronic mRNA — more than one ORF on one transcript — is bacterial (and some protists). Eukaryotes use monocistronic mRNA, one ORF per transcript. Getting that backwards also breaks the logic of why eukaryotic gene regulation must be per-gene.

stem: Which feature distinguishes transcription from DNA replication?
options: Transcription proceeds 3' → 5' while replication proceeds 5' → 3', which is the only difference of substance between them, and both require a primer laid down by primase before synthesis can begin at all on either strand

Transcription needs no primer, has only limited proofreading, and copies only the part of the genome needed at that moment, while replication requires a primer, proofreads carefully, and copies the entire genome
Transcription consumes the template while replication conserves it
Transcription requires a primer and replication does not
Both processes copy the entire genome, differing only in the product
rationale:
Three real differences, each with a reason:
No primer. RNA polymerase can start from scratch — which is precisely why RNA can serve as the primer for DNA synthesis.
Limited proofreading, because the product is not passed to progeny and generally has a short half-life: it is used and destroyed.
Selective copying — only what the cell needs now, unlike replication which must copy everything.

Both are alike in synthesising 5' → 3', and in both the template is conserved, neither used up nor changed.

The trap: the option reversing the primer requirement is the single most examinable fact here, and the direction option is simply false for both.

stem: The RNA product of transcription is complementary to which DNA strand, and reads the same as which?
options: Complementary to the coding strand; reads the same as the template strand
Complementary to the template (antisense) strand; reads the same as the non-template (coding, sense) strand, with U in place of T
Complementary to both strands simultaneously
Complementary to the sense strand; reads the same as the antisense strand
Identical to the template strand
rationale:
Polymerase reads the template strand, so the RNA is complementary to the template — which is also called the antisense strand. Since the two DNA strands are complementary to each other, the RNA therefore matches the non-template strand, called the coding or sense strand, except that U replaces T.

That is why you can read a protein sequence straight off the coding strand — it already reads like the mRNA.

The trap: four names for two strands, and half of them are synonyms. Fix one pair and derive the rest: template = antisense = the one that gets read; coding = sense = the one the RNA looks like.

stem: In E. coli, what does the sigma (σ) factor add to the core RNA polymerase, and why does the cell need it?
options: Sigma supplies the catalytic activity required to polymerize RNA
Sigma recognizes promoter sequences and directs the core polymerase to transcription start sites
Sigma proofreads the RNA transcript through 3′→5′ exonuclease activity
Sigma terminates transcription by recognizing the polyadenylation signal
Sigma adds the 5′ cap before the core polymerase begins elongation
rationale:
Core polymerase is catalytically active but blind — it can make RNA and has no idea where to start. Add σ factor and you have the holoenzyme, which recognises the promoter and starts at the right place.

Her rationale for why this matters is the same asymmetry as before: replication copies everything, so a single origin suffices, but transcription must copy only the bit needed at that moment — so where and how often to start is the whole regulatory problem. Different σ factors recognising different promoters is how bacteria switch whole programmes on.

The trap: “adds catalytic activity” inverts the relationship. The core does the chemistry; σ supplies the address.

stem: What does a promoter specify, and what does variation in its sequence change?
options: It specifies which protein is made; variation changes the protein sequence
It specifies WHEN a gene is transcribed and HOW MUCH — the gene sequence says what to make — and sequence variation changes the promoter's strength
It specifies where transcription terminates; variation in it changes the length of the transcript produced, and therefore the stability of the message
It specifies the reading frame; variation causes frameshifts
It specifies the splice sites; variation causes intron retention
rationale:
Her sentence is worth memorising verbatim: the gene sequence tells the cell WHAT to make; the promoter tells the cell WHEN to make it and HOW MUCH.

A promoter is a sequence element, usually upstream of the +1 start site (drawn as a broken arrow), recognised by σ in bacteria. It tolerates variation, and that variation sets the strength of the promoter — how often polymerase initiates there.

That is why promoter mutations cause disease without touching a single codon: her TATA box mutation cutting β-globin mRNA by 80% and causing β-thalassemia changes the amount, not the sequence, of the protein.

The trap: every wrong option relocates the promoter's job to another part of the gene. Promoters control quantity and timing, never identity.

stem: A child with a Wilms' tumour is treated with actinomycin D. How does it work, and how does that differ from rifampicin?
options: Actinomycin D binds RNA polymerase and prevents mRNA extension; rifampicin blocks DNA unwinding
Actinomycin D blocks the unwinding of DNA by RNA polymerase
Both bind the 30S ribosomal subunit and block translation initiation
Actinomycin D is a folic acid analog; rifampicin is a nucleoside analog
Both act as aminoacyl-tRNA mimics causing premature chain termination
rationale:
Her two classes of RNA polymerase inhibitor, split by what they bind:
DNA-binding — actinomycin D (dactinomycin, Cosmegen) blocks the unwinding of DNA by RNA polymerase. Because it targets the DNA, it works on bacterial and eukaryotic cells alike — which is exactly why it is useful as an anti-tumour drug and why it is not a safe antibiotic.
Enzyme-binding — rifampicin binds the polymerase itself and is selective for the bacterial enzyme, hence its use in TB and leprosy.

Her third inhibitor belongs to the eukaryotic section: α-amanitin from Amanita phalloides, a potent inhibitor of RNAP-II — abdominal cramps, vomiting and diarrhoea within 12–24 hours, fatal in 20% of cases.

The trap: the ribosome and folate options describe entirely different drug classes; the first option swaps the two mechanisms you are actually being asked to distinguish.

stem: Which enzyme synthesises hnRNA in eukaryotes, and what happens if it is inhibited by α-amanitin?
options: E. coli RNA polymerase; bacterial transcription stops
RNA polymerase II; synthesis of protein-coding transcripts stops, which is why Amanita phalloides poisoning is fatal in about 20% of cases
RNA polymerase I; ribosomal RNA synthesis stops
RNA polymerase III; tRNA synthesis stops
DNA polymerase δ; replication stops
rationale:
RNA polymerase II transcribes protein-coding genes, and its immediate product is hnRNA (heteronuclear RNA), not mRNA — it becomes mRNA only after processing. RNAP-II is a 10–12 subunit complex, sharing some subunits with RNAP-I and RNAP-III.

Eukaryotes have three functionally distinct nuclear polymerases. Note her aside that mitochondrial and chloroplast polymerases more closely resemble the bacterial enzyme — consistent with their endosymbiotic origin.

The trap: the question is really testing whether you keep hnRNA and mRNA distinct. Calling RNAP-II's product “mRNA” skips the three processing events that are the bulk of this lecture.

stem: What is the function of the TATA box in a eukaryotic promoter?
options: To bind the sigma subunit of the bacterial RNA polymerase holoenzyme
To bind a basal transcription factor for RNA polymerase II
To mark an internal promoter for RNA polymerase III
To specify the position of transcriptional termination
To specify the position of cleavage and polyadenylation
rationale:
The TATA box binds TFII-D, also called TBP (TATA binding protein), which then recruits the transcription initiation complex and directs RNAP-II to the proper start site. Her keyed answer.

She notes TBP is a slight misnomer — subunits of TFII-D also bind the initiator element and the downstream promoter element. Not every core promoter has all three elements, and the initiator element alone is enough to recruit RNAP-II and start at the right site, though it makes a weak promoter by itself.

The clinical anchor: a TATA mutation cuts β-globin mRNA by 80%, causing β-thalassemia.

The trap: σ factor is the bacterial equivalent and the TATA box is explicitly analogous to the −10 and −35 boxes of bacteria — which makes σ the most attractive wrong answer on the page.

stem: How do basal and regulatory transcription factors differ?
options: Basal factors are gene-specific and differ at every promoter; regulatory factors are the same at every gene that is transcribed, which is the reverse of the arrangement found in bacteria

Basal factors (TFII-A, B, D, E, F, H) are the same at every gene to be transcribed; regulatory factors are specific to particular genes and may bind far away in sequence, positively or negatively controlling initiation
Basal factors bind DNA; regulatory factors bind only RNA
Basal factors act only in bacteria; regulatory factors only in eukaryotes
Both are identical in function, differing only in name
rationale:
Basal factors — TFII-A, B, D, E, F, H — are the same at every gene. They assemble the initiation complex and position RNAP-II. That is a general-purpose machine and it has no opinion about which gene should be on.

Regulatory factors are gene-specific, and their binding sites can be far from the start site in sequence — but, as she stresses, close in three-dimensional space once DNA loops. They positively or negatively regulate initiation, which is what makes selective transcription possible: we do not want to transcribe every gene all the time.

The trap: the swapped option. Anchor on the word basal — a base is what everything sits on, so basal factors are the universal ones.

stem: Which components carry out the post-transcriptional processing of hnRNA into mRNA?
options: RNA polymerase holoenzyme
The basal transcription factors, TFII-A through TFII-H
rRNA
snRNPs (small nuclear ribonucleoprotein particles)
The RNA-induced silencing complex (RISC)
rationale:
snRNPs — “snurps” — are the working parts of the spliceosome. Her keyed answer. There are five snRNPs, each built around a unique snRNA plus its own set of proteins, and together with several hundred other proteins they carry out the endonuclease cleavage and ligation of splicing.

She draws the analogy deliberately: the spliceosome is to splicing what the ribosome is to translation — a large RNA-protein machine.

Medical significance worth keeping: snRNPs can be antigens in autoimmune disease, notably systemic lupus erythematosus (anti-Smith antibodies).

The trap: RISC is the other RNA-protein complex in this lecture and it acts on mature mRNA in the cytoplasm to silence it, not on hnRNA in the nucleus to process it.

stem: Name the three processing events that convert hnRNA into mature mRNA, and state what the 5' cap is.
options: Capping, polyadenylation and splicing; the cap is a guanylate residue attached by an unusual 5'-to-5' linkage
Capping, methylation and reverse transcription
Splicing, editing and translation; the cap is a methylated cytosine
Polyadenylation, ubiquitination and export; the cap is a phosphate group
Capping, splicing and proofreading; the cap is a short RNA primer
rationale:
Her three events: capping of the 5' end, polyadenylation of the 3' end, and splicing.

The cap is a guanylate residue joined by a 5'-to-5' linkage — she flags this as true in her own true/false question, and the linkage is the point. Every other bond in a nucleic acid is 5'-to-3'; a 5'-to-5' cap leaves no free 5' end, which is what protects the transcript from 5' exonucleases.

The mature transcript then reads, left to right: 5' cap · 5' UTR · AUG start · ORF · stop codon · 3' UTR · poly-A tail.

The trap: “translation” and “export” are things that happen to mRNA but are not processing events — processing is what turns hnRNA into mRNA, and it all happens in the nucleus.

stem: The untranslated regions of an mRNA carry no codons. Why do they still matter, and what is her example?
options: They do not matter; they are removed before translation
They carry regulatory elements
They are the binding sites for the spliceosome
They contain the promoter
They are where the poly-A tail is translated into polylysine
rationale:
UTRs are part of the mature mRNA and are not removed — they simply are not translated. They are regulatory real estate.

Her example is iron metabolism: iron responsive elements (IREs) sit in the 3' UTR of transferrin receptor mRNA and in the 5' UTR of ferritin mRNA, so the same iron signal can push the two in opposite directions and let the cell respond to local iron.

The 3' UTR turns up again later in the lecture as where RISC usually binds its target — so the same region is used for two different regulatory systems.

The trap: confusing untranslated with removed. Introns are removed; UTRs are kept and are functional.

stem: Regions of hnRNA removed during processing are called introns. Why must their removal be so precise?
options: Because introns contain the promoter
Because an imprecise cut leaves the reading frame out of register, so every codon downstream is misread
Because introns must be preserved for export
Because introns carry the poly-A signal
Because introns contain the binding site for the ribosome on the mature message, without which translation cannot start
rationale:
Introns are intervening sequences that are removed; exons are the sequences kept and joined. Removal has to be exact to the nucleotide, because the code is read in non-overlapping triplets — lose or gain even one or two nucleotides at a junction and the reading frame shifts, and everything downstream is nonsense.

She notes the splice sites are specified by sequences in the hnRNA itself — the transcript carries its own instructions for how to be cut — and that splicing of multiple introns is normally ordered: with 3 exons and 2 introns, 1 joins to 2 and 2 to 3, without skipping.

The trap: the promoter option confuses a DNA element that is never transcribed with an RNA region that is transcribed and then cut out.

stem: A mutation changes the 5' donor sequence of an intron from GT to AT. What happens to the transcript?
options: An artificially short transcript
A normal transcript
An artificially long transcript
A deletion of base pairs
No transcript at all
rationale:
Longer. Her keyed answer, and it is worth reasoning rather than memorising: the spliceosome recognises the 5' donor and 3' acceptor sequences. Destroy the donor and the spliceosome cannot find the start of that intron, so the intron is never removed and stays in the mRNA — the transcript is longer, not shorter.

Downstream consequences follow: the retained intron usually puts the message out of frame and introduces a premature stop, so the protein is short, unstable and non-functional, and the transcript is often destroyed by nonsense-mediated decay. Her disease table shows exactly this — LGMD1B and FPLD2 are both 5' splice-site mutations causing intron retention and NMD.

The trap: “shorter” is the intuitive answer because mutation reads as loss. Here the failure is a failure to cut, so material is retained.

stem: How does alternative splicing differ from ordered splicing, and why does it matter clinically?
options: It joins exon 1 to exon 3, skipping exon 2, producing different polypeptides from one gene — often tissue-specific, and the majority of human multi-exon genes are alternatively spliced
It removes exons instead of introns, always producing a non-functional protein from every transcript, which is why it is regarded as a splicing error rather than a normal regulatory mechanism
It occurs only in bacteria
It is a rare error, affecting fewer than 1% of genes
It joins two different genes' transcripts together
rationale:
Ordered splicing joins consecutive exons. Alternative splicing skips one — joining 1 to 3 — and so produces different polypeptides from a single gene. Her scale claim matters: the majority of human multi-exon genes are alternatively spliced, so this is a normal mechanism, not an error.

Her example is tropomyosin: one product in striated muscle and another in smooth muscle, so the calcium sensitivity differs between the two tissues. That is how one gene serves two physiologies. Regulatory sites that enhance or suppress inclusion of a given exon are what choose between the versions.

The trap: filing alternative splicing under “disease mechanism”. It is a normal source of proteome diversity — although her table shows what happens when it goes wrong, e.g. Hutchinson-Gilford progeria, where an alternative 5' splice site deletes 150 nt from exon 11 and generates progerin.

stem: What is the fundamental difference between siRNA and miRNA?
options: siRNA is longer than miRNA
siRNA acts in the nucleus, miRNA in the cytoplasm
The difference is primarily the SOURCE
siRNA blocks transcription, miRNA blocks replication
siRNA is protein-coding and miRNA is not
rationale:
Her exact framing: the difference between siRNA and miRNA is based primarily on their source.

siRNA — exogenous, generated from a foreign challenge such as a DNA or RNA virus. Its keyed function in her practice set is defence against viral infection.
miRNA — endogenous, transcribed from the organism's own genome, must be self-complementary (it folds into a stem-loop), and miRNA genes are plentiful — some sit inside introns of protein-coding genes, where they are called mirtrons.

The trap: both are 18–24 nt and both work through RISC, so length and mechanism cannot separate them. Only origin does.

stem: One strand of a small RNA is loaded into RISC and guides it to a target mRNA, usually in the 3' UTR. What are the possible outcomes, and why is this called a knock-down rather than a knock-out?
options: The gene is deleted from the genome by RISC, so the term silencing is arbitrary and no transcript is ever made, which is why the effect is permanent and cannot be reversed by removing the small RNA from that cell at any later point in time

Either translational interference — ribosomes are physically blocked, sometimes reversibly — or marking the mRNA for nuclease cleavage and degradation; the gene itself is untouched, so protein level falls rather than being abolished
The mRNA is spliced differently, producing a shorter protein
Transcription of the gene is prevented in the nucleus
The protein is degraded after translation by the proteasome
rationale:
The guide strand in RISC base-pairs with its target, usually in the 3' UTR, and the outcome is one of two things: translational interference — the bound complex physically blocks ribosomes, and this can be reversible — or nuclease cleavage beginning mRNA degradation.

Either way protein expression falls but is not abolished, and the gene is never altered — hence knock-down, not knock-out. That distinction is the reason this is therapeutically attractive: it is tunable and reversible.

Scale and applications: ~1/3 of all genes are estimated to be regulated by miRNA; roles in stem cell pluripotency, cell fate, neurogenesis; and FDA-approved siRNA drugs already exist for hereditary transthyretin amyloidosis, acute hepatic porphyria, primary hyperoxaluria type 1, and for lowering LDL-C.

The trap: the option describing a genomic deletion is what a knock-out is — and that is CRISPR's territory, not RISC's.

stem: How does CRISPR-Cas9 achieve genome editing, and what is its natural function?
options: The CRISPR RNA guides Cas9 to a site marked by a PAM sequence, where Cas9 makes a double-strand break that cellular repair then modifies or fills with new sequence; naturally it is a bacterial and archaeal immune system against viruses
Cas9 binds mRNA and blocks translation, as RISC does
CRISPR RNAs are spliced into the host genome by the spliceosome
Cas9 is a reverse transcriptase that copies RNA into the genome
CRISPR works only in bacteria and cannot be used as a tool in human cells, because the Cas9 protein is degraded by mammalian proteases before it can reach the nucleus
rationale:
Clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats — naturally, small non-coding RNAs in bacteria and most archaea acting as an immune system against viruses.

As a tool, the parts divide cleanly: the CRISPR RNA is the address, guiding Cas9, an endonuclease, to a site demarcated by a conserved proto-spacer adjacent motif (PAM). Cas9 makes a double-strand break, and it is the cell's own repair machinery that then modifies the site or inserts new sequence.

The trap: conflating CRISPR with RNA silencing because both are guided by a small RNA. RISC targets mRNA and lowers protein — a reversible knock-down. Cas9 cuts DNA — a permanent, heritable knock-out or edit. Same guiding principle, entirely different level of the central dogma.

stem: An actively dividing cell suffers extensive DNA damage. What does it do to prevent mutation?
options: Leaves the cell cycle and enters G0
Pauses in G1 before committing to initiate replication
Pauses in G2 before entering mitosis
Pauses in mitosis just before chromosome segregation begins
Inhibits apoptosis until the damage is repaired
rationale:
The G1/S checkpoint assesses DNA damage before replication starts. Her keyed answer, and the logic is worth holding: replicating damaged DNA copies the damage into both daughter cells and fixes it permanently. Stopping beforehand is the only way to prevent a mutation rather than merely detect one.

There are later checkpoints — S (slows synthesis if damage appears mid-replication), G2 (is replication complete?), and metaphase (spindle assembly and chromosome segregation) — but they are damage control, not prevention.

The trap: the last option inverts the response. Apoptosis is the intended outcome when repair fails, not something to be suppressed — that suppression is what a p53 mutation achieves, and it is how tumours survive.

stem: Two drugs are compared: one inhibits DNA replication, the other is Taxol, a spindle poison binding tubulin. Which phase does each target?
options: Both target S phase
The replication inhibitor targets S; Taxol targets M
The replication inhibitor targets G1; Taxol targets G2
The replication inhibitor targets G2; Taxol targets S
Both target M phase
rationale:
DNA replication happens in S phase, so a replication inhibitor must act there — the nucleoside analogs from the replication lecture are exactly this class. Taxol disrupts the mitotic spindle, so it blocks chromosome segregation in M phase. Both are her keyed answers.

The phases in one line: G1 growth and preparation to replicate · S replication, giving two chromatids per chromosome · G2 growth, some DNA repair, chromosome condensation, accumulation of mitotic proteins · M prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase.

The trap: phase-targeting questions reward knowing what physically happens in each phase rather than the phase names. Ask what the drug interferes with, then find the phase where that event occurs.

stem: Which cells are terminally differentiated and permanently in G0, as opposed to quiescent?
options: Fibroblasts
Liver cells, the hepatocytes of the lobule
Neurons and skeletal muscle
Embryonic stem cells
Endothelial cells
rationale:
Her distinction, and it matters clinically. Quiescent cells — fibroblasts, hepatocytes, smooth muscle, endothelium — have left the cycle but CAN re-enter G1 under the right conditions. That is why the liver regenerates so well after injury or partial resection.

Terminally differentiated cells — skeletal muscle and neurons — cannot re-enter the cycle at all. That is why myocardial and neuronal loss is permanent while liver injury is often recoverable.

Her cycle-length figures make the same point: epithelial cells ~10 hours, liver cells about a year, and the huge variation is almost entirely in the length of interphase.

The trap: hepatocytes divide so rarely that they look terminally differentiated. Rarely dividing and unable to divide are different states — the whole capacity for liver regeneration depends on it.

stem: Which statement about the relationship between cyclins and CDKs is correct?
options: CDK levels fluctuate while cyclin abundance is constant; CDK synthesis controls phase transitions
Cyclin levels fluctuate while CDK abundance is relatively constant; cyclin binding controls CDK activity
Cyclins phosphorylate their partner CDKs and are therefore the catalytic subunits
Each cyclin binds only one unique CDK, and neither partner is reused in another phase
Cyclins inhibit CDKs until both proteins are degraded at the same checkpoint
rationale:
CDKs are serine/threonine kinases made constantly — their concentration does not change. Cyclins are made at the start of a phase and destroyed at its end, so their concentration rises and falls, and CDK activity therefore tracks cyclin availability. That is what makes the cycle a clock rather than a switch.

Mechanically: cyclin binds CDK → the CDK is phosphorylated and its kinase activity turns on → it phosphorylates the proteins, transcription factors and cytoskeletal subunits needed for that phase → the phase completes → the cyclin is destroyed by ubiquitin-mediated proteasome degradation and the next cyclin takes over. The four families are D, E, A and B, and note that cyclin A pairs with both CDK2 and CDK1 to regulate different portions of the cycle.

The trap: “cyclins are the kinases” — her own keyed foil explanation says it plainly: cyclins are not kinases. The name means cyclical, not catalytic.

stem: At the end of each phase, the cyclin that drove it is inactivated irreversibly. By what mechanism?
options: Multiple phosphorylations
Dephosphorylation
Binding of the CDK inhibitors of the INK4 family
Destruction by proteolysis in the proteasome
Export from the nucleus
rationale:
Ubiquitin-mediated proteasomal degradation. Her keyed answer, and the word irreversibly in the stem is the clue: phosphorylation and inhibitor binding are reversible; destroying the protein is not.

That irreversibility is the design feature. A cycle that could run backwards would let a cell re-replicate its DNA, so each transition is made one-way by throwing away the protein that permitted the previous step.

The trap: CDK inhibitors are a real and prominent mechanism in this lecture — but they modulate cyclin-CDK activity, they do not irreversibly end a phase. Read the adverb.

stem: A new oral cancer drug inhibits CDK4 and CDK6, arresting cells in G1. Which endogenous inhibitor family does it mimic, and how do the two CKI families differ?
options: The Cip/Kip family; both families are specific for cyclin D–CDK4/6
The INK4 family (p15, p16, p18, p19), which is specific for cyclin D–CDK4/6; the Cip/Kip family (p21, p27, p57) has broad specificity and inhibits multiple cyclin–CDK complexes
The INK4 family, which has broad specificity across all of the cyclin–CDK pairs in the cycle
Neither — CDK inhibitors act only on CDK1
The Cip/Kip family, which is specific for cyclin B–CDK1
rationale:
Two families, distinguished by breadth:
INK4 — p15 (CDKN2B), p16 (CDKN2A), p18, p19 — the name literally means INhibitors of CDK4, and they are specific for cyclin D–CDK4/6.
Cip/Kip — p21 (CDKN1A), p27 (CDKN1B), p57 (CDKN1C) — broad specificity, inhibiting multiple cyclin–CDK complexes.

The CDK4/6 inhibitor drugs reproduce INK4 function pharmacologically: they arrest cells in G1, leading to senescence and apoptosis.

The trap: p21 belongs to Cip/Kip and is also the effector p53 induces, so it is the most memorable CKI — which makes Cip/Kip the tempting answer for anything CKI-related. The name INK4 encodes its own answer: inhibitor of CDK4.

stem: Tumour suppressor genes are divided into gatekeepers and caretakers. Which assignment is correct?
options: Gatekeepers repair DNA damage (BRCA1, BRCA2); caretakers control cell cycle checkpoints and growth inhibition (p53, pRb), which is the assignment used throughout the lecture
Gatekeepers are directly involved in cell cycle checkpoints and growth inhibition (p53, pRb, PTEN); caretakers encode the DNA repair apparatus (BRCA1, BRCA2)
Both classes encode DNA repair proteins, differing only in tissue
Gatekeepers are oncogenes; caretakers are tumour suppressors
Gatekeepers act only in G2; caretakers only in M
rationale:
Gatekeepers sit at the checkpoints and directly inhibit growth — p53, pRb, PTEN. Caretakers maintain the genome by repairing DNA — BRCA1, BRCA2 — and her point is the indirect route to cancer: mutations in DNA repair genes lead to mutations in other genes.

The metaphor holds: a gatekeeper stops the cell going through the gate; a caretaker keeps the building from falling apart. Lose a gatekeeper and proliferation is unrestrained directly; lose a caretaker and damage accumulates until a gatekeeper is hit.

More broadly, tumour suppressor products apply brakes to proliferation and may act as transcription factors, cell cycle inhibitors, signalling molecules, cell surface receptors or regulators of the DNA damage response.

The trap: the swapped option — and the oncogene option is a category error worth naming: oncogenes are accelerators, tumour suppressors are brakes. Both classes here are brakes.

stem: How does the pRb–E2F interaction control the G1 checkpoint?
options: Hypophosphorylated pRb releases E2F, driving the cycle forward; hyperphosphorylation traps E2F and arrests the cell in G1 instead, so growth factor signalling acts by keeping pRb in its unphosphorylated state
Hypophosphorylated pRb binds E2F and blocks progression; growth factor signalling activates cyclin D–CDK4/6, which hyperphosphorylates pRb, releasing E2F to transcribe the genes needed to progress
pRb is a kinase that phosphorylates E2F directly
E2F degrades pRb via the proteasome each cycle
pRb and E2F act only at the G2/M transition
rationale:
pRb is a brake held on by its unphosphorylated state. Hypophosphorylated pRb binds E2F, keeping that transcription factor off the genes needed for cycle progression. The release pathway is her chain: growth factor stimulation → MAP/PI3 kinase signalling → activation of cyclin D–CDK4/6 → phosphorylation of pRb → hyperphosphorylated pRb lets E2F go, and E2F switches on the genes for S phase.

Notice that this is where the restriction point sits: before it, progression depends on extracellular mitogens and growth factors; after it, the cell no longer needs them.

Clinically: hereditary retinoblastoma is caused by mutant pRb that cannot stop the cycle in G1, so progression is unregulated.

The trap: the first option reverses the phosphorylation states, and it is genuinely counter-intuitive — phosphorylating the brake RELEASES it. Phosphorylation does not mean activation; here it means inactivation of pRb's inhibitory function.

stem: Which of the following is a function of p53?
options: Halting replication in cells that have suffered DNA damage
Targeting successfully repaired cells for apoptosis regardless
Stimulating cyclin production
Stimulating CDK production
Stimulating phosphorylation of pRb
rationale:
p53 is phosphorylated and activated by DNA damage. Once active it is a transcription factor that induces p21, an inhibitory protein that stops cycle progression, giving the cell time to repair. If the damage cannot be repaired, p53 triggers apoptosis. Her keyed answer.

Follow the chain and the last two distractors collapse: p53 induces p21, p21 inhibits cyclin–CDK complexes, which prevents pRb phosphorylation, so E2F stays bound and DNA replication stops. p53 therefore does the opposite of stimulating cyclins, CDKs or pRb phosphorylation.

The trap: “targeting repaired cells for apoptosis” is her own foil, and it is precisely one word wrong. Repaired cells are released; unrepaired cells are killed.

stem: More than 50% of human tumours carry a p53 mutation or deletion. Why are some of these tumours resistant to radiotherapy?
options: Mutant p53 repairs radiation damage more efficiently
Radiotherapy works partly by causing DNA damage severe enough to trigger p53-dependent apoptosis; without functional p53 that apoptosis is not triggered, so the damaged cells survive
Mutant p53 prevents radiation from reaching the DNA
p53 mutation increases the rate of cell division beyond anything radiation can affect, so the tumour simply outgrows the treatment
p53 mutations cause cells to enter G0, where radiation has no effect
rationale:
Radiotherapy kills by damaging DNA badly enough that the cell's own machinery elects to die. p53 is the protein that makes that decision, so a tumour without functional p53 sustains the same damage and simply fails to trigger apoptosis. Her explicit point.

Two related facts she gives: those who inherit only one functional copy will most likely develop tumours in early adulthood, and inherited p53 mutation causes Li-Fraumeni syndrome, characterised by multiple types of tumour.

The trap: the G0 option describes a real mechanism of radioresistance — non-dividing cells are genuinely less radiosensitive — attached to the wrong cause. p53 loss does not push cells into G0; it removes the death decision.

stem: HPV strains 16 and 18 are associated with cervical cancer. What do the viral proteins E6 and E7 do?
options: E6 binds pRb and E7 binds p53, in that order
E6 binds p53 and targets it for proteasomal degradation; E7 binds pRb and prevents it from inhibiting proliferation — so both brakes are removed
Both E6 and E7 activate cyclin D directly
E6 and E7 integrate the viral genome directly into a tumour suppressor gene, disrupting it and abolishing its function permanently in the infected cell
E6 and E7 inhibit apoptosis by blocking caspases
rationale:
E6 → p53 → degraded via the proteasome. E7 → pRb → held inactive. Both of her named gatekeepers are neutralised, so the cell has neither the G1 brake nor the damage-triggered death pathway, and the cycle runs unchecked toward malignancy.

The economy of it is worth appreciating: the virus needs the host cell to replicate its DNA, so it forces the cell into S phase — and cancer is the side effect of a viral replication strategy.

The trap: the E6/E7 assignment is exactly the kind of two-item pairing that a distractor reverses, and both orders sound equally plausible. A hook: E6 → p53 (both have a ‘6’ shape in the number line before pRb), E7 → pRb — or simply learn the pair as one unit, since they always appear together.

stem: What does the G2 checkpoint ask, and how is CDK1 controlled there?
options: Is DNA damaged? CDK1 is degraded to prevent entry into S phase

Is replication complete? CDK1 is held inactive by inhibitory tyrosine phosphorylation until cdc25C phosphatase removes it, letting CDK1 bind cyclin B and phosphorylate mitotic structures such as microtubules

Are all chromosomes attached to the spindle? CDK1 checks kinetochore tension at every attachment site, and holds the cell until every chromosome is under equal tension from both poles of the spindle apparatus
Has cytokinesis finished? CDK1 licenses the next G1
Are growth factors present? CDK1 senses mitogens
rationale:
The G2 question is “is replication complete?” — S phase must be finished and the DNA fully duplicated before mitosis, or the genome will be torn apart unevenly.

The control is a double negative, which is why it is easy to misstate: CDK1 is phosphorylated on tyrosine residues, and that phosphorylation INHIBITS it through G1, S and into G2. cdc25C phosphatase removes the inhibitory phosphates, the now-dephosphorylated CDK1 binds cyclin B, and the active complex phosphorylates the components of mitosis such as microtubules.

The trap: phosphorylation usually reads as activation, and here it is the opposite — the same inversion as pRb. Also note the spindle option describes the metaphase checkpoints: spindle-assembly (are all chromosomes attached?) and chromosome-segregation (have they separated correctly?).

stem: Put the five stages of prophase I in order and state what defines each.
options: Zygotene (condense) → leptotene (synapsis) → pachytene (crossing over) → diakinesis (chiasmata) → diplotene (separation), with the same events simply assigned to different stages, which is the order most students remember incorrectly because the names are alphabetically misleading

Leptotene (chromosomes become visible as they condense) → zygotene (homologs align, synapsis) → pachytene (tightly coiled bivalents/tetrads, crossing over) → diplotene (homologs begin to separate but stay joined at chiasmata) → diakinesis (maximal condensation for metaphase I)
Pachytene → leptotene → zygotene → diplotene → diakinesis
Leptotene → pachytene → zygotene → diakinesis → diplotene
Diplotene → diakinesis → leptotene → zygotene → pachytene
rationale:
Leptotene · Zygotene · Pachytene · Diplotene · Diakinesis.
Leptotene — chromosomes become visible as they condense.
Zygotene — homologs align opposite one another: synapsis.
Pachytene — each pair is tightly coiled; the unit of two homologs is a bivalent and of four chromatids a tetrad; crossing over happens here.
Diplotene — homologs begin to separate but stay attached at the chiasmata where crossing over occurred.
Diakinesis — maximal condensation, ready for metaphase I.

Anchor the two that carry the examinable content — pachytene = crossing over, diplotene = chiasmata — and the sequence around them follows.

The trap: options that put pachytene before zygotene are asking whether you know homologs must pair before they can exchange. Synapsis has to precede recombination.

stem: At the end of prophase I a chromosome pair that has undergone one crossover consists of what, and why does she link reduced recombination to trisomy 21?
options: Four identical chromatids; reduced recombination has no known consequence

Two parental chromatids, one of egg and one of sperm origin, plus two recombinant chromatids each carrying both egg- and sperm-derived alleles; absent or reduced recombination has been found in 45% of females who produced trisomy 21 offspring but is very rare in females with normal offspring
Two recombinant chromatids only, the parental ones being destroyed

Four recombinant chromatids; reduced recombination increases crossover frequency elsewhere in the genome to compensate, so the total number of exchanges per meiosis stays constant no matter how many crossovers occur on any one bivalent
Two chromatids in total, one from each parent
rationale:
One crossover involves two of the four chromatids, so you end with two parental chromatids (one egg-derived, one sperm-derived, unchanged) and two recombinant chromatids, each carrying a complementary mix of egg- and sperm-derived alleles. Crossing over is exchange between non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes.

Her mechanistic point is the important one: each pair of homologs needs at least one crossover in every meiosis, because the chiasma is what physically holds the homologs together until anaphase I. No chiasma, no tether, and the pair can mis-segregate. Hence achiasmate or reduced recombination in 45% of women who had a trisomy 21 child, and very rarely in those who did not.

The trap: assuming all four chromatids are recombinant. Crossing over is a pairwise exchange, which is exactly why two parental chromatids survive intact.

stem: After meiosis I, what does each resulting cell contain?
options: 46 chromosomes and 46 chromatids
23 chromosomes and 23 chromatids
23 chromosomes and 46 chromatids
46 chromosomes and 92 chromatids
23 chromosomes and 92 chromatids
rationale:
23 chromosomes and 46 chromatids. Her keyed answer. Meiosis I separates homologs, so the chromosome number halves from 46 to 23 — the parent cell is diploid and each daughter is haploid. But the sister chromatids are still attached, so each of those 23 chromosomes is still a dyad: 23 × 2 = 46 chromatids.

Meiosis II then separates the sister chromatids, leaving 23 chromosomes and 23 chromatids in each gamete. Note her related keyed point: division of the centromeres occurs in mitotic anaphase and meiotic II anaphase — not meiosis I anaphase, where centromeres stay intact.

The trap: assuming halving the chromosome number halves the DNA. It does not — chromosome number and chromatid number come apart during meiosis I, and that is the entire content of this question. Also note crossing over occurs in prophase I, never prophase II.

stem: An individual is heterozygous at a locus, and a crossover occurs involving that gene. At what stage of meiosis does segregation of those alleles become evident?
options: Prophase I of meiosis
Metaphase I
Anaphase I
Prophase II
Telophase II
rationale:
Telophase II. Her keyed answer, and the reasoning is the useful part. If a crossover has occurred at that locus, the two sister chromatids of one chromosome now carry different alleles — they are no longer identical there. Anaphase I separates homologs, so both alleles are still travelling together in the same cell. Only when meiosis II separates the sister chromatids do the two alleles finally end up in different cells.

So: not until the end of cell division in the second meiotic cycle have the two different alleles been separated.

The trap: anaphase I is the answer when there is no crossover at that locus, and it is what most people answer reflexively. The crossover in the stem is what moves the answer from meiosis I to meiosis II — read the stem for whether recombination happened at that gene.

stem: Which statement best reflects Mendel's law of segregation, and how does it differ from independent assortment?
options: The separation of one pair of homologs is independent of another pair — that is segregation
The two members of a single gene pair always separate and pass to different gametes; independent assortment is the separate claim that different gene pairs segregate independently of one another
Wild-type alleles for all genes go to one gamete and mutant alleles to the other
Alleles exchanged by recombination are not segregated into separate gametes
Each daughter cell from mitosis contains the same genome
rationale:
Segregation — Mendel's 2nd Law: the two alleles of a single gene are never found in the same gamete; they always separate. Physically this is homologs separating at anaphase I.

Independent assortment — Mendel's 3rd Law: different gene pairs assort independently — the segregation of one pair of homologs does not affect another's. Physically this is the random orientation of each bivalent at metaphase I, and the arithmetic is worth carrying: 2²³, more than 8 million combinations from 23 chromosomes, before crossing over adds any more.

The trap: the “wild-type to one gamete, mutant to the other” option is what independent assortment specifically denies — genes on different chromosomes are shuffled, not inherited as blocks. And the first option states the 3rd law while calling it the 2nd.

stem: At the completion of meiosis, a single oogonium gives rise to what — and a single secondary oocyte to what?
options: Four ova; and two ova
One ovum plus two or three polar bodies; and one ovum plus one polar body
One ovum only; and one ovum only
Two ova and two polar bodies from the oogonium; and one ovum plus one polar body
Four polar bodies; and one polar body
rationale:
Both are her keyed answers, and the difference is where in the sequence you start.

From an oogonium: it becomes a primary oocyte, which divides into a secondary oocyte plus a polar body; the secondary oocyte divides into an ovum plus another polar body; and the first polar body may itself divide in two. Total: one ovum plus two or three polar bodies.

From a secondary oocyte — meiosis I is already done — only meiosis II remains: one ovum plus one polar body.

Contrast spermatogenesis, which yields four gametes from one precursor. Oogenesis discards cytoplasm-poor polar bodies to keep all the cytoplasm in one egg.

The trap: the two versions of this question look identical and have different answers. Read whether the stem starts at the oogonium or at the secondary oocyte.

stem: Which statement describes a real difference between male and female gametogenesis?
options: Synaptonemal complexes form only in females
Mitotic division of germ-cell precursors occurs only in males
Dictyotene occurs during meiosis I in females but not in males
Meiosis in males begins in the fetus, whereas female meiosis begins at puberty
Oocytes complete meiosis before fertilisation, whereas spermatocytes complete it afterwards
rationale:
Dictyotene is a female-only stage — a special form of diplotene at which meiosis I is arrested from the 9th month of gestation until ovulation, 10 to 50 years later. Her keyed answer.

The two processes differ on almost every axis. Spermatogenesis: spermatogonia arise from primordial germ cells through ~200 mitoses, ~1,000 sperm per second, ~30 billion a year — and all that repeated replication brings an increased risk of accumulating deletions and duplications, which is why paternal age is associated with FGFR3 mutations causing achondroplasia. Oogenesis: ~30 mitoses, and women are born with all the primary oocytes they will ever have (~2 million), ~400,000 by puberty, of which only ~400 mature over a lifetime.

The trap: the timing option gets the direction exactly backwards — female meiosis begins in the fetus and stalls; male meiosis begins at puberty and runs continuously. That decades-long arrest is also the accepted explanation for the maternal age effect on non-disjunction.

stem: A cell with three pairs of chromosomes shows homologous chromosomes paired along the equatorial plate, each chromosome still consisting of two sister chromatids joined at the centromere. What stage is this?
options: Metaphase of mitosis
Metaphase I of meiosis
Metaphase II of meiosis
Anaphase of mitosis
Prophase I of meiosis
rationale:
Metaphase I of meiosis. Her keyed answer. The decisive feature is that homologs are PAIRED at the equator — lined up as bivalents, side by side.

That single observation separates all three metaphases. In mitotic metaphase, chromosomes line up individually, never paired with their homolog. In metaphase II, the cell is already haploid, so there is no homolog present to pair with. Only metaphase I has homologs side by side.

The second detail — sister chromatids still joined at the centromere — confirms that no centromere has divided yet, consistent with meiosis I.

The trap: mitotic metaphase and metaphase I look nearly identical in a diagram, and the only difference is whether the chromosomes at the plate are single files or pairs. Count the rows before naming the stage.

stem: Gene expression is regulated at three levels. Which list correctly assigns the examples?
options: Transcriptional — alternative splicing and mRNA stability; post-transcriptional — transcription initiation

Transcriptional — transcription initiation, the main site of control; post-transcriptional — RNA elongation, processing, transport, alternative splicing, stability and translational efficiency; post-translational — protein processing, transport, stability and targeting

Transcriptional — protein targeting and secretion; post-transcriptional — chromatin remodelling; post-translational — RNA processing and splice site selection, with the main site of control being the final one in every eukaryotic cell studied so far, regardless of tissue
All three levels act on the mRNA, differing only in timing
Post-translational regulation is the main site of control in eukaryotes
rationale:
Her three levels, and she names the dominant one explicitly: transcription initiation is the MAIN site of control, which is why most of the lecture is about assembling the RNA polymerase complex.

Post-transcriptional acts on the mRNA — elongation, processing, transport, alternative splicing, stability, translational efficiency. Post-translational acts on the protein — translation, processing, transport, stability, targeting.

The useful organising question is what molecule is being acted on? DNA/nascent transcript → transcriptional. Finished mRNA → post-transcriptional. Protein → post-translational.

The trap: the first option puts alternative splicing under transcriptional regulation. Splicing acts on an RNA that already exists, so it is post-transcriptional, even though it happens while transcription is still going on.

stem: Which of these signals takes its functional form in DNA rather than RNA?
options: Polyadenylation signal
Transcriptional promoter
E. coli transcriptional termination signal
Prokaryotic ribosome binding site
5' splice site consensus sequence
rationale:
The promoter — a DNA-based signal that recruits RNA polymerase to the start site. Her keyed answer, and her explanation is one line: all of the other choices function in RNA, not DNA.

Check them: the polyadenylation signal is recognised in the transcript; the E. coli termination signal works as an RNA hairpin; the ribosome binding site is read on the mRNA; the 5' splice site is recognised by the spliceosome in the hnRNA.

This distinction is worth keeping because it is why promoter mutations and splice-site mutations behave so differently — one changes how often a transcript is made, the other changes what the transcript becomes.

The trap: every one of these sequences is present in the DNA. The question asks where it is recognised and acted upon.

stem: What is the role of an enhancer, and how can it work from thousands of bases away?
options: To increase replication of a specific gene; distance is irrelevant to replication
To increase transcription of a specific gene
To increase the half-life of a specific mRNA
To increase translation of a specific mRNA
To increase the half-life of a specific polypeptide
rationale:
An enhancer is a DNA sequence that transcriptional activator proteins bind, and its role is to stimulate transcription of the nearby gene. Her keyed answer. A silencer is the mirror image — bound by repressors, decreasing transcription.

Distance is the interesting part. Her regulatory sites come in two ranges: promoter-proximal, hundreds of bases from +1, and distant regulatory sites, thousands or tens of thousands of bases away. She resolves it with the same point made in the RNA lecture — remember the 3-D structure: elements far apart in sequence may be quite close in space once the DNA loops.

The trap: three distractors move the effect onto RNA or protein stability. Enhancers act on transcription only, and by definition they act on DNA.

stem: A transcriptional regulatory protein has two distinct domains. What does each do?
options: The DNA-binding domain binds the enhancer or responsive element; the transcription regulatory domain interacts with basal transcription factors and recruits co-activators that modify chromatin
The DNA-binding domain binds the hormone; the regulatory domain binds DNA
Both domains bind DNA, at different sequences
The DNA-binding domain acetylates histones; the regulatory domain methylates DNA at CpG islands nearby, so both domains act on chromatin rather than on the transcription machinery itself at any point
The two domains are functionally identical and provide redundancy
rationale:
Two jobs, two domains: the DBD is the address — it binds the specific DNA element — and the TRD is the effect.

Her TRD does two things. It makes direct interactions with basal transcription factors, and it recruits co-activators that modify chromatin — either ATP-dependent remodelling enzymes that slide nucleosomes along the DNA to widen the gaps so RNAP-II and TFII-D can reach the DNA, or enzymes that covalently modify histones (acetylation, methylation, phosphorylation).

Her figure question tests exactly this: the domain touching the enhancer in the DNA is the DBD; the one touching the basal transcription factors is the TRD.

The trap: a steroid receptor has three domains — ligand-binding, DBD and TRD — so the option swapping hormone-binding onto the DBD is built from real anatomy in the wrong order.

stem: Eukaryotic transcriptional activator proteins stimulate gene expression mainly by:
options: Binding the TATA box in place of the basal transcription machinery
Directly unwinding the entire gene so RNA polymerase II no longer needs a promoter
Adding the 5′ cap and poly-A tail before transcription begins
Recruiting co-activators and general transcription factors that make the promoter accessible to RNA polymerase II
Covalently modifying the DNA sequence to create a new promoter
rationale:
Her keyed answer: activators recruit co-activator proteins that “loosen” the chromatin structure to allow RNA polymerase II to access the promoter DNA, and recruit general transcription factors to that promoter.

The key idea is indirection. An activator does not do the chemistry itself and does not transcribe anything — it binds a specific site and brings in the machinery. That is why one activator can control genes it has no enzymatic relationship with.

The trap: “binding to the TATA box” is what a basal factor does — TFII-D/TBP — not a gene-specific activator, which binds enhancers and responsive elements. And “recruiting histones to form nucleosomes” would compact chromatin and repress transcription: right vocabulary, wrong direction.

stem: Trace cortisol from outside the cell to a change in gene expression. Which sequence is correct?
options: Cortisol binds a cell-surface receptor → a second messenger is generated → a kinase cascade follows → transcription changes, exactly as a peptide hormone such as insulin or glucagon does, since all hormones act through membrane receptors and none of them enter the cell under any circumstances

Cortisol crosses the plasma membrane → binds the glucocorticoid receptor in the cytosol → the hormone-receptor complex translocates to the nucleus → its DBD binds the glucocorticoid responsive element → its TRD recruits the machinery, activating PEP carboxykinase and hence gluconeogenesis
Cortisol binds DNA directly at the glucocorticoid responsive element
Cortisol is transported into the nucleus by a carrier protein and binds RNA polymerase II
Cortisol activates NF-κB by degrading IκB
rationale:
The receptor-as-transcription-factor pathway. Steroid hormones are hydrophobic, so they cross the membrane and find their receptor in the cytosol. The receptor has three domains — ligand-binding, DBD and TRD. Binding triggers translocation to the nucleus, the DBD docks on a hormone-responsive element, and the TRD recruits the activating machinery.

Her two worked examples:
Cortisol → glucocorticoid receptor → GRE → PEP carboxykinase → gluconeogenesis.
Estradiol → estrogen receptor → ERE → ovalbumin → oviduct function.

The trap: “cortisol binds DNA directly” skips the receptor. The hormone never touches DNA — the receptor is the DNA-binding protein, and that is exactly why blocking the receptor works as therapy.

stem: Tamoxifen is used in breast cancer because some tumours depend on estrogen for proliferation. How does it work, and what does an ER-positive biopsy report mean?
options: It binds the estrogen responsive element to repress transcription; ER-positive means the tumour has that element
It binds the estrogen receptor as a competitive inhibitor, blocking estrogen from binding; ER-positive means the cancer cells contain estrogen receptor, so the pathway is present and can be blocked

It prevents estrogen from entering the cell at all; ER-positive means that circulating estrogen levels are high in that patient, which is what makes that tumour hormone-dependent in the very first place
It binds estrogen and causes it to be degraded; ER-positive means estrogen is detectable
It inhibits estrogen synthesis in the ovary; ER-positive refers to serum estrogen
rationale:
Tamoxifen is a competitive inhibitor (antagonist) of the estrogen receptor. Her keyed answer. It occupies the ligand-binding domain so estradiol cannot, the receptor never translocates, the ERE is never bound, and the estrogen-driven proliferation programme is not switched on.

Pathologists grade breast cancer ER-positive or ER-negative on whether the receptor is present in the biopsy cells — which is precisely a test of whether there is anything for tamoxifen to block. That is why the receptor status determines the treatment.

The trap: “binds the estrogen responsive element” targets the right pathway at the wrong molecule. The ERE is DNA; tamoxifen is a small molecule that competes with a hormone for a protein pocket. Ask what a drug can physically bind.

stem: SREBP and NF-κB are both described as variations on the receptor-as-transcription-factor theme. What actually activates each?
options: Both are activated by a hormone binding a cytosolic receptor

SREBP sits in the ER membrane and, when cholesterol is LOW, moves to the Golgi where two proteases cleave off its cytoplasmic domain, which then enters the nucleus; NF-κB is held in the cytoplasm by IκB until LPS or a cytokine such as IL-1β triggers ubiquitin-tagging and degradation of IκB, releasing NF-κB
SREBP is activated by high cholesterol; NF-κB is activated by IκB binding
Both are activated by phosphorylation of a receptor tyrosine kinase

SREBP is released when IκB is degraded by the proteasome; NF-κB is released by two successive proteolytic cleavages in the Golgi apparatus, so the two factors use each other's activation mechanisms, and both respond to falling cholesterol rather than to inflammatory signals of any kind at all within the cell
rationale:
Same endpoint — a transcription factor with a DBD and a TRD reaching the nucleus — reached two different ways, and both by releasing a factor rather than making one.

SREBP: a transmembrane protein in the ER. Low cholesterol sends the precursor to the Golgi, where two proteases cleave the cytoplasmic domain free; it translocates to the nucleus, its DBD binds the sterol regulatory element, and its TRD activates cholesterol-metabolism genes. Note the logic: low cholesterol turns the pathway ON, which is how a cell restores its supply.

NF-κB: anchored in the cytoplasm by IκB. Bacterial LPS or a cytokine such as IL-1β causes IκB to be ubiquitin-tagged and degraded, freeing NF-κB to enter the nucleus and switch on inflammatory genes.

The trap: the option swapping the two mechanisms, and the one making SREBP respond to high cholesterol — a plausible-sounding inversion that gets the physiology backwards.

stem: Which is the site of DNA methylation?
options: A guanine base paired to a cytosine
A cytosine linked to a guanine by a phosphodiester bond (5'-CpG)
A cytosine base paired to a guanine
A guanine linked to a cytosine by a phosphodiester bond (5'-GpC)
A cytosine linked to another cytosine by a phosphodiester bond (5'-CpC)
rationale:
Methylation adds a methyl group to the C5 position of the cytosine ring of a CpG dinucleotide — and the p is the whole point: it denotes a phosphodiester bond along one strand, cytosine followed by guanine, not a C–G base pair across the two strands. Her keyed answer, with her own foil note that methylation does not occur on the guanine.

Getting this right is what makes maintenance methylation make sense: because CpG on one strand pairs with CpG on the other, the site is symmetric, so after replication the old strand's methyl mark tells DNMT1 exactly where to methylate the new one.

The trap: “a cytosine base paired to a guanine” is the intuitive reading of “CpG” and is wrong. Read the p as ‘phosphate, same strand’.

stem: How does DNA methylation relate to chromatin state and transcription?
options: Heterochromatin is heavily methylated and tightly packed and is not expressed; euchromatin has much less methylation, is loosely packed and is expressed
Heterochromatin is unmethylated and actively expressed; euchromatin is heavily methylated and transcriptionally silent, which is the reverse of what is observed
Methylation has no relationship to chromatin packing
Methylation loosens chromatin by adding negative charge
Only euchromatin can be methylated
rationale:
Heavily methylated → tightly packed → heterochromatin → not expressed. Less methylated → loosely packed → euchromatin → expressed.

Her two mechanisms for the silencing: directly, by inhibiting the binding of specific transcription factors, and indirectly, by recruiting proteins carrying repressive chromatin-remodelling activity.

Methylation also has a job beyond gene regulation — genome stability: silencing repetitive and centromeric DNA, suppressing recombination between repeats, and silencing transposons. It is found predominantly in repetitive regions (satellite DNA, LINEs, SINEs) and to a lesser extent at imprinted genes.

The trap: the charge option borrows the argument that is true of histone acetylation (which removes positive charge and loosens chromatin) and misapplies it to DNA methylation. Two different mechanisms in the same lecture, pulling the same direction for different reasons.

stem: Distinguish DNMT1 from DNMT3A/3B, and name a disease linked to each.
options: DNMT1 does de novo methylation, DNMT3A/3B maintenance; DNMT1 mutation causes ICF syndrome
DNMT1 maintains existing patterns
All three do de novo methylation; the numbers refer only to tissue distribution
DNMT1 removes methyl groups; DNMT3A/3B add them
DNMT enzymes methylate histones, not DNA
rationale:
DNMT1 = maintenance. Replication makes a hemimethylated CpG — the old strand carries the mark, the new one does not — and DNMT1 copies the mark onto the new strand. That is how an epigenetic pattern is heritable through cell division without being in the sequence.

DNMT3A and DNMT3B = de novo, laying down new patterns early in embryogenesis, around implantation.

All three transfer the methyl group from SAM (S-adenosyl-methionine).

Clinically: DNMT3A is mutated in about 20% of acute myeloid leukemia; DNMT3B mutations cause ICF syndrome — Immunodeficiency, Centromeric instability, Facial anomalies — with hypomethylation localised mostly to the centromere-adjacent heterochromatin of chromosomes 1 and 16.

The trap: the swapped option. Hook it on the number — DNMT3 is the “3” that starts from scratch in the embryo; 1 comes after and keeps what exists.

stem: Epigenetic alterations contribute to cancer in two opposite directions. Which pairing is correct?
options: Hypomethylation silences tumour suppressor genes; hypermethylation activates oncogenes and reactivates transposable elements, so the two changes push in opposite directions but by the reverse mechanisms
Hypomethylation causes genomic instability, loss of imprinting, activation of oncogenes and reactivation of transposons; hypermethylation of CpG islands silences genes, usually tumour suppressors
Only hypermethylation contributes to cancer
Only hypomethylation contributes to cancer
Both push in the same direction, silencing all genes
rationale:
Both directions are pathogenic and they damage different things.

Hypomethylation — the brakes come off the genome: genomic instability, loss of imprinting (LOI), activation of oncogenes, reactivation of transposons. Consistent with methylation's normal genome-stability role.

Hypermethylation — CpG islands aberrantly methylated, silencing genes, usually tumour suppressors. This is a way to lose p53 or pRb function without any mutation in the sequence.

That last point is why epigenetics matters therapeutically: a silenced gene is intact and can in principle be reactivated, which a deleted gene cannot.

The trap: the first option has both mechanisms with their effects swapped. Methylation silences — so hypermethylation silences what should be on, and hypomethylation un-silences what should be off. Derive it rather than memorising the list.

stem: What is genomic imprinting, and what does “improper imprinting” produce?
options: A mutation that silences one allele permanently in all of the tissues of the body, inherited from one parent only, so the silencing is written into the DNA sequence itself and cannot be reversed by any change in methylation state during development or later life at all

Modification of a gene — such as a methylation pattern — as it is transmitted through the sperm or the egg, so that normally only ONE copy of an imprinted gene is active; improper imprinting can leave two active copies or two inactive copies, disturbing development
The random inactivation of one X chromosome in females
The deletion of one parental copy of a chromosome region
A change in the DNA sequence inherited from one parent only
rationale:
Imprinting is parent-of-origin marking. You inherit two copies of every gene, but for imprinted genes the egg-derived copy of some and the sperm-derived copy of others is silenced, so only one copy is normally active. Break the marking and you get two active copies or two inactive copies, and either dosage is abnormal.

The regions where this happens are differentially methylated regions (DMRs), containing imprinting control regions (ICRs) that govern expression across the imprinted domain.

The trap: X-inactivation is the neighbouring concept and both silence one copy of something — but X-inactivation is random with respect to parental origin, while imprinting is determined entirely BY parental origin. And note the whole point of the definition: no change in the DNA sequence occurs, which is what makes imprinting epigenetic rather than genetic.

stem: A patient with Prader-Willi syndrome has a 15q11 deletion on the sperm-derived chromosome 15. Which enzyme class is responsible for the normal imprinting pattern that makes this deletion pathogenic?
options: Histone acetyl transferases
DNA methyltransferases
Histone methyltransferases
The E1, E2, E3 ubiquitin ligases
Histone deacetylases
rationale:
DNA methyltransferases. Her keyed answer, and the reasoning is what makes the imprinting diseases derivable rather than memorisable.

In 15q11, the first four genes — ZNF127, NDN, SNRPN, IPW — are methylated and silent on the egg-derived chromosome and active on the sperm-derived one. Delete the sperm-derived copy and the only remaining copy is the egg-derived one, where those four genes are already switched off by methylation. So the patient expresses none of them — and that loss is Prader-Willi.

The enzymes that laid down that silencing methylation are the DNMTs.

The trap: the deletion is the obvious lesion, so it is easy to answer as though the question were about the deletion. The question asks what made the remaining copy silent — and the answer is normal, correctly-performed imprinting.

stem: In 15q11, UBE3A is expressed from the egg-derived chromosome, while ZNF127, NDN, SNRPN and IPW are expressed from the sperm-derived one. Using only that, which loss gives Angelman and which gives Prader-Willi?
options: Loss of UBE3A activity from the egg-derived chromosome gives Angelman; loss of the four sperm-derived genes gives Prader-Willi
Loss of UBE3A gives Prader-Willi; loss of the four genes gives Angelman
Both syndromes result from loss of UBE3A alone
Both result from loss of the four sperm-derived genes; the two syndromes differ only by the sex of the patient
Neither syndrome involves imprinting
rationale:
Her one-line rule: in Prader-Willi, gene activity that normally comes from the SPERM is missing; in Angelman, gene activity that normally comes from the EGG is missing.

Apply it to the gene map. The four genes are active on the sperm-derived chromosome, so losing them → Prader-Willi. UBE3A is active on the egg-derived chromosome, so losing it → Angelman.

This is why her practice question works: a reprogramming defect that imprints UBE3A in a female's germ cells silences the copy that should have been active, and her child gets Angelman — from a mother who is entirely healthy.

The trap: memorising which syndrome goes with which parent without the gene map is fragile, and the two syndromes are always presented together precisely so they can be confused. Anchor UBE3A to the egg and derive the rest.

stem: There are two epigenetic reprogramming events in development. How do they differ, and why do somatic cells only undergo the first?
options: The zygote preserves both methylation and imprints; primordial germ cells later erase only non-imprinted methylation
The zygote erases most methylation but protects imprints; primordial germ cells later erase and reset imprints
Both events erase genomic imprints, but only the zygote restores totipotency
Both events preserve genomic imprints while removing histone acetylation
Only somatic cells undergo the second event, allowing tissue-specific imprinting
rationale:
Two erasures with different scopes, and the exception in the first is the examinable detail.

Zygote, pre-implantation: extensive demethylation of the genome to re-establish totipotency — but imprints are protected. If imprints were wiped here, every cell in the embryo would lose parent-of-origin dosage control.

Primordial germ cells, post-implantation: imprints are erased, so they can be reset according to the sex of the developing embryo — a man must put male imprints on all his sperm, including on the chromosome he inherited from his mother.

That last point resolves her worked tables: in somatic cells, an egg-derived chromosome 15 keeps the egg pattern forever; in a male's sperm cells, that same egg-derived chromosome has been reset to the male pattern.

The trap: the option that has the zygote erasing imprints. Both events erase methylation, but only the germline event touches imprints.

stem: Histone acetylation activates transcription. What is the charge argument, and what reverses it?
options: Acetylation adds positive charge to lysines, tightening the histone–DNA contact and compacting chromatin; HATs reverse it by removing the acetyl groups again, so acetylation represses transcription and deacetylation activates it, which is the opposite of the arrangement usually described and the reason HDAC inhibitors are used to silence genes rather than to activate them

Acetylation of lysine residues on the N-terminal tails of H3 and H4 REDUCES the histones' positive charge, weakening their attraction to the negatively charged phosphate backbone of DNA and loosening nucleosome packing; histone deacetylases (HDACs) remove the acetyl groups, recompacting chromatin and repressing transcription
Acetylation methylates the DNA directly; DNMTs reverse it
Acetylation cleaves the histone tails; ligases reverse it
Acetylation has no effect on charge and acts purely as a signal
rationale:
The mechanism is electrostatic and worth being able to state. Histones are positively charged (lysine-rich); the DNA backbone is negatively charged (phosphates). That attraction is what holds DNA on the nucleosome. Acetylating lysines neutralises positive charge, the grip weakens, and packing loosens. Enzymes: histone acetyl transferases (HATs) add, histone deacetylases (HDACs) remove and thereby repress.

There is a second, non-electrostatic effect she lists: acetylated histones act as a binding site for ATP-dependent remodelling enzymes, which slide nucleosomes to widen the gaps so RNAP-II and TFII-D can reach the DNA.

The tails carry other marks too — methylation, phosphorylation, ubiquitylation, sumoylation — which can create or disrupt binding sites for non-histone proteins.

The trap: the first option reverses the charge logic. Anchor it: acetyl groups are not positive, so adding them can only REDUCE net positive charge. That single fact regenerates the whole answer.

stem: Epigenetic modifications are described as heritable. Heritable in what sense, and what makes that possible?
options: Heritable because they change the primary DNA sequence, which is then copied faithfully at every round of replication, so the modification is passed on in exactly the same way as any ordinary mutation would be in the germline

Heritable through cell division without any change to the primary DNA sequence — because CpG sites are symmetric, DNMT1 reads the methylation on the parental strand after replication and copies it onto the new strand
Heritable only through the germline, never through mitosis
Not truly heritable — the term is used loosely
Heritable because histones are copied nucleotide by nucleotide
rationale:
Her definition insists on both halves: epigenetic modifications are heritable and do not amount to changes in the primary DNA sequence. The mechanism that reconciles them is maintenance methylation.

Because a CpG on one strand faces a CpG on the other, replication leaves a hemimethylated site — the old strand marked, the new one bare. DNMT1 reads the parental mark and copies it, so the daughter cells inherit the pattern.

That is the same phenomenon as the tissue-specific chromatin differences from the DNA lecture: stably inherited changes in chromatin structure, maintained through cell division, without a sequence difference. It is how a liver cell's daughters stay liver cells.

The trap: “heritable” is read as passed to offspring. Here it primarily means passed to daughter CELLS — and the germline reprogramming event exists specifically to erase imprints before they reach the next generation.

stem: Match the definition: different mutant alleles at the SAME locus cause the same disease, versus mutations at DIFFERENT loci cause the same disease.
options: The first is locus heterogeneity and the second is allelic heterogeneity, which is the reverse of the usual definitions, since heterogeneity at one locus must mean different alleles of that same gene by definition

The first is allelic heterogeneity (cystic fibrosis, with over 1000 CFTR mutations at 7q31), the second is locus heterogeneity (non-syndromic hearing loss, several genes with different inheritance patterns)
Both describe pleiotropy
The first is pleiotropy, the second epistasis
The first is variable expressivity, the second reduced penetrance
rationale:
Allelic = same gene, different mutations. Cystic fibrosis is her example: over 1000 known mutations at CFTR (7q31), of varying severity, with ΔF508 accounting for 70% in the Caucasian population.

Locus = different genes, same disease. Non-syndromic hearing loss, where several different genes are involved and the inheritance pattern differs between them. She notes this often happens when two different genes make a compound gene product — break either subunit and the product fails.

Clinically, locus heterogeneity is the reason a negative test for one gene does not exclude the diagnosis.

The trap: the two words are near-identical in shape. Anchor on the roots — allele = a version of a gene; locus = a place on a chromosome.

stem: Cystic fibrosis is used as an example of both allelic heterogeneity and pleiotropy. What does the pleiotropy consist of, and what is the underlying mechanism?
options: Different CFTR mutations cause different diseases
One gene produces diverse effects
Different patients inherit CFTR from different parents
CFTR is regulated by another gene at a different locus
The environment mimics cystic fibrosis in some patients
rationale:
Pleiotropy is one gene producing diverse phenotypic effects, and CF shows why it happens: CFTR moves sodium and chloride across epithelial cells, and epithelium lines almost everything. One transport defect → salt imbalance → thick, sticky, obstructing mucus → disease in the lungs, pancreas, intestine, reproductive tract, and more.

CF is her worked example of three modifiers at once: allelic heterogeneity (1000+ CFTR mutations), variable expressivity (most have respiratory and digestive disease, some only respiratory), and pleiotropy. Median survival is in the 30s, usually from end-stage lung disease.

The trap: “different mutations cause different diseases” is allelic heterogeneity restated, not pleiotropy. Pleiotropy is ONE genotype fanning out to many organs; allelic heterogeneity is MANY genotypes converging on one disease.

stem: Hereditary retinoblastoma is autosomal dominant and about 90% penetrant. What is the chance that the child of an affected person develops retinoblastoma?
rationale:
Two independent probabilities, so multiply: 1/2 chance of inheriting the mutant allele × 9/10 chance of expressing it if inherited = 9/20 ≈ 45%. Her worked answer.

Penetrance is the probability that someone with the genotype expresses the phenotype to any degree — an all-or-nothing measure, given as a percentage. Reduced penetrance is why a dominant condition can appear to skip generations and why an unaffected person can have an affected child.

Her counselling point is worth keeping: reduced penetrance does not change the risk of inheriting the mutation, only the risk of developing the disease — and for an unaffected relative you may not know whether they are at 50% risk or no risk at all.

The trap: 50% answers only the transmission half and ignores the penetrance; 90% answers only the expression half and assumes the allele was inherited. Both gates must be passed.

stem: A woman is completely unaffected but clearly inherited a dominant mutation and passed it to two affected children. What is the most likely explanation, and how does it differ from variable expressivity?
options: Reduced penetrance — she has the genotype and expresses nothing at all, which is all-or-nothing; variable expressivity would mean she shows the condition but mildly
Variable expressivity — she has a very mild form
Germline mosaicism — she does not carry the mutation in her somatic cells at all, only in a subpopulation of her gametes, which is why she is unaffected herself despite transmitting it
Non-paternity
A phenocopy in the children
rationale:
Reduced penetrance. Her keyed answer for exactly this pedigree, and her wording matters: this indicates an all-or-nothing situation. She is completely unaffected, but seems to have passed the gene to her children.

The contrast with variable expressivity is the whole point of the pair: variable expressivity means the manifestation varies among people with the same genotype — different features, different severity, from mild and possibly unnoticed to severe — but there is a manifestation. Penetrance asks WHETHER; expressivity asks HOW MUCH.

Her caution about expressivity is clinically important: mildly affected individuals may never come to clinical attention, so an apparently unaffected relative may just be under-examined. Note also that the majority of genetic conditions show variable expressivity.
