The trap: germline mosaicism also produces affected children of an unaffected parent — but the stem says she clearly inherited the mutation, so it is in her somatic cells, which rules mosaicism out.

stem: A man is diagnosed with an autosomal dominant disease; neither parent has any symptoms. Which explanations remain possible?
options: Variable expressivity, reduced penetrance and skewed X-inactivation in a female parent of his
De novo mutation, germline mosaicism in a parent, reduced penetrance, and non-paternity
Only a de novo mutation
Skewed X-inactivation and phenocopy only
None — a dominant disease requires an affected parent
rationale:
Her keyed question, answered by ruling in and out one at a time:
De novo mutation — possible. Very common in some diseases; the parents carry no increased risk for further children.
Germline mosaicism — possible. A parent could have the mutation in a portion of their gametes only, with no symptoms, and could have more than one affected child.
Reduced penetrance — possible, though you would then expect the disease somewhere else in the family.
Non-paternity — possible; the biological father may be affected. She puts the rate at 4–10%.
Variable expressivity — NO, because a parent would then show some symptoms, and the stem says neither has any.
Skewed X-inactivation — NO, twice over: it applies only to X-linked conditions, and the patient is male with a single X.

The trap: variable expressivity is the reflex answer for “unaffected parent”, and the two words any symptoms in the stem are what exclude it.

stem: Compare de novo mutation, somatic mosaicism and germline mosaicism by when the mutation occurs and who is at risk.
options: All three occur before fertilisation and carry the same recurrence risk

De novo: arises in the egg or sperm at conception, so it is in ALL the proband's cells — parents not at increased risk, but the proband can transmit it. Somatic mosaicism: arises AFTER fertilisation in body cells, so only a subpopulation carries it. Germline mosaicism: arises after fertilisation in a parent's germ cells only, so the unaffected parent CAN have several affected children
De novo mutations occur only in autosomal recessive conditions

Somatic mosaicism means the germ cells are affected and the body cells are not, so the recurrence risk for the proband's siblings is high while the proband shows no features at all, and the mutation cannot be detected in a blood sample from either parent or from the affected child at any stage of life, which is why the distinction between the three mechanisms has no bearing on counselling
Germline mosaicism carries no recurrence risk
rationale:
Timing determines who carries the mutation, and that determines the counselling.

De novo — in the gamete at conception, so every cell of the proband has it. Parents are not at increased risk for future pregnancies, but the proband transmits at the same rate as anyone who inherited it. Commoner in autosomal dominant and X-linked conditions; her figures: neurofibromatosis 50%, tuberous sclerosis 67%, and DMD, being genetically lethal, must have a 1/3 new mutation rate just to maintain its frequency.

Somatic mosaicism — after fertilisation, in body cells. Disease appears only if enough cells are affected, is often milder or regionally limited — her example, segmental NF1, where café-au-lait spots and neurofibromas are confined to one area and do not cross the midline.

Germline mosaicism — after fertilisation, in the germ cells only. The parent is unaffected but a proportion of gametes carry the mutation, so several affected children are possible. Risk figures: 15% for DMD when the proband is the only affected member; 5–6% in osteogenesis imperfecta; ≤1% for most conditions.

The trap: her explicit warning — with only ONE affected child you cannot tell a de novo mutation from parental germline mosaicism, and the recurrence risk you quote depends entirely on which it is.

stem: A woman carries a Duchenne muscular dystrophy mutation and has definite muscle weakness. DMD is X-linked recessive, so how can a carrier be symptomatic?
options: She must have inherited two mutant alleles
Skewed X-inactivation
DMD is actually autosomal in females
She has a de novo mutation on her second X
Germline mosaicism causes her symptoms
rationale:
All females are mosaic for X expression — normally ~50% of cells inactivate the maternal X and ~50% the paternal. Inactivation is random at the time it happens; skewing is what you observe afterwards, and her careful phrasing is that we only see “the survivors”. The more skewed the proportion, the more likely an effect, up to 100%.

For X-linked recessive: if most cells have the abnormal X active, a carrier expresses some or all features — about 1/3 of DMD carriers have muscle weakness.

For X-linked dominant it cuts both ways, and Rett syndrome is her example: if the normal X is preferentially inactivated the phenotype is more severe; if the mutated X is, it is milder or apparently absent — which is why a mildly affected or unaffected woman can have a severely affected child. Affected males rarely survive infancy.

The trap: “recessive” is taken to guarantee that carriers are unaffected. In an X-linked condition, a female is not a uniform heterozygote — she is a mosaic, and the proportions can go against her.

stem: Two people with achondroplasia have children. What are the expected outcomes, and what does this illustrate?
options: All children have achondroplasia; this is co-dominance
25% homozygous and lethal, 50% achondroplasia, 25% unaffected
All children are unaffected; this is epistasis
50% affected and 50% unaffected, as for any dominant condition
25% affected, 75% unaffected; this is a recessive pattern
rationale:
Aa × Aa gives 25% AA : 50% Aa : 25% aa. In achondroplasia, AA is lethal, Aa is achondroplasia, and aa is unaffected. Her worked Punnett square.

Incomplete dominance means the heterozygote's phenotype is different from and intermediate to both homozygotes — heterozygotes are affected, homozygotes far more severely, often lethally. It is a reminder that “dominant” describes the heterozygote, and says nothing about the homozygote.

Background: achondroplasia is the commonest inherited dwarfism, with rhizomelic (proximal) shortening of the limbs and normal intelligence and lifespan, and it turned up in the cell cycle lecture as the paternal-age-associated FGFR3 mutation.

The trap: the plain-dominant answer of 50/50 ignores the lethal homozygote. Whenever both parents are affected by a dominant condition, check what AA does before writing the ratio.

stem: In the ABO system, A and B are co-dominant and O behaves as recessive. Which statement follows?
options: Genotype AO gives an intermediate phenotype between A and O
Genotype AB expresses BOTH A and B antigens and makes neither anti-A nor anti-B antibody, because neither allele is dominant over the other
Genotype OO expresses a weak A antigen
Co-dominance means the heterozygote is intermediate between the two homozygotes, exactly as in incomplete dominance
Type O individuals have neither anti-A nor anti-B antibodies
rationale:
Co-dominance: different alleles have an EQUAL effect and both are expressed — neither masks the other. So AB expresses both antigens and, having both as self, makes neither antibody — which is why AB is the universal recipient.

Her table completes it: AA/AO = type A, A antigen, anti-B antibody · BB/BO = type B, B antigen, anti-A · OO = type O, neither antigen, BOTH anti-A and anti-B.

The trap: the distinction from incomplete dominance is the point of putting these two sections side by side. Co-dominance = both alleles fully expressed at once (A and B antigens both present). Incomplete dominance = a single blended intermediate phenotype (achondroplasia). The AB heterozygote is not intermediate between A and B — it is both.

stem: A patient types as blood group O, but genetic testing shows they carry an A allele. What explains this, and what is the general phenomenon?
options: A laboratory error; genotype and blood type always agree
The Bombay phenotype
Incomplete dominance between A and O
Co-dominance between H and A
A phenocopy caused by transfusion
rationale:
Epistasis: the expression of one gene is prevented or modified by a gene at a different locus.

The chemistry makes it concrete. The H gene encodes fucosyl transferase, which builds the H antigen (a terminal fucose-galactose disaccharide) on the red cell. The A and B enzymes are glycosyl transferases that MODIFY the H antigen into A or B antigen; O does not modify it. H antigen is present in HH or Hh, absent in hh.

So in hh — the Bombay phenotype — there is no H substrate to modify, and even with functional A or B enzymes no A or B antigen can form. The person types as O whatever their ABO genotype: AA, AO, BB, BO, OO and AB all present as type O.

Clinically this matters: a Bombay individual will react against ordinary group O blood, because that blood still carries H antigen.

The trap: reading this as a co-dominance or dominance problem within ABO. Epistasis is between loci — the H locus overrides the ABO locus entirely.

stem: Distinguish a sex-influenced from a sex-limited condition.
options: Sex-influenced traits are X-linked; sex-limited traits are Y-linked
Sex-influenced traits occur in both sexes at different frequencies; sex-limited traits are expressed in only one sex
Sex-influenced traits occur in one sex only; sex-limited traits occur in both at different frequencies
Sex-influenced traits require hormones; sex-limited traits require mitochondrial inheritance
Sex-influenced and sex-limited are equivalent terms for autosomal traits
rationale:
Both are autosomal — that is the first thing to fix, because both are routinely mistaken for X-linkage.

Sex-influenced — expressed in both sexes, at significantly different frequencies. Her example is male pattern baldness, explicitly NOT an X-linked trait: it behaves as autosomal dominant in males and autosomal recessive in females, so men need one mutant allele and women need two.

Sex-limited — expressed in ONE sex only, generally associated with primary or secondary sexual characteristics: beard growth, milk production in a lactating mother, and — the clinically useful one — mild CFTR mutations causing congenital bilateral absence of the vas deferens (CBAVD) in males.

The trap: a sex bias in a pedigree pulls hard toward X-linkage. Recall her rule-out logic from the modes lecture: a sex bias makes autosomal inheritance less likely but does not rule it out — and these two categories are exactly why.

stem: A woman in a family with hereditary breast cancer develops breast cancer but tests negative for the family's BRCA mutation. What is this, and what is the counselling consequence?
options: A de novo mutation; her children are at increased risk
A phenocopy
Reduced penetrance; the mutation is present but undetected
Germline mosaicism
Non-paternity
rationale:
A phenocopy is a phenotype produced by something other than the genetic cause it resembles — an environmental influence mimicking a genetic disorder, occurring sporadically within a family. Her two examples are sporadic cancer in a hereditary cancer family and environmental (infection, antibiotic) versus genetic hearing loss.

The counselling consequence is her stated one: the individual may be thought to have the genetic condition when they do not, and so may be given a higher recurrence risk than is accurate. Affected individuals with a phenocopy are not at increased risk of affected offspring from that cause.

The trap: “reduced penetrance” assumes a false negative test. Penetrance describes people who have the genotype and do not express it — the opposite direction from someone who expresses the phenotype without the genotype. Sporadic disease is common enough that it will occasionally land in a family that also carries a mutation.

stem: Huntington disease illustrates delayed age of onset. What is her precise claim, and what problem does it create?
options: The mutation appears in adulthood, so the children of an affected person are not at risk until they reach the same age themselves, and testing before that age cannot detect anything at all, since the mutation is not yet present in their cells, which is why predictive testing is offered only to adults

ALL heritable conditions are present at birth, but not all are EXPRESSED at birth — Huntington's cognitive, psychiatric and motor decline generally begins after age 30 — which makes recurrence risk hard to predict, because you do not yet know whether an at-risk adult is affected
The disease is acquired in adulthood from environmental exposure
Delayed onset means the mutation accumulates over time
Delayed onset only occurs in recessive conditions
rationale:
Her exact wording: all heritable conditions are present at birth, but not all are expressed at birth. The genotype was fixed at conception; only the phenotype waits.

Huntington disease shows progressive cognitive, psychiatric and motor decline, generally not before age 30. The counselling difficulty is real: it is hard to predict recurrence risk for the children of an at-risk adult, because you do not yet know whether that adult will be affected. She notes genetic testing may be available to predict who will develop the disease — which is why Huntington testing is the classic case study in whether a person wants to know.

The trap: “the mutation appears in adulthood” is a genuine misconception and the reason the distinction is worth stating. The gene does not change; its expression is what is delayed.

stem: Hereditary haemochromatosis is her capstone example. Which set of modifiers does it demonstrate?
options: Only reduced penetrance and delayed onset, since the other modifiers described in the lecture apply to dominant conditions and haemochromatosis is recessive in its inheritance pattern, which excludes all of them

Reduced penetrance, variable expressivity, pleiotropy, locus heterogeneity, allelic heterogeneity, delayed age of onset, phenocopies and sex-influence — eight modifiers in one autosomal recessive disease
Only epistasis and co-dominance
Only sex-limited expression
None — its inheritance is purely Mendelian
rationale:
One disease, eight modifiers, and each is worth being able to name:
Reduced penetrance — not everyone with two mutations develops it.
Variable expressivity — presentations differ widely.
Pleiotropy — iron loads the liver, skin, pancreas, heart, joints and testes.
Locus heterogeneity — usually HFE, but mutations in three other genes are known.
Allelic heterogeneity — three common HFE mutations, C282Y the most severe, plus H63D and S63C.
Delayed age of onset — iron takes years to accumulate.
Phenocopies — alcoholic liver disease or hepatitis can produce iron overload.
Sex-influenced — commoner in males, with menstruation protective.

It is also the most common inherited condition in the US and often unrecognised early — 1/9 Caucasians carry the severe C282Y mutation and 1/4 carry some mutation — and it is preventable with therapeutic phlebotomy. That combination is what makes it a favourite exam disease: common, treatable, and easy to miss.

The trap: assuming one disease illustrates one modifier. The reason she ends the lecture here is that real inheritance patterns are modified by several factors at once, which is what makes a pedigree hard to read.

stem: A child has café-au-lait spots and neurofibromas confined to one region of the body, not crossing the midline, with no family history. What is this, and what is the recurrence risk?
options: Classic NF1 from a de novo mutation; the parents' risk is not increased
Segmental neurofibromatosis type 1 from SOMATIC mosaicism
Germline mosaicism in a parent; several sibs will be affected
A phenocopy; there is no genetic basis
Skewed X-inactivation; NF1 is X-linked
rationale:
Segmental NF1 — somatic mosaicism. Her example. The mutation occurred after fertilisation, so only a subpopulation of cells carries it, and the clinical signature is a regional distribution that does not cross the midline — a map of which cells descended from the mutated one.

Two consequences she states: expression may be less severe because normal cells are also present, and it may affect only certain features or certain regions. And the counselling problem: the recurrence risk is difficult to determine, because you do not know whether the germ cells are also affected.

The trap: the timing distinguishes this from every neighbouring answer. De novo means the mutation was in the gamete, so it would be in every cell and the disease would not be segmental. Germline mosaicism is in a parent's gametes, which affects the sibs, not the distribution on this child's skin. Read where the mosaicism sits.

stem: What does the law of large numbers state, and what sample size does he say should be accepted with caution?
options: That larger samples always give a statistically significant result, so any study failing to reach significance must simply have been too small, and he cautions against trusting any result below n = 100 for that reason, since power alone determines whether a finding is real

That repeating an experiment enough times yields a metric representative of the whole population — as sample size increases the sample mean approaches the population mean; as a general rule a study with a sample size below 30 should be accepted with caution
That the population mean approaches the sample mean as the population grows
That the standard deviation falls to zero as sample size increases
That any sample above 30 is guaranteed to be representative
rationale:
As the number of samples increases, the sample mean approaches the population mean. His coin-flip demonstration is the illustration: with 30 flips heads can dominate, with 240 the proportion converges on 50%, which is what an unbiased coin should give.

His practical rule: a study with a sample size below 30 should be accepted with caution.

The framing to keep is why sampling exists at all — a population is a group where measuring every member is impractical or impossible, so you take an appropriately sized sample and generalise.

The trap: the last option turns a caution into a guarantee. n ≥ 30 removes one specific worry; it does not make a sample representative — a large biased sample is still biased, which is exactly the skin-cancer example later in the same lecture.

stem: Classify each: eye colour (brown/blue/red) · skill level (beginner/intermediate/expert) · blood pressure in mmHg · smoker yes/no.
options: Nominal · ordinal · numerical continuous · binary
Ordinal · nominal · numerical discrete · binary
Binary · nominal · ordinal · numerical
All four are categorical
Nominal · binary · ordinal · numerical
rationale:
Numerical (quantitative) data can be discrete (1, 2, 3) or continuous (any measurable value) — blood pressure is continuous. Categorical (qualitative) splits three ways: binary, two values (smoker yes/no); nominal, three or more values with no natural order (eye colour); ordinal, three or more values with a natural order (beginner/intermediate/expert).

His one-line test: if the data can only be grouped into categories, it is categorical.

This is not vocabulary for its own sake — it determines the analysis. Numerical → Student's t-test. Categorical, usually expressed as a proportion → chi-square.

The trap: nominal and ordinal both have three or more values, so the count cannot separate them. Only the presence of a natural order does.

stem: In a study of whether hours of sleep affect exam score, which variable is dependent and which independent, and how does he define the terms?
options: Exam score is independent because it is the variable being measured; hours of sleep is dependent because it is the one the investigator chooses to vary in the design
Exam score is dependent — it may be affected by other measured variables; hours of sleep is independent — it is not changed by the other factors being measured
Both are dependent, since both are measured
Both are independent, since neither is manipulated
The classification depends on whether the data are numerical or categorical
rationale:
His definitions: a dependent variable might be affected by other variables that are measured; an independent variable is not changed by other factors that might be measured. His own examples are exactly these — exam score might be affected by hours of sleep; age is not affected by diet.

By convention the independent variable goes on the X axis and the dependent on the Y axis. In his spin-angle work, spin-angle stays dependent throughout while the independent variable changes from time to temperature — which is a useful reminder that the labels describe the question, not the measurement.

The trap: “both are measured, so both are dependent”. Being measured is not what makes a variable dependent — being potentially affected by the other variable is.

stem: Which statistical test does he pair with which data type?
options: Numerical data → chi-square; categorical data, often expressed as a proportion → Student's t-test, which is the standard pairing
Numerical data → Student's t-test; categorical data, often expressed as a proportion or fraction → chi-square
Both data types → Student's t-test
Both data types → chi-square
Test choice depends only on sample size, not data type
rationale:
Numerical (quantitative) → Student's t-test. Categorical (qualitative), often expressed as a proportion or fraction → chi-square.

The reason is what each test compares. A t-test compares means, which requires numbers you can average. Categorical data have no meaningful mean, so they are summarised as proportions and compared with chi-square.

That is also why so much of epidemiology is proportion arithmetic — as he puts it, risk, risk ratios, odds ratios, sensitivity, specificity and predictive values are all based on proportions, which is to say they are all summaries of categorical data.

The trap: the swapped option. Anchor it on the word mean — t-test compares means, so it needs numbers.

stem: You draw an ace from a 52-card deck. What is the probability of drawing a second ace, with and without replacing the first?
options: 7.7% with replacement; 5.9% without
5.9% with replacement; 7.7% without
7.7% in both cases
5.9% in both cases
3.8% with replacement; 7.7% without
rationale:
Probability is allowed outcomes divided by possible outcomes. First draw: 4/52 = 7.7%.

Without replacement, both numbers fall — one ace gone and one card gone — so 3/51 = 5.9%. With replacement, the deck is restored and it is 4/52 = 7.7% again.

The general point is the one that matters clinically: replacement determines whether successive events are independent, and independence is what licenses multiplying probabilities. It is the same idea as the product rule in the genetics lecture.

The trap: the two numbers are both correct and the whole question is which goes with which condition. Removing a card changes both the numerator and the denominator — check both before answering.

context: Rick enrolls 1,000 people who have their teeth cleaned every six months. 100 have had a knee replacement in the past five years (the Replacement group); the other 900 are Controls. Over two years, 30 of the Replacement group and 18 of the Control group develop a bone infection.
stem: Build the 2×2 contingency table using his cell labels, then compute the risk of infection in each group and the relative risk. State the conclusion in a sentence a patient could use.
rationale:
Infection   No Infection   Totals
  Replacement        30            70          100
  Control            18           882          900
  Totals             48           952         1000
His cell labels are A B / C D, with row totals A+B and C+D, column totals A+C and B+D, and grand total A+B+C+D. Check the arithmetic both ways before using the table — rows and columns must both sum to 1000.

Risk in the exposed = 30/100 = 0.30.
Risk in the unexposed = 18/900 = 0.02.
Relative risk = 0.30 / 0.02 = 15.

His sentence: the risk of getting an infection is 15 times greater for those who have had knee replacement surgery than for those who have not.

Note what the denominator does for you. RR accounts for the background rate — infections happen in unexposed people too, and dividing by that baseline is what separates “this exposure matters” from “this outcome is common”.

Two other probabilities he asks from the same table, worth keeping distinct: pick one person from the replacement group and P(infection) = 30/100 = 30%; pick one person from the whole study and P(infection) = 48/1000 = 4.8%. The denominator is set by the group you sampled from.

context: Rick enrolls 1,000 people who have their teeth cleaned every six months. 100 have had a knee replacement in the past five years (the Replacement group); the other 900 are Controls. Over two years, 30 of the Replacement group and 18 of the Control group develop a bone infection.
stem: If you pick one person at random from everyone in the study, what is the probability they had an infection — and how does that differ from the risk quoted to a replacement patient?
options: 4.8% overall and 4.8% for a replacement patient — they are the same, because the denominator does not change with the group you sample from
4.8% overall, but 30% for someone in the replacement group, because the denominator changes with the group you sample from
30% overall and 2% for a replacement patient
48% overall and 30% for a replacement patient
It cannot be calculated without the relative risk
rationale:
Whole study: 48 infections in 1000 people = 4.8%.
Replacement group only: 30 in 100 = 30%.
Control group only: 18 in 900 = 2%.

Same table, three different answers, and the only thing that changed is which group you drew the person from. This is the single most common source of error in 2×2 questions: reading the right cell and dividing by the wrong total.

It is also why the overall figure is nearly useless for counselling. 4.8% is dominated by the 900 controls and badly understates the risk to the patient actually sitting in front of you.

The trap: 48% is what you get by treating a raw count as a percentage in a 100-person mental model. Always write the denominator down.

stem: Define the three measures of central tendency and say which is most useful for nominal data.
options: Mean = middle value; median = most frequent; mode = average — and the mean is the one that suits nominal data, since naming a category requires an arithmetic average of the numeric codes that were assigned to each category before any analysis

Mode = most frequently occurring value, and it is the one useful for nominal data since it names the most popular category; median = the middle value, or the mean of the middle two if the count is even; mean = the sum divided by N
All three require numerical data and none applies to nominal data
Median = most frequent; mode = middle value; mean = the range
The mode is the value at the centre of a Gaussian distribution by definition
rationale:
Mode — the most frequently occurring value. It is the only one of the three that works on nominal data, because you can count categories but cannot average or rank them; it tells you which category was most popular. On a bar chart it is simply the tallest bar.

Median — the middle value; for an even-sized data set, the mean of the middle two.
Mean — the sum of all values divided by N, i.e. the average.

His own spin-angle data set shows all three separating slightly: mean 3.823, median 3.855, mode 3.98 — close but not equal, which is what a nearly-but-not-quite symmetric distribution looks like.

The trap: the last option is a real misconception. Mean, median and mode coincide only in a perfectly symmetric distribution — in a skewed one they separate, and that separation is how you detect the skew.

stem: How does the standard error of the mean differ from the standard deviation?
options: They are two names for the same quantity

SD measures the dispersion of the data about its own mean; SEM measures how much the sample mean is likely to differ from the population mean, and is the SD divided by the square root of the sample size

SEM measures the dispersion of the data about its own mean; SD measures how much the sample mean would vary between repeated samples, so SD is the one that falls as the sample grows larger in any study of the same population
SEM is the SD multiplied by the sample size
SD applies to categorical data and SEM to numerical data
rationale:
They answer different questions. SD describes the data you have — a small SD means values cluster closely about the mean; a large SD means they are spread farther away. SEM describes your uncertainty about the population — how much discrepancy there is likely to be between your sample mean and the mean you would get if you could measure everyone.

SEM = SD / √n. The √n is the important part: collecting more data shrinks SEM but not SD. More measurements make you more confident about where the mean is; they do not make the underlying variable less variable.

The trap: papers often report SEM because it is the smaller number and makes error bars look tighter. When you read a figure, check which one is plotted — the two carry entirely different claims.

stem: A distribution has a long tail extending to the right. What is it called, and where does the mean sit relative to the median?
options: Left-skewed or negatively skewed; the mean is left of the median
Right-skewed or positively skewed; the mean is shifted to the right of the median
Right-skewed; the mean and median are identical
Left-skewed; the mean is right of the median
Gaussian; skew does not affect the mean
rationale:
Skew is named for the longer tail. A tail extending right = right-skewed = positively skewed, and his own hook for the name is that the mean becomes shifted to the right of the median.

The reason is worth understanding rather than memorising: the mean is pulled by extreme values because every value enters the sum, while the median only counts positions. A few very large values drag the mean toward the tail and leave the median where it is.

That is also the practical consequence — report the median for skewed data (income, length of stay, survival time), because the mean is misleading there.

The trap: naming the skew for where the bulk of the data sits rather than where the tail points. The tail names the skew.

stem: What distinguishes a histogram from a bar chart, given that both use columns?
options: They are the same; the names are interchangeable

A bar chart compares magnitudes across categories, with bar length proportional to the value it represents; a histogram shows a frequency distribution, with bar length proportional to the COUNT of observations falling in a bin, where bins have equal width

A histogram is used for categorical data and a bar chart for numerical data, so the columns of a histogram may be of unequal width while those of a bar chart are always equal, and the two therefore answer entirely different questions about the same dataset in practice
A histogram has no axes labels
A bar chart shows counts and a histogram shows magnitudes
rationale:
Same shape, different meaning on the Y axis. Bar chart: length ∝ the value being represented, best for comparing magnitude across categories. Histogram: length ∝ the COUNT of observations in a bin, showing the frequency distribution of one variable.

His construction detail: the data are grouped into bins of equal width, each width being the range divided by the number of bins, where the range is max minus min. In his spin-angle set the bins run [2.00, 2.76], (2.76, 3.52] and so on.

A histogram is also what let him recognise the Gaussian shape of his data, which is why the graph choice mattered.

The trap: the option assigning histograms to categorical data reverses it — a histogram needs a continuous variable to bin, and it is the bar chart he calls the preferred chart for qualitative data.

stem: Match graph to purpose. Which pairing is correct?
options: Scatter plot — to show the five-number summary of a single variable, with the independent variable plotted on the vertical axis by convention
Scatter plot — to observe the relationship between two variables and reveal any correlation, with the independent variable on the X axis
Box plot — to reveal correlation between two variables
Line graph — to show the frequency distribution of a variable
Dot plot — to compare magnitudes across categories
rationale:
His set, each with a job:
Dot plot — the simplest way to see the spread of a small-to-moderate data set. It is what showed him spin-angle ranged from 2.00 to 5.34.
Line graph — connects sequential points so you can see the rate of change (slope) between them; horizontal lines would have meant a constant value.
Bar chart — compares magnitude across categories.
Histogram — frequency distribution.
Scatter plot — relationship between two variables, revealing correlation.
Box plot — the five-number summary of one variable.

The narrative is the lesson: the same data told him nothing as a dot plot, showed drift as a line graph, and revealed the cause only as a scatter plot against temperature. The graph you choose determines the question you can answer.

The trap: every wrong option is a real graph paired with another graph's purpose.

stem: A study finds a statistically significant positive correlation between exercise and skin cancer in a Western Australian population, without recording time spent exercising outdoors. What is wrong with concluding that exercise causes skin cancer?
options: Nothing — a significant correlation establishes causation
Correlation does not establish causation: a third variable — sunlight exposure — plausibly explains both, and the population already has a high baseline incidence of skin cancer
The sample size must have been below 30
The correlation coefficient must have been negative
Skin cancer is categorical, so a correlation between it and exercise cannot be calculated at all, and the reported association must therefore be a computational artefact of the analysis
rationale:
His worked cautionary tale. A correlation between variables does not automatically mean the change in one causes the change in the other; causation means one event is the result of the other.

The reviewer's objection has two parts and both matter. There is a lurking third variable — sun exposure, which drives both outdoor exercise and skin cancer. And the sample came from a population with an already high baseline incidence, so the association could reflect the setting rather than the exposure.

Note his honest position on his own data: he concludes temperature causes the spin-angle change “in the absence of other possibilities” — a controlled experiment where he can vary temperature deliberately, not an observational association.

The trap: “statistically significant” is heard as “real, therefore causal”. Significance tells you the association is unlikely to be chance; it says nothing about what produced it.

stem: Regression gives spin-angle = 0.0331(Temperature) + 0.2212 with R² = 0.9833. What does R² tell you, and what does the correlation coefficient R add?
options: R² gives the slope; R gives the intercept
R² is a goodness-of-fit measure
R² indicates causation; R indicates correlation
R² can be negative, indicating an inverse relationship
R and R² are the same quantity expressed on different scales, and both carry direction
rationale:
R² is goodness of fit: the closer R² is to 1, the better the linear equation models the data. At 0.9833 he judges the fit “good enough” to build a temperature-compensation equation into his instrument.

R, the correlation coefficient, carries direction as well as strength: greater than zero is a positive relationship, less than zero negative, with −1 a perfect negative and +1 a perfect positive correlation. His definition of a positive association: high values of one variable tend to accompany high values of the other.

The distinction that matters: squaring destroys the sign, so R² alone cannot tell you whether the relationship runs up or down.

The trap: “R² can be negative” — it is a square, so it cannot. And note that a high R² still says nothing about causation, which is the previous slide's whole point.

stem: What is alpha, and what does he emphasise about where it comes from?
options: Alpha is calculated from the data and represents the strength of the observed effect, so a larger effect gives a smaller alpha, and the investigator has no say in what it turns out to be once the study has been analysed, which is why it is reported alongside the p-value

Alpha is a threshold the investigator CHOOSES — the probability of rejecting the null hypothesis when it is in fact true — so it has nothing to do with the data and everything to do with how confident you want to be that you are not making a Type I error
Alpha is the probability that the null hypothesis is true
Alpha is the p-value returned by the statistical test
Alpha is fixed at .05 by convention and cannot be changed
rationale:
His moment of realisation is the teaching point: alpha has nothing to do with his data — it is a threshold he sets in advance, specifying how confident he wants to be that he is not making a Type I error.

Setting α = .05 means that 1 time in 20 you would expect to reach the wrong conclusion and reject a true null hypothesis.

Keep alpha and p distinct: alpha is chosen by the investigator before the test; p is computed from the data. Everything about a significance test is the comparison between one number you picked and one number you measured.

The trap: “alpha is the probability that the null hypothesis is true” is the classic misstatement. It is the probability of REJECTING the null GIVEN that it is true — a conditional in the opposite direction.

stem: Rick's test returns p = .037. He first sets α = .05, then decides α should have been .03 and re-runs it. What happens, and what is the lesson?
options: The p-value changes to .03 and the conclusion is therefore unchanged, because lowering alpha shifts the p-value with it, and the two always move together whenever the threshold is redefined after the data have been collected and analysed

The p-value stays .037. At α = .05, p < α so the null is rejected and the samples are significantly different; at α = .03, p > α so the null is accepted and they are not — the same data give opposite conclusions purely by moving a threshold the investigator chose, which is why alpha must be set BEFORE the analysis
The test cannot be re-run with a different alpha
Lowering alpha makes significance easier to achieve
A p-value of .037 is not significant at any alpha
rationale:
This is the demonstration the lecture is built around. The p-value is a property of the data and does not move: .037 both times. What moves is the threshold.

p < α → reject the null → the two sets are significantly different. At α = .05, .037 < .05, so reject.
p > α → accept the null → not significantly different. At α = .03, .037 > .03, so accept.

His summary: in a simple sleight of hand Rick has gone from rejecting to accepting the null hypothesis from the identical two sets of data, simply by changing the threshold. He quotes Twain — facts are stubborn things, but statistics are pliable.

Hence the discipline: alpha is declared before the analysis, which is what study pre-registration exists to enforce.

The trap: “lowering alpha makes significance easier” is backwards. A lower alpha is a stricter threshold and makes significance HARDER — which is precisely how Rick rescued his instrument.

stem: What is a Type I error, and why did Rick particularly want to avoid one?
options: Failing to detect a real difference; he would have missed a fault in his instrument
Rejecting a true null hypothesis
Choosing the wrong statistical test
Using a sample size below 30
Reporting a p-value without an alpha
rationale:
A Type I error occurs when we decide there is a significant difference between two samples when in fact there is not — rejecting a null hypothesis that is true. A false positive.

Rick's null hypothesis was that there is no significant difference between the two samples, and any observed difference is due to sampling or experimental error. Since he re-made the solutions and cleaned the equipment, the only thing carried over was the Spinometer itself — so a “difference” would be an indictment of his instrument's reproducibility, and his hopes for promotion rode on it.

His test choice follows the same logic: a two-tailed independent-samples t-test — independent because nothing carried over, two-tailed because he could not predict whether the second mean would be higher or lower.

The trap: the first option describes a Type II error, failing to detect a real difference. Type I = false alarm; Type II = missed detection.

context: His spin-angle box plot reports: minimum 2.00 · 1st quartile 3.36 · median 3.855 · 3rd quartile 4.28 · maximum 5.34, with mean 3.823 and mode 3.98.
stem: Answer his four questions from the box plot, then state what the mean-vs-median comparison suggests.
rationale:
Largest and smallest values: maximum 5.34, minimum 2.00. Range = 3.34.

Inter-quartile range: Q3 − Q1 = 4.28 − 3.36 = 0.92. The IQR is the spread of the middle half of the distribution — quartiles cut the data into four equal parts of 25% each.

50% of the data is less than what value? The median, 3.855 — that is what a median is.

75% of the data is greater than what value? The 1st quartile, 3.36. Below Q1 lies 25%, so above it lies 75%.
   min      Q1     median     Q3      max
   2.00    3.36    3.855     4.28    5.34
     |--25%--|--25%--|--25%--|--25%--|
Mean 3.823 vs median 3.855: close but not equal, with the mean slightly BELOW the median — a hint of mild left skew, consistent with the low outlier at 2.00 pulling the mean down. In a perfectly symmetric Gaussian they would coincide.

The habit worth building: box-plot questions are answered by asking what fraction lies on each side of this line, not by recalling definitions. Each of the four segments is 25%, so any percentage question maps onto a boundary.

stem: Which statement about the Gaussian distribution and its summary statistics is correct?
options: A Gaussian distribution is characterised by its mode and range
A Gaussian distribution is characterised by a mean and a standard deviation, where a small SD means values cluster closely about the mean and a large SD means they are spread farther from it
A Gaussian distribution has no standard deviation because it is perfectly symmetric about its mean, so dispersion has to be described by the range instead in any dataset that follows it closely
Gaussian data are always skewed to the right
The chi-square distribution is a special case of the Gaussian
rationale:
Mean and standard deviation are the two parameters — the mean fixes where the distribution sits and the SD fixes how wide it is. Small SD → values clustered closely about the mean; large SD → spread farther away.

Recognising the Gaussian shape in his histogram is what licensed everything downstream: the t-test assumes approximately normal data, so “that nice Gaussian appearance” was not an aesthetic observation.

He notes there are other probability distribution functions — chi-square being one — which is a separate distribution, not a special case of the normal.

The trap: “symmetric, therefore no standard deviation” confuses symmetry with spread. Two Gaussians can share a mean and be perfectly symmetric while differing enormously in width — and that difference is the entire point of quoting an SD.

stem: Which figures does he give for the clinical footprint of genetics?
options: Genetic disease is rare enough that a general practitioner will rarely encounter it, so the figures he gives relate to specialist referral centres rather than to ordinary practice, and the proportion of admissions attributable to congenital anomaly is well under one percent in most hospitals

About 30% of pediatric hospital admissions relate to a congenital anomaly, ~11% of pediatric and ~12% of adult admissions are for genetic disorders, 10% of adult chronic disease has a significant genetic component, and 5–10% of common cancers have an inherited susceptibility
Genetic disorders account for fewer than 1% of all hospital admissions
Only pediatricians need to understand genetics
Genetic disease affects fewer than 100,000 Americans
rationale:
He opens by naming three misconceptions — we can't cure a gene defect so what's the use, this is so rare I'll never see it, these syndromes all look the same — and answers them with numbers.

~30% of pediatric hospital admissions relate to a congenital anomaly; 11% of pediatric and 12% of adult admissions are for genetic causes; 10% of adult chronic disease (heart, diabetes, arthritis) has a significant genetic component; 5–10% of common cancers have inherited susceptibility; 50% of cognitive impairment has a genetic basis. Collectively, >15,000 recognised disorders affecting 25–30 million Americans. And ~70% of adults say they would ask their primary care physician first about a family genetic disorder.

His answer to why bother diagnosing: it is essential for management, early recognition prevents complications through pre-emptive screening, and it enables genetic counselling — recurrence risks, alternatives such as adoption, at-risk testing for relatives, and avoiding unnecessary evaluations in unaffected family members.

The trap: “individually rare” is true and “collectively rare” is not — that gap is the entire point of the section.

stem: Match trisomy to its distinguishing features. Which line is correct?
options: Trisomy 21 — rocker-bottom feet, clenched hands, prominent occiput
Trisomy 18 (Edwards) — feeble activity, hypertonia, rocker-bottom feet, prominent occiput, tightly clenched hands
Trisomy 13 (Patau) — congenital heart disease in 40%, requiring echocardiography in all
Trisomy 21 (Down) — cyclopia, proboscis and polydactyly
Trisomy 18 — elfin facies and a chatty personality
rationale:
Edwards (trisomy 18): feeble activity, hypertonia, rocker-bottom feet, prominent occiput, tightly clenched hands.
Patau (trisomy 13): severe motor and cognitive delay with striking midline defects — cyclopia, proboscis, polydactyly of all extremities.
Down (trisomy 21): distinctive dysmorphic features allowing diagnosis at birth, developmental delay obvious by the end of the first year, and — the actionable one — congenital heart disease in about 40% of liveborns, so every one should have an echocardiogram.

That echo recommendation is the kind of detail exams like, because it is a management decision that follows directly from a diagnosis.

The trap: the distractors rotate correct features onto the wrong trisomy. Hook one memorable feature to each: 21 → heart, 18 → clenched hands and rocker-bottom feet, 13 → midline/cyclopia.

stem: A male has testicular atrophy, gynecomastia, a eunuchoid body shape and female hair distribution. Which karyotype fits, and where does the extra chromosome come from?
options: 47,XXY
rationale:
Klinefelter, 47,XXY. His keyed answer. The extra X comes from mother or father with about equal chance, and his emphasis is that the presence of the Y is the decisive factor in male development — one Y makes a male regardless of how many Xs are present.

Clinical course: patients are tall and thin with relatively long legs and appear physically normal before puberty; then signs of hypogonadism appear, the testes remain small and secondary sexual characteristics stay underdeveloped unless treated with exogenous testosterone. Usually infertile.

The trap: the pre-pubertal normality is why the diagnosis is often missed — the phenotype is time-dependent, so a normal childhood examination does not exclude it.

stem: He insists that Turner syndrome is a phenotype, not a karyotype. What does he mean, and what are the features?
options: Every Turner patient is 45,X without exception; the phrase about phenotype refers only to the variable severity seen between patients with that identical karyotype, and no mosaic or structural variant has ever been reported in a patient who meets the full clinical criteria for the syndrome as he defines them in the lecture

Only about 55% are monosomy X (45,X); the rest are mosaic 45,X/46,XX (10%), isochromosome 46,X,i(X) (20%), ring 46,X,r(X) (5%) or deletion 46,X,del(Xp) (5%) — the shared features are lymphedema at birth, webbed neck, short stature (average 145 cm without growth hormone) and absent secondary sexual characteristics
Turner syndrome affects males and females equally
Turner syndrome is caused by an extra X chromosome
The karyotype is always normal; the diagnosis is clinical only
rationale:
Several different chromosomal routes converge on one clinical picture — which is why the phenotype is the diagnosis and the karyotype merely explains it. His distribution: 45,X 55% · mosaic 45,X/46,XX 10% · isochromosome 46,X,i(X) 20% · ring 46,X,r(X) 5% · deletion 46,X,del(Xp) 5% · other 5%. Note the last four are exactly the structural abnormalities from L005.

Features: lymphedema at birth is the tip-off, webbed neck, short stature — average 145 cm (4'10") without growth hormone, and absent secondary sexual characteristics, which is what brings many to attention in the early teens; estrogen therapy at puberty is required to induce them.

His conceptual question is worth carrying: why does 45,X have a phenotype at all, if the second X is normally inactivated? Because a second sex chromosome, X or Y, is needed — so it must express genes that escape inactivation.

The trap: “always 45,X” is the textbook simplification, and 45% of cases are something else.

context: A 10-year-old has periorbital puffiness, a large mouth and small chin giving an elfin appearance, short stature, microcephaly, an aortic stenosis repaired in infancy, treated hypercalcaemia, mild cognitive delay, and an unusually friendly, chatty manner with everyone in the office.
stem: You order a routine chromosome analysis. What result do you expect, and why?
options: Trisomy 13
A normal karyotype
Trisomy 18
Triploidy
A karyotype containing XXY
rationale:
A normal karyotype. His keyed answer, and the point of the question. The picture — periorbital fullness, elfin face, and what he calls a “bar-room” charming/chatty personality — is Williams syndrome, caused by a microdeletion at 7q11.23 that is too small to detect by routine karyotyping. You need FISH or chromosome microarray. Every other option listed would be easily visible on a karyogram.

The mechanism ties the features together: the deleted region contains the elastin gene, a connective tissue protein, which is thought to account for much of the phenotype including the cardiac problems such as supravalvular aortic stenosis. Also characteristic: “stellate” lace-like iris, wide mouth with a full drooping lower lip, and a noted proclivity for music.

The trap: the question tests test selection, not syndrome recognition. Recognising Williams and then ordering the test that cannot see it is the clinical error being examined.

context: A 5-year-old girl has nasal, poorly intelligible speech, a repaired cleft palate, a repaired heart defect, long slender fingers, and a facial appearance unlike the rest of her family.
stem: Which disorder is most likely?
options: Cri-du-chat syndrome (5p deletion)
Down syndrome (trisomy 21)
Velocardiofacial syndrome (22q11.2 deletion)
Williams syndrome (7q11 deletion)
Wolf-Hirschhorn syndrome (4p deletion)
rationale:
Velocardiofacial syndrome — also called DiGeorge, Shprintzen, or Sedláčková syndrome — a microdeletion at 22q11.2. His keyed answer.

The name encodes the triad: velo (palate) + cardio + facial. His features are exactly the stem: cleft lip, cleft palate or submucosal cleft producing hypernasal speech, conotruncal heart defects, broad tubular nose, small chin, long slender fingers — plus thymic aplasia with immune deficiency.

Contrast the other deletion syndromes in his set: Wolf-Hirschhorn (4p16.3) — profound cognitive impairment, ocular hypertelorism, broad or beaked nose, micrognathia, cleft lip/palate. Cri-du-chat (5p) — the weak high-pitched “cat cry” in the newborn, with microcephaly, micrognathia, hypertelorism, epicanthal folds, low-set ears.

The trap: as he notes in his own answer, features overlap between these syndromes — several involve cleft palate and hypertelorism. The discriminator here is the combination of hypernasal speech with a conotruncal heart defect.

stem: Which syndrome is due to mutations in the fibrillin gene, and what makes it different in kind from the others in this lecture?
options: Edwards syndrome
Marfan syndrome
Patau syndrome
Turner syndrome
Wolf-Hirschhorn syndrome
rationale:
Marfan syndrome — mutations in fibrillin (FBN-1) at 15q21.1. His keyed answer with his own reasoning: every other syndrome listed involves too much or missing genetic material from an extra chromosome or a deletion; Marfan has a full complement of genetic information that has been altered — a missense mutation (single nucleotide change altering an amino acid) or a nonsense mutation (premature termination). Over 600 FBN-1 mutations are described, mostly missense.

Mechanism to phenotype: fibrillin is an extracellular matrix protein that scaffolds elastin deposition in connective tissue, so the systems affected are the ones that depend on elastic connective tissue — skeletal, cardiovascular, optic, and the lumbosacral dural sac.

His Measurable Outcome E is the inheritance profile: autosomal dominant, 100% penetrant at some point in life, with variable expressivity and variable age of onset — which is exactly the L014 vocabulary applied to one disease.

The trap: knowing Marfan clinically and missing that it is being contrasted as a category — single gene versus chromosomal.

stem: The age of onset of Huntington disease becomes progressively earlier in successive generations. What is this, and what is its molecular basis?
options: Genomic imprinting caused by progressive promoter methylation
Genetic anticipation caused by expansion of an unstable trinucleotide repeat
Variable expressivity caused by random X-inactivation
Locus heterogeneity caused by new genes contributing each generation
Reduced penetrance caused by age-dependent loss of the mutant allele
rationale:
Genetic anticipation: increased frequency of affected relatives, increased severity, or earlier age of onset in successive generations. His keyed answer for the molecular basis is an increase in the number of repeats of certain trinucleotides, with the instability attributed to stuttering of DNA polymerase during replication or dysfunctional DNA repair.

His historical note is a good reasoning check: anticipation was long dismissed as “bias of ascertainment” — severely affected people get noticed, mildly affected ones have more children. That was a genuinely reasonable alternative explanation, and it was wrong; the repeats really do expand.

The trap: the imprinting option is the neighbouring topic in the same lecture, and both are parent-of-origin-flavoured phenomena. Anticipation changes across generations because the DNA physically lengthens; imprinting changes because methylation marks are reset.

stem: How do Fragile X and Huntington disease differ in the location of their repeat expansion, and what does that predict about the protein?
options: Fragile X is coding and produces polyglutamine; Huntington is non-coding
Fragile X is non-coding; Huntington is coding and produces a polyglutamine tract
Both expansions are coding and therefore produce polyglutamine tracts
Both expansions are non-coding and silence their genes by methylation
Both occur in promoters, but only Huntington alters transcript abundance
rationale:
His Measurable Outcome G asks exactly this. Of the ~15 clinically significant repeat disorders, the split is:
Non-coding expansions — Fragile X syndrome, myotonic dystrophy. The repeat lies outside the reading frame, so the protein sequence is unchanged; the damage is to expression or RNA handling.
Coding (exonic) expansions — Huntington disease. Most are repeats of the codon CAG, giving a polyglutamine tract in the protein — an abnormal protein rather than an absent one, which is why these tend to be dominant and involve toxic gain of function.

The trap: the two disorders are always taught together, so the pairing is the question. Anchor on CAG = glutamine = coding = Huntington, and put Fragile X on the other side.

stem: Which syndrome results when the egg-derived allele at chromosome 15q11 carries a deletion, and what is its phenotype?
options: Prader-Willi syndrome — neonatal hypotonia and poor feeding followed later by hyperphagia and obesity, with the egg-derived allele being the one that is lost in this condition rather than the sperm-derived one at that particular locus

Angelman syndrome — normal at birth then progressive microcephaly, severe cognitive delay with no speech onset, gait ataxia (once called “happy puppet”), abnormal EEG with seizures usually by age 3, sometimes albinism
Fragile X syndrome
Marfan syndrome
Turner syndrome
rationale:
Angelman syndrome. His keyed answer: if the egg-derived allele is deleted, chromosome 15 expresses only the sperm-derived imprint — and that is Angelman. Same rule as L012, from the other direction.

Angelman: normal at birth, then progressive microcephaly, severe cognitive delay with no speech onset, gait ataxia (the old “happy puppet” name), abnormal EEG with seizures usually by age 3, sometimes albinism.

Prader-Willi (only the egg-derived imprint present) is the mirror: neonatal hypotonia — which he warns looks a lot like trisomy 21, don't be fooled — poor feeding and failure to thrive to age 2, then voracious eating and food-stealing, short stature, small hands and feet, hypogonadism, microcephaly, obesity, sometimes albinism, inability to regurgitate, and being notably good at puzzles.

The trap: the two syndromes share a chromosome region and sometimes albinism, and the parent-of-origin assignment is the whole answer. Read which parent's copy is LOST, then ask which parent's genes were doing the work there.

stem: Which statement about multifactorial inheritance is true?
options: It always involves many genes combined with environmental variables
It may demonstrate a threshold of liability for phenotypic expression in an individual
Down syndrome is a classic example
Recurrence risk decreases as more family members are affected
Recurrence risk decreases if the affected individual is of the less commonly affected sex
rationale:
His keyed answer. The clinical observation that defines multifactorial inheritance: conditions that recur in families at an incidence higher than chance predicts, but do not follow Mendelian patterns. The manifestation itself is often either/or, while the individual's liability shows a threshold effect.

Each distractor is wrong in an instructive way. “Always many genes” overstates — it may involve many genes or just one gene in combination with environmental variables. Down syndrome is chromosomal, not multifactorial. And both recurrence-risk options are backwards: risk increases with more affected family members and increases when the affected individual is of the less commonly affected sex.

Worth noting what “environment” covers: teratogens (medications, maternal conditions, alcohol), sex hormones — and frequently a non-genetic contributor that is simply unknown.

stem: Concordance for BMI is 0.95 in MZ twins and 0.53 in DZ twins. Calculate heritability and state what it does and does not tell you.
options: H = 0.42; BMI is not influenced by genes
H = 1.48; BMI is entirely genetic
H = 0.84, which proves a large number of genes are responsible
Heritability cannot be calculated from concordance rates
rationale:
H = 2(CMZ − CDZ) = 2(0.95 − 0.53) = 0.84. His keyed answer: a pretty strong genetic component — but it is not all genetic.

The formula's logic: MZ twins share ~100% of genes, DZ twins ~50%, so the gap between the concordance rates is what genes contribute; doubling it scales for the halved sharing. A purely genetic trait gives ~100% MZ and ~50% DZ; a purely environmental one gives similar rates in both.

His three explicit limits, each a distractor here: heritability tells you nothing about how many genes are involved, how much each contributes, or the mode of inheritance. Nor does it identify a mechanism such as a teratogen.

The trap: forgetting the factor of 2, which gives 0.42 and understates it by half.

stem: Which concordance pattern best represents an environmentally caused phenotype, and which of his examples proves that high concordance does not mean high heritability?
options: MZ 100% / DZ 25%; fingerprints, because high MZ concordance proves environmental causation
MZ 25% / DZ 25%; measles, because similar concordance can coexist with low heritability
MZ 65% / DZ 27%; schizophrenia, because any MZ–DZ gap proves purely environmental causation
MZ 100% / DZ 100%; multiple sclerosis, because equal concordance proves high heritability
MZ 0% / DZ 0%; cleft lip, because absent concordance proves a shared exposure
rationale:
Equal concordance in MZ and DZ twins means genes are contributing nothing to the difference — the trait tracks the shared environment, which DZ twins share just as much as MZ twins do. His keyed answer is the 25%/25% row.

Measles is his worked case for Outcome E: MZ 0.95, DZ 0.87 — both very high, so twins nearly always share it — yet H = 2(0.95 − 0.87) = 0.16. High concordance rate does not always equal “highly genetic”. Living in the same house during an outbreak explains it.

Compare from his table: fingerprints 0.95/0.49 → H 0.92; schizophrenia 0.47/0.12 → H 0.70; spina bifida 0.72/0.33 → H 0.78; cleft lip/palate 0.38/0.08 → H 0.60; multiple sclerosis 0.28/0.03 → H 0.50. Note that MS has LOW concordance and moderate heritability — the reverse trap.

The trap: reading the MZ number alone. Only the GAP between MZ and DZ carries information about genes.

stem: Siblings of glaucoma patients have glaucoma 25% of the time; siblings of controls, 2%. Which mode of inheritance does this best fit?
options: Autosomal dominant
Autosomal recessive
X-linked recessive
Multifactorial inheritance
It cannot be determined from these data
rationale:
Multifactorial. His keyed answer. The reasoning is his definition applied directly: the condition recurs in families far above the population rate — 25% versus 2%, a more than ten-fold excess — so it is clearly familial, yet 25% fits no clean Mendelian expectation.

Sanity-check the alternatives: autosomal dominant sibling risk would be ~50%; autosomal recessive ~25% with two carrier parents, but across 100 unrelated families that pattern would be extraordinary for a common adult disease; X-linked recessive would show a marked male excess, which is not described.

The trap: 25% is the autosomal recessive number, so the figure itself baits that answer. Look at the study design — an aggregate across many unrelated families with a common condition is the signature of multifactorial inheritance, not of a single recessive gene.

stem: Explain the threshold model and why cleft lip is used as an example rather than height.
options: Both height and cleft lip follow the threshold model identically

Height is a quantitative trait measured on a continuous scale with a bell-shaped distribution; cleft lip is present-or-absent, so what is bell-shaped is not the phenotype but the number of predisposing genetic and environmental factors — the disease appears only when an individual's liability exceeds a threshold
The threshold model applies only to traits with a bell-shaped phenotype
Cleft lip is Mendelian and height is multifactorial

The threshold is the number of affected family members needed before a diagnosis can be made, so cleft lip is used as the example because it requires a specific count of affected relatives, whereas height cannot be diagnosed at all and therefore has no threshold of any kind attached to it anywhere in the model as described
rationale:
Two shapes of multifactorial trait. Quantitative traits — height, blood pressure — are measured on a continuous scale and are bell-shaped in a large enough population. But cleft lip, cleft palate and omphalocele are either/or: there is no spectrum of cleft.

The threshold model resolves it: what is bell-shaped is the number of predisposing factors, genetic and environmental, that an individual carries — from a few to many. The disease manifests only when an excessive number are present, i.e. when liability exceeds the threshold. So liability is continuous while the phenotype is binary.

Note his related distinction: polygenic = variation from the combined effect of multiple genes; multifactorial = when environmental influences also contribute.

The trap: assuming a continuously distributed cause requires a continuously distributed effect. The threshold is precisely what converts one into the other.

stem: Hip dysplasia has a male-to-female ratio of 1:6. Which child has the lowest risk?
options: A female born to an affected female
A male born to an affected female
A female born to an affected male
A male born to an affected male
All four have equal risk
rationale:
Two rules combine, and both must be applied.

Rule 1 — the sex of the CHILD. The more commonly affected sex has the LOWER threshold and therefore always the higher risk. Hip dysplasia is 6× commoner in females, so a female child is always at higher risk than a male child.

Rule 2 — the sex of the AFFECTED PARENT. If the affected individual is of the less commonly affected sex (here, male), they had a higher threshold to cross, so more predisposing factors must be present in that family — and the recurrence risk to all relatives is higher.

Lowest risk therefore needs both to point down: a male child (higher threshold) of an affected female (lower-threshold parent, so less family burden implied).

His pyloric stenosis table shows the same arithmetic, males being more commonly affected at 1/200: affected male → brothers 4%, sisters 2%; affected FEMALE → brothers 10%, sisters 3%. Note that brothers outrank sisters in both columns — the lower-threshold sex always carries the higher risk — while an affected female roughly doubles everyone's risk.

The trap: applying only one rule. Ask both which sex is the child and which sex was the affected relative.

stem: What raises the recurrence risk of a multifactorial condition in a family, and what is his ventricular septal defect example?
options: Only the number of affected relatives matters

Risk rises if the affected relative is CLOSE, if MORE family members are affected, if the disease is MORE SEVERE in that family, and if the affected individual is of the LESS commonly affected sex — VSD recurrence is 3% with one affected child, 10% with two, and nearly 25% with three
Risk falls as more family members are affected

Risk is fixed at the population incidence regardless of family history, because multifactorial conditions have no familial clustering, and the number or closeness of affected relatives makes no difference to the recurrence risk quoted to any family, nor does the severity of the condition in the proband
Only severity matters; the number of affected relatives is irrelevant
rationale:
All four factors point at the same underlying quantity: how much genetic and environmental liability this family carries. A close relative shares more genes and more environment; more affected members, more severe expression (hypoplastic left heart versus ASD), and an affected member of the less commonly affected sex all imply a heavier burden.

His VSD numbers make it concrete: 3% with one affected child, 10% with two, nearly 25% with three — and his own aside is the useful one: think about the latter — this is almost like families with an autosomal recessive form of VSD. A sufficiently loaded family starts to look Mendelian.

He also flags that these are empiric figures from recurrence studies, generally difficult to quantify and varying between populations — not derived from a model.

The trap: importing the Mendelian intuition that past children do not change future risk. In multifactorial disease, each additional affected child is evidence about the family's liability, so the risk estimate genuinely moves.

stem: What is the recurrence risk for an open neural tube defect in a first-degree relative, and what is the folic acid recommendation?
options: Recurrence is 1/500, exactly the same as the population risk, since a neural tube defect in one child says nothing about the risk in the next, and folic acid supplementation has never been shown to be effective in preventing recurrence in any randomised trial reported to date anywhere in the literature

Population risk is 1/500–1/1000 and recurrence rises to about 3% (1/33) in a first-degree relative; 0.4 mg folic acid for all women and 4 mg with a history of NTD, from one month before pregnancy through the first two months of gestation, potentially avoiding 50–70% of cases
Recurrence is 25%, consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance
Folic acid should be started only after pregnancy is confirmed
Neural tube defects are entirely environmental with no genetic contribution
rationale:
Spina bifida and anencephaly arise from failure of the neural tube to close at ~4 weeks' gestation. That single fact drives the whole recommendation: at four weeks many women do not yet know they are pregnant, which is why supplementation must start one month BEFORE conception and continue through the first two months.

Numbers: population risk 1/500–1/1000; first-degree relative ~3% (1/33). Dose 0.4 mg for all women, 4 mg with a prior NTD history — a ten-fold increase. Effect: 50–70% of open NTDs may be avoided.

This is the clearest case in the course of an environmental factor moving liability across a threshold — and it connects straight to the folate lecture, where THF supplies one-carbon units for nucleotide synthesis in the fastest-dividing tissue in the embryo.

The trap: starting folate at the first prenatal visit. By then the neural tube has already closed.

stem: Type I diabetes shows 35–40% MZ and 5–10% DZ concordance; type II shows ~59% MZ and ~27% DZ. What do these tell you, and what modifies risk in type I?
options: Type I diabetes is entirely genetic and type II entirely environmental, which is why the concordance rates differ between them, and heritability need not be computed for either since the answer is already known from the twin data

Both have substantial genetic components — H ≈ 0.6 for both — and type I risk is modified by HLA class II alleles DR3 and DR4: sibling risk may rise to 18% if both HLA haplotypes are shared and 20–25% if DR3/4
Neither shows any genetic contribution
Type II is Mendelian autosomal dominant in all families
Concordance rates cannot be compared between the two types
rationale:
Apply H = 2(CMZ − CDZ) to both: type I ≈ 2(0.375 − 0.075) = 0.60; type II ≈ 2(0.59 − 0.27) = 0.64. Substantial and similar genetic contributions — and critically, neither is anywhere near 1.0, so environment matters in both.

Type I: strong association with HLA class II alleles DR3 and DR4, over 20 other candidate genes, population risk 1/500, first-degree relative risk 1/14 for siblings and 1/25 for offspring. Risk is refined by HLA typing — sharing both haplotypes raises sibling risk to 18%, and DR3/4 to 20–25%; sharing neither lowers it.

Type II: obesity and lack of exercise are the environmental factors; population risk 6.2% in Caucasians, 10.2% in African Americans, up to 50% in some Native American groups; first-degree relatives at 2× risk. A few families carry rare autosomal dominant forms, but most are multifactorial.

The trap: the folk belief that type I is “the genetic one”. By concordance, type II is at least as heritable — the difference is that type II's environmental drivers are modifiable.

stem: What are the main limitations of twin studies, and what do adoption studies add?
options: Twin studies have no limitations worth noting, and adoption studies add nothing beyond what twin studies already establish, since separating genetic from environmental contributions is straightforward once concordance rates for both twin types are known in any population studied, which is why heritability estimates from twins are treated as definitive

MZ twins' environments may be more similar than DZ twins', post-fertilisation somatic mutations mean MZ twins are not entirely identical, and the in-utero environment may differ between MZ pairs; adoption studies help separate shared genes from shared environment, but are limited because the in-utero environment is never fully separated
Twin studies overestimate environmental effects only
Adoption studies are free of confounding
MZ twins share only 50% of their genes
rationale:
Every limitation attacks the assumption the method depends on — that MZ and DZ twins differ in genes but not in environment.

MZ environments may be MORE similar (dressed alike, treated alike, closer friendships), which inflates MZ concordance and so overstates heritability. Post-fertilisation somatic mutations mean MZ twins are not perfectly identical. And the in-utero environment may differ between MZ pairs — shared versus separate placentas, unequal blood supply.

Adoption studies attack this from the other side: compare adopted offspring of affected parents with adopted offspring of unaffected parents, so genes and rearing environment are separated. Their limitation is that the in-utero environment is never separated — the biological mother supplied nine months of it.

The trap: “MZ twins share only 50%” is the DZ figure. MZ ~100%, DZ ~50% — and that difference is the entire basis of the calculation.

stem: Red blood cell membranes are impermeable to solute X. Placing them in which solution makes them shrivel, and what is the driving force?
options: A hypertonic solution; water leaves the cell down its water-concentration gradient
A hypotonic solution; water leaves the cell down its osmotic gradient
An isotonic solution; water leaves while impermeant solute enters
A hypertonic solution; impermeant solute leaves and pulls water with it
A hypotonic solution; extracellular osmotic pressure compresses the cell
rationale:
Hypertonic means the solution has a higher solute concentration than the cytosol, and therefore a lower water concentration. Osmosis is the movement of water from higher [H₂O] to lower [H₂O] across a membrane permeable to water but not solute, driven by osmotic pressure and using aquaporins. So water leaves and the cell shrinks.

Her three-beaker set: hypertonic → cells shrink · isotonic → no change · hypotonic → cells swell.

Osmosis sits under passive transport (“diffusion”), energy-independent, alongside simple diffusion — which follows Fick's law: the rate is proportional to the concentration difference across the membrane and inversely proportional to its thickness.

The trap: tracking the solute instead of the water. The membrane is impermeable to solute — only water can move, so name the direction water goes and the answer follows.

stem: Which statement most accurately describes a carrier protein, and how do carriers differ from channels?
options: It may carry out passive OR active transport, binds its solute on one side and releases it on the other after a conformational change, is saturable and competitively inhibitable, and does not form a pore — whereas channel transport is always passive, may form a pore, does not bind its cargo, and is about 1,000 times faster
It only carries out passive transport
It always forms a hydrophilic pore
It is another name for an ion channel

It transports substances about 1,000 times faster than a channel, because binding its solute on one side and releasing it on the other is quicker than allowing free diffusion through an open pore, and this is what makes carriers rather than channels the route used whenever a high rate of throughput is required in any tissue of the body
rationale:
Her keyed answer, and she flags the crucial clause herself: a carrier may involve passive OR active transport, while channel-mediated transport is ALWAYS passive and cannot be coupled to an energy source.

Carrier mechanism: high-affinity binding of the solute on one side → conformational change → release on the other side. Hence structural specificity, saturability and competitive inhibition — the same behaviour as an enzyme, for the same reason: a finite number of binding sites.

Channel mechanism: a conformational change in the subunits creates a pore, shielding ions from the hydrophobic tails of the bilayer. Channels do not bind what they transport, which is why they are ~1,000× faster. Driving force is always downhill, along the electrochemical gradient.

The trap: “only passive” is the answer for channels and is the single most attractive wrong option. The Na⁺/K⁺/ATPase is a carrier — an actively pumping one.

stem: Channel pores are not continuously open. What controls them, and which examples does she give?
options: Pores are always open once formed

Gates — either voltage differences (voltage-gated Na⁺, K⁺ and Ca²⁺ channels) or ligand-receptor binding (ligand-gated, also called transmitter-gated or chemically-gated, e.g. acetylcholine-gated Na⁺ channels)

ATP hydrolysis opens and closes each pore, so every channel is effectively a pump that spends energy each time it changes state, and neither voltage nor ligand binding has any part in controlling when a channel is open
Carrier proteins open channel gates
Osmotic pressure alone
rationale:
Pores may be open or closed but not continuously open, and the conformational change that opens them is controlled by gates. Two kinds:
Voltage-gated — opened by a change in membrane potential: voltage-gated Na⁺, K⁺ and Ca²⁺ channels.
Ligand-gated (also transmitter-gated or chemically-gated) — opened by ligand binding: acetylcholine-gated Na⁺ channels.

Gating is what makes a channel a signalling device rather than a hole. Note that gating does not make transport active — energy controls the gate, never the direction of flow, which is always downhill.

The trap: the ATP option. Gating and pumping are different things, and this distinction is exactly what separates a channel from a primary active transporter.

stem: Which set are all hereditary channelopathies she names?
options: Long QT syndrome, polycystic kidney disease, malignant hyperthermia, periodic paralysis (hyper- and hypokalemic), cystic fibrosis
Marfan syndrome, Down syndrome, Turner syndrome
Diabetes mellitus, hypertension, obesity
Pellagra, scurvy, beriberi
Bloom syndrome, xeroderma pigmentosum, Fanconi anaemia
rationale:
Her six, all caused by mutations in channel proteins: long QT syndrome (cardiac K⁺/Na⁺ channels) · polycystic kidney disease · malignant hyperthermia (ryanodine receptor, a Ca²⁺ release channel) · periodic paralysis, hyperkalemic and hypokalemic · cystic fibrosis.

Cystic fibrosis is the one worth noticing, because it has already appeared twice in this course as an example of allelic heterogeneity and pleiotropy — and here it turns up as a channelopathy, since CFTR is a chloride channel. One gene, three lectures, three different framings.

The unifying clinical logic: channelopathies produce episodic, excitability-related disease — arrhythmia, paralysis, a hypermetabolic crisis under anaesthesia — because channels govern how fast a tissue can change state.
