Phosphofructokinase 1 (PFK1)
Phosphoglucoisomerase
Glucokinase or hexokinase; the tests cannot distinguish them
rationale:
Both isozymes phosphorylate glucose using ATP, so the discriminator is the product inhibition: hexokinase is switched off by glucose 6-phosphate, which stops a muscle cell importing more glucose than it can use.

The trap: glucokinase is deliberately not product-inhibited, because the liver must clear all the glucose arriving in the portal blood and either burn it or store it.

stem: In two of the last three reactions of glycolysis the phosphate group is switched from carbon 3 to carbon 2 and the molecule is then dehydrated to form an enol. Why are these steps necessary?
rationale:
To turn the phosphate into a good leaving group. An alcohol phosphate is a poor leaving group, so 3-phosphoglycerate cannot be used to phosphorylate ADP. Moving the phosphate to C2 and then dehydrating raises its leaving-group potential to that of an enol phosphate (phosphoenolpyruvate), which is now energetic enough to drive ATP synthesis at pyruvate kinase.

These steps do a second job as well: when the phosphate finally leaves, the enol collapses to a keto group on the alpha carbon. That alpha-keto arrangement is what allows the carboxyl group to be removed later by the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex, should the pyruvate reach the mitochondrion.

stem: Briefly explain why molecular oxygen (O₂) controls the glycolytic pathway, that is, aerobic versus anaerobic glycolysis.
rationale:
Everything follows from whether the ETC can run.

Without oxygen: the ETC stops, so oxidative phosphorylation makes no ATP and the TCA cycle also halts, because its NADH and FADH₂ have nowhere to unload and NAD⁺/FAD are never regenerated. Glycolysis becomes the only pathway still yielding ATP directly. But glycolysis itself needs cytosolic NAD⁺ for GAPDH, and the shuttles cannot work with the ETC down. So an eleventh step is added: lactate dehydrogenase re-oxidizes NADH to NAD⁺, letting glycolysis continue.

With oxygen: the ETC runs, so the malate-aspartate and glycerol phosphate shuttles carry the electrons of cytosolic NADH into the mitochondrion and return NAD⁺ to the cytosol. GAPDH keeps working, lactate is not needed, and the pyruvate goes on to PDH and the TCA cycle.

stem: A 22-year-old student begins chewing a piece of bread. As the bread is mixed with saliva, which enzyme begins the digestion of its starch content?
options: Lactase
Maltase
Pancreatic α-amylase
Salivary α-amylase
Sucrase
rationale:
Salivary α-amylase starts hydrolysing the α(1→4) bonds of starch in the mouth, producing shorter dextrins.

The trap: its contribution is brief, because gastric HCl inactivates it once the bolus is swallowed. Maltase, sucrase, and lactase are brush-border disaccharidases that act much later, on the products.

stem: A 45-year-old patient undergoes pancreatic surgery and subsequently develops difficulty digesting carbohydrates. Which enzyme normally provides the major enzymatic digestion of dietary starch in the small intestine?
options: Salivary amylase
Pancreatic α-amylase
Lactase
Isomaltase
Sucrase
rationale:
Pancreatic α-amylase secreted into the duodenum does the bulk of starch digestion, which is why losing pancreatic exocrine function impairs it.

The trap: salivary amylase starts the job but is destroyed in the stomach; the disaccharidases finish the job but cannot attack polysaccharides.

sourceRef: Wilkins Problem Set (007 Vitamins) Q8 distractor E, expanded
stem: An adult develops bloating, cramping, and osmotic diarrhoea within an hour of drinking milk. Which enzyme is deficient, and where does it normally act?
options: Lactase, at the intestinal brush border
Sucrase, in pancreatic secretions
Salivary amylase, in the mouth
Pancreatic amylase, in the duodenal lumen
Isomaltase, in the gastric mucosa
rationale:
Lactose is a disaccharide, so it cannot be absorbed intact; lactase on the enterocyte brush border must split it into glucose and galactose. Undigested lactose stays osmotically active and is fermented by colonic bacteria.

The trap: the disaccharidases are membrane-bound enzymes of the enterocyte surface, not pancreatic or gastric secretions.

stem: A patient presents with lack of energy and very low haemoglobin. His red blood cells show a high level of phosphoenolpyruvate with little pyruvate produced and decreased ATP. A mutation in which glycolytic enzyme best explains this?
options: Glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate dehydrogenase
Glucokinase
Phosphofructokinase
Enolase
Pyruvate kinase
rationale:
Substrate piles up immediately upstream of a block. PEP is the substrate of pyruvate kinase, so PEP accumulation with little pyruvate localizes the defect there; losing that step also costs the cell ATP, and red cells with no mitochondria cannot compensate, hence the haemolytic anaemia.

The trap: an enolase block would accumulate 2-phosphoglycerate instead, because enolase is the enzyme that makes PEP.

stem: A 19-year-old woman has been anaemic since birth. Analysis of her red blood cell glycolytic intermediates shows that all intermediates from glucose 6-phosphate onward are lower than normal. A mutation in which glycolytic enzyme best explains this?
options: Glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate dehydrogenase
Hexokinase
Phosphofructokinase
Phosphoglycerate kinase
Pyruvate kinase
rationale:
When everything downstream of and including G6P is low, the block must be at the step that produces G6P. In the red cell that step is hexokinase, which traps glucose on entry.

The trap: a block further down the pathway would raise the intermediates above it while lowering those below. Read the pattern, not just the lowest value.

stem: Two parents are carriers of the same autosomal recessive disorder. What is the probability that their next three children will all be unaffected?
rationale:
Each pregnancy independently carries a 3/4 chance of an unaffected child. The product rule for several future events gives (3/4)³ = 27/64.

The trap: the product rule applies only to predicting future events together. It is never used to revise the risk of one pregnancy on the basis of how earlier children turned out.

context: A 5-year-old child is being treated for acute lymphoblastic leukaemia with chemotherapy that includes cytosine arabinoside (cytarabine, araC), a nucleoside analog.
stem: Which of the following enzymes will incorporate this drug into growing chains of DNA?
options: RNA polymerase II
DNA polymerase
Primase
Ligase
Topoisomerase I
rationale:
AraC is a deoxycytidine analog. Once the cell phosphorylates it to the triphosphate, DNA polymerase accepts it as a substrate and inserts it into the growing strand, where its arabinose sugar stalls further extension.

The trap: the drug is given as a nucleoside because a charged nucleotide could not cross the membrane; it is the cell’s own kinases that activate it.

context: A prenatal patient presents for counselling at 15 weeks with a family history of a rare autosomal recessive lipodystrophy; her sister died of it. The condition occurs in 1 in 10,000,000 individuals. Consanguinity with her partner is denied.
stem: What is the risk to this couple's fetus of being affected?
rationale:
Three independent factors multiply. The patient is unaffected with two carrier parents, so she is a carrier with probability 2/3. For her partner, q² = 1/10,000,000 gives q = 1/3162, so the carrier frequency 2pq is about 1/1581. If both carry it, the chance both transmit is 1/4. Multiplying: (2/3)(1/1581)(1/4) = 1/9486.

The trap: the sister's diagnosis tells you about the patient's own risk, but her partner is from the general population, so only Hardy-Weinberg can supply his.

stem: A Caucasian woman has cystic fibrosis with two mutant alleles. The population incidence is 1 in 400 among Caucasians. She marries an unrelated Caucasian man. What is the likelihood that they will have a fetus affected with CF?
rationale:
q² = 1/400, so q = 1/20 and the carrier frequency 2pq is about 1/10. Because the mother is affected she transmits a mutant allele to every child, so her factor is 1. The father contributes (1/10 carrier) × (1/2 transmission) = 1/20.

The trap: do not put a 1/4 in this calculation. A 1/4 applies to carrier × carrier; here one parent is homozygous affected.

context: In a clinical study, 100 subjects are genotyped at a locus hypothesized to be associated with cancer: AA in 30, AB in 25, BB in 45.
stem: What is the frequency of the B allele?
rationale:
Count alleles directly: each AB contributes one B and each BB contributes two, giving 25 + 90 = 115 B alleles out of 200 total alleles in 100 diploid people, so 115/200 = 0.575.

The trap: Hardy-Weinberg is not needed and would be wrong to invoke here. The genotypes were counted, so the allele frequency is a matter of arithmetic, not of assuming equilibrium.

context: A birth defect results from a parasitic infection during pregnancy. A parasite resistance allele occurs in 20% of the population and is autosomal dominant.
stem: What percentage of the population is predicted to be resistant to the parasite?
rationale:
You are given p = 0.20, so q = 0.80. Because resistance is dominant, resistant people are both the homozygotes and the heterozygotes: p² + 2pq = 0.04 + 0.32 = 0.36.

The trap: 20% is the allele frequency, not the phenotype frequency, and 4% counts only the homozygotes. A dominant phenotype always needs the 2pq term as well.

stem: Among the African-American population the allele frequency of the sickle-cell mutation is about 4%. Assuming Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, what are the expected frequencies of affected individuals and of carriers?
options: Affected about 0.0016; carriers about 0.077
Affected about 0.04; carriers about 0.16
Affected about 0.0016; carriers about 0.0032
Affected about 0.08; carriers about 0.0016
Affected about 0.16; carriers about 0.48
rationale:
q = 0.04, so affected homozygotes are q² = 0.0016 and carriers are 2pq = 2(0.96)(0.04), about 0.077.

The trap: carriers outnumber affected individuals by roughly 2/q, which for a rare allele is a very large factor. That ratio is the whole reason carrier screening exists.

stem: The incidence of Tay-Sachs disease, an autosomal recessive disorder, is about 1/3600 in Ashkenazi Jewish populations. What is the carrier frequency in these populations?
rationale:
q² = 1/3600 gives q = 1/60. Carriers are 2pq, and with p close to 1 this is about 2/60 = 1/30.

The trap: 1/60 is the allele frequency, not the carrier frequency. For a rare recessive the carrier frequency is roughly twice the allele frequency.

stem: Familial hypercholesterolemia is autosomal dominant with a prevalence of about 1 in 400 in Caucasian populations. What is the mutant allele frequency, and what is the frequency of affected homozygotes?
options: Allele about 1/800; homozygotes about 1/640,000
Allele about 1/400; homozygotes about 1/160,000
Allele about 1/200; homozygotes about 1/40,000
Allele about 1/800; homozygotes about 1/1600
Allele about 1/20; homozygotes about 1/400
rationale:
For a rare dominant, essentially all affected people are heterozygotes, so 2pq = 1/400 with q close to 1 gives p = 1/800. Homozygotes are p² = 1/640,000.

The trap: for a dominant condition the disease frequency is 2pq, not p². Reaching for p² is the standard error, and it is why homozygous dominant disease is vanishingly rare.

stem: Hemophilia A, an X-linked disorder of coagulation, has a prevalence of about 1 per 10,000 in males but a much lower frequency among females. Which is the most likely explanation for this difference?
options: Females are less prone to mutation
Females are less likely to have coagulation problems
Females have two X chromosomes, whereas males have only one
Females can receive the disease gene only from their fathers, whereas males can receive it from either parent
X-inactivation in females selectively turns off the defective gene
rationale:
A male needs only the one mutant X to be affected, so the male frequency equals the allele frequency q. A female needs two, so her frequency is q². With q = 1/10,000 that predicts about 1 in 100,000,000 females.

The trap: X-inactivation is random, not selective; it cannot preferentially silence the mutant allele, though skewing can occasionally make a carrier symptomatic.

context: In some regions of Africa where malaria is endemic, the prevalence of G6PD deficiency, an X-linked recessive condition, is nearly 25% among males.
stem: Assuming Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, what are the allele frequencies and how does the frequency of affected females compare with affected males?
options: q = 0.25 and p = 0.75; affected females 0.0625, carrier females 0.375
q = 0.5 and p = 0.5; affected females 0.25, carrier females 0.5
q = 0.25 and p = 0.75; affected females 0.25, carrier females 0.75
q = 0.125 and p = 0.875; affected females 0.0156, carrier females 0.22
q = 0.0625 and p = 0.9375; affected females 0.25, carrier females 0.117
rationale:
For an X-linked trait the male frequency is the allele frequency, so q = 0.25 and p = 0.75. Affected females are q² = 0.0625 (1 in 16) and carriers are 2pq = 0.375.

The trap: when q is this large, affected females are not rare at all — the usual intuition that X-linked disease is a male problem depends on q being small.

context: A population shows the following genotype frequencies: A/A = 0.59, A/a = 0.19, a/a = 0.02.
stem: Is this population in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium?
options: Yes; the frequencies satisfy p² + 2pq + q² = 1
No; the genotype frequencies sum to only 0.80 rather than 1.0
Yes, but only if the population is small
No; because 2pq is smaller than p²
It cannot be determined without knowing the allele frequencies
rationale:
The three genotype frequencies must account for everyone. These sum to 0.80, so the population cannot be at equilibrium. Selection against homozygotes, assortative mating, or migration could explain it.

The trap: 2pq being smaller than p² is perfectly normal when one allele is common, so that observation proves nothing on its own. Check the sum first.

stem: The Old-Order Amish community in Pennsylvania arose from a small band of people with common religious beliefs who tended to marry within their faith. The frequency of maple-syrup urine disease among them is markedly higher than in the surrounding population. This most likely represents:
options: Reduced fitness
Founder effect
Random mating
Geographic stratification
Heterozygote advantage
rationale:
A founder effect: a small group carried an unrepresentative sample of alleles, and subsequent endogamy preserved those frequencies instead of diluting them into the wider population.

The trap: heterozygote advantage would require the carrier state to confer a survival benefit, as it does for sickle cell in malarial regions. Nothing here suggests MSUD carriers are advantaged.

stem: The frequency of an X-linked recessive trait among males is 0.0009 in a population at Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium. What is the frequency of the trait among females, and the expected carrier frequency?
options: Affected females about 1 in 1,250,000; carriers about 1 in 550
Affected females 0.0009; carriers 0.0018
Affected females about 1 in 550; carriers about 1 in 1,250,000
Affected females 0.03; carriers 0.06
Affected females 0.0018; carriers 0.0009
rationale:
q = 0.0009 because male frequency equals the allele frequency. Affected females are q² = 0.00000081, about 1 in 1,250,000. Carriers are 2pq = 0.0018, about 1 in 550.

The trap: squaring a small number makes it dramatically smaller, while doubling it barely changes it — which is why carriers outnumber affected females by more than a thousandfold.

context: A family has multiple members with a degenerative disorder of muscle; some affected individuals also have vision loss and migraines, while others are only mildly affected. All the children of affected women are affected; none of the children of affected men are affected.
stem: What is the BEST explanation for the variability observed in this family?
options: Allelic heterogeneity
Reduced penetrance
Locus heterogeneity
Heteroplasmy
Skewed X-inactivation
rationale:
Transmission exclusively through women identifies this as mitochondrial. Within that pattern, the varying severity is explained by heteroplasmy: cells carry a mixture of mutant and normal mitochondrial genomes, and different individuals and tissues sit at different mutant loads relative to the threshold for disease.

The trap: reduced penetrance is all-or-nothing and would not produce a graded range of severity within one family.

context: A 33-year-old man has microphthalmia, a narrow nose, absent teeth, sparse hair, and fusion of fingers 4 and 5 on both hands. Neurologic evaluation notes spasticity and speech difficulty.
stem: The condition this man has is BEST described as one that exhibits:
options: Pleiotropy
Allelic heterogeneity
Anticipation
Locus heterogeneity
rationale:
Pleiotropy is one mutant gene producing multiple, apparently unrelated effects across different organ systems — here eye, face, teeth, hair, limb, and nervous system.

The trap: allelic and locus heterogeneity describe several genotypes converging on one phenotype. Pleiotropy is the opposite direction: one genotype fanning out into many phenotypes.

context: Hereditary breast cancer is inherited as autosomal dominant with reduced penetrance. Females with a mutant allele have about an 80% lifetime risk of developing breast cancer. A woman has an affected mother and an affected maternal grandmother.
stem: What is this woman's lifetime risk of developing breast cancer?
rationale:
Two steps multiply: a 1/2 chance of inheriting the allele from her affected mother, then an 80% chance of expressing it. (1/2)(8/10) = 2/5.

The trap: the grandmother adds nothing once the mother is known to be affected — the mother's status already accounts for that branch of the pedigree. And 1/2 alone would ignore penetrance.

stem: A man and a woman each born with autosomal recessive hearing loss have children together; all the children have normal hearing. What is the BEST explanation?
options: Reduced penetrance
Variable expressivity
Locus heterogeneity
Allelic heterogeneity
Somatic mosaicism
rationale:
Locus heterogeneity: the parents are homozygous at two different deafness loci, say d1d1D2D2 and D1D1d2d2. Every child is then a double heterozygote, carrying one normal allele at each locus, and is affected at neither.

The trap: reduced penetrance is the tempting catch-all, but it would require every one of the children to escape by chance. Do not reach for penetrance whenever a pedigree breaks the expected rule.

stem: In a particular population, autosomal dominant retinoblastoma has a population frequency of 1/25,000. What is the allele frequency in this population?
rationale:
For a rare dominant, affected individuals are essentially all heterozygotes, so disease frequency = 2pq with q close to 1. Then 2p = 1/25,000 and p = 1/50,000.

The trap: 1/158 and 1/316 come from taking a square root, which is the recessive manoeuvre. Square roots belong to q², not to 2pq.

stem: A woman whose sister died with Tay-Sachs disease, an autosomal recessive condition, marries a man with no family history of it. The gene frequency of this condition is 1/60. What is the chance they will have an affected child?
rationale:
Both of the woman's parents must be carriers, and since she is unaffected her carrier risk is 2/3. The man comes from the general population, so his carrier risk is 2pq, about 1/30. Two carriers have a 1/4 chance per child. (2/3)(1/30)(1/4) = 1/180.

The trap: 1/60 is the allele frequency; using it directly as the man's carrier risk halves the answer.

stem: A woman with hemochromatosis marries a man with no such history. Hemochromatosis is autosomal recessive with a carrier frequency of 1/8. What is the chance this couple will have an affected child?
rationale:
The woman is affected, so she transmits a mutant allele to every child. The man is a carrier with probability 1/8 and would transmit with probability 1/2: (1/8)(1/2) = 1/16.

The trap: the carrier frequency is given directly here, so there is no Hardy-Weinberg step to perform. Read carefully whether a problem hands you q or 2pq.

context: A three-generation family has a neurologic disorder inherited as an autosomal dominant. The proband is a 35-year-old man; other affected members include one of his daughters, his sister, his brother's son, his father, and his father's sister. The brother, who is the father of the affected nephew, is unaffected.
stem: Which of the following best explains why the proband's brother is unaffected?
options: Germline mosaicism
Incomplete penetrance
New mutation in the nephew
Variable expressivity
Wild-type genotype
rationale:
The allele is clearly segregating through three generations, and the brother sits between two affected relatives, so he is an obligate transmitter who does not express the phenotype: incomplete penetrance.

The trap: a de novo mutation in the nephew would be a remarkable coincidence in a family already carrying the allele. Prefer the explanation that uses the segregation you can already see.

stem: In some populations approximately 1/30 women are carriers for the X-linked trait G6PD deficiency. What is the disease frequency in males?
rationale:
Female carriers are 2pq = 1/30, and with p close to 1 that gives q = 1/60. For an X-linked trait the frequency of affected males equals the allele frequency, so 1/60.

The trap: the male frequency is q itself, never q². Males are hemizygous, so there is no second allele to inherit.

context: G6PD catalyses the step of the pentose phosphate pathway that produces NADPH, which maintains red cell morphology. G6PD-deficient red cells are sensitive to oxidative stress but are also less amenable to growth of the malarial parasite.
stem: Given that G6PD deficiency is much more common in parts of the world where malaria is prevalent, what is the best explanation for that observation?
options: Founder effect
Natural selection
Consanguinity
New mutation
Assortative mating
rationale:
Natural selection through heterozygote advantage. Low NADPH leaves glutathione oxidized, hydrogen peroxide accumulates, and denatured haemoglobin forms Heinz bodies that distort the cell — a cell the parasite grows in poorly. Where malaria is endemic that survival benefit keeps the allele frequency high.

The trap: a founder effect would explain a high frequency in one isolated community, not a frequency that tracks the geography of malaria across many unrelated populations.

stem: If a male with G6PD deficiency has children with a woman who has no family history of G6PD deficiency, what is the most likely outcome in his offspring?
options: Half of the girls are carriers, all the boys are affected
All the girls are carriers, half of the boys are affected
Half of the girls are carriers, none of the boys are affected
All the girls are carriers, none of the boys are affected
None of the girls are carriers, all the boys are affected
rationale:
He has one X, and it carries the mutation. Every daughter receives that X and is therefore an obligate carrier; every son receives his Y instead, so no son is affected.

The trap: affected fathers cannot produce affected sons for an X-linked condition. That absence of male-to-male transmission is the diagnostic feature of X-linkage on a pedigree.

context: A 1-year-old girl has failure to thrive, cognitive impairment, and poor motor function. Both parents and a brother and sister are healthy. A second brother died of a similar condition at age 18 months.
stem: This pattern of inheritance is MOST CONSISTENT with:
options: Autosomal dominant
Autosomal recessive
X-linked recessive
X-linked dominant
Mitochondrial
rationale:
The condition is absent in the parents' generation but present in the next, affects a girl and a boy, and is lethal in early childhood. Unaffected parents with affected children of both sexes is the signature of autosomal recessive inheritance.

The trap: X-linked dominant would require the mother to show something, via skewed X-inactivation or mosaicism, and would not so neatly give two similarly affected children of different sexes. Prefer the simpler explanation.

stem: A man with hemophilia B, an X-linked recessive disorder, wants to know his chance of having a similarly affected son. The BEST response is:
rationale:
To father a son he must pass his Y chromosome. His mutant X goes only to daughters, every one of whom becomes an obligate carrier.

The trap: the answer is 0% only because the mother's carrier status is not in play; if she were a carrier, sons could be affected through her. The question asks about what he transmits.

context: In a pedigree for an autosomal recessive condition, two first cousins have a daughter who is affected and is homozygous for two identical copies of the same mutant allele, derived from a common ancestor. The cousins' parents are a brother and sister from the second generation; their own parents form the first generation.
stem: Which conclusion is best supported?
options: The two second-generation siblings who are the cousins' parents must both be obligate carriers
Both first-generation grandparents must be carriers
The condition must be X-linked because it appears in only one branch of the family
Neither cousin can be a carrier, since both are unaffected
All of the affected child's siblings will also be affected
rationale:
The child's two identical alleles trace back to one common ancestor, so each cousin must have inherited the allele through their own parent. Those two siblings are therefore obligate carriers.

The trap: in the first generation only one of the two grandparents needs to carry the allele. These diseases are rare, so assuming both grandparents carry it multiplies an already small probability without warrant.

context: A patient is diagnosed with an autosomal dominant genetic disease, but neither of his parents has any symptoms of the disease.
sourceRef: Factors Modulating Inheritance Practice Questions (014) Q7
stem: Which of the following is NOT a possible explanation for this scenario?
options: A de novo mutation in the patient
Germline mosaicism in one parent
Reduced penetrance in one parent
Non-paternity
Skewed X-inactivation in the mother
rationale:
X-inactivation only bears on X-linked conditions, and this one is autosomal; the patient is male in any case, with a single X, so skewing could not apply to him.

The trap: the other four are all genuinely possible, and de novo mutation and germline mosaicism carry very different recurrence risks for the parents — near baseline for the first, meaningfully raised for the second.

context: D-glucose and L-glucose differ in configuration at every chiral carbon. α-D-galactose and β-D-galactose differ only at carbon 1.
stem: These two pairs are, respectively:
options: Enantiomers and anomers
Epimers and enantiomers
Anomers and epimers
Diastereomers and enantiomers
Enantiomers and epimers that are not anomers
rationale:
Enantiomers are non-superimposable mirror images, so they differ at every chiral centre. Epimers differ at exactly one, and anomers are the special case of epimers differing at the anomeric (former carbonyl) carbon, C1 in an aldose.

The trap: α-D-glucose and α-D-galactose are epimers too, differing at C4, but they are not anomers. Every anomer pair is an epimer pair; the reverse does not hold.

context: A disaccharide is formed from two β-D-galactose units joined by a 1→4 linkage.
stem: Which end is the reducing end, and why?
options: The anomeric carbon of the second galactose, because its hydroxyl is not tied up in the glycosidic bond
The anomeric carbon of the first galactose, because it donated its hydroxyl to the bond
Neither end, because both anomeric carbons are committed to the glycosidic bond
Carbon 4 of the second galactose, because that hydroxyl is free
Both ends, because galactose is an aldose
rationale:
A reducing end needs a free anomeric carbon that can open back to the aldehyde. In a 1→4 linkage the first sugar's C1 is committed to the bond, so the reducing end is the second sugar's C1.

The trap: sucrose is the classic non-reducing disaccharide precisely because its linkage ties up both anomeric carbons. Being an aldose is not sufficient on its own.

sourceRef: Carbohydrate Tutorial (Refresher 6) with Wilkins Problem Set (007) Q9
stem: Humans hydrolyse the α(1→4) bonds of starch but not the β(1→4) bonds of cellulose, yet we digest lactose perfectly well even though it also contains a β(1→4) bond. What explains this?
options: We have one specific brush-border enzyme, lactase, for that galactosidic bond, but none for the glucosidic bonds of cellulose
Cellulose bonds are converted to the α configuration in the gut lumen
Pancreatic amylase cleaves β bonds only at intestinal pH
Cellulose is absorbed intact across the enterocyte and excreted unchanged
Lactose is cleaved by salivary amylase before it reaches the intestine
rationale:
Specificity belongs to individual enzymes, not to a whole class of bond. Lactase cleaves the one particular β-galactosidic bond of lactose; we have no enzyme for the β-glucosidic bonds of cellulose, which is why cellulose passes through as dietary fibre.

The trap: “humans cannot digest β(1→4) bonds” is the usual shorthand, and lactose is the exception that shows why the shorthand is imprecise.

stem: A fasting hepatocyte breaks fatty acids into a common two-carbon product before the citric acid cycle. Which stage and product are paired correctly?
options: Stage 1; acetyl-CoA
Stage 2; acetyl-CoA
Stage 2; NADPH
Stage 3; carbon dioxide
rationale:
Stage 2 converts building blocks, including fatty acids, into common products such as acetyl-CoA; stage 3 then feeds acetyl-CoA into the TCA cycle.

The trap: stage 3 produces reducing power, but it is not the stage that first makes the shared acetyl-CoA product.

stem: A cell diverts reducing power toward lipid synthesis instead of ATP production. Which change best keeps that reducing power out of the electron transport chain?
options: Converting NADPH to NADH
Adding phosphate to NADH
Using NADPH as the reductant
Using FADH2 as the reductant
rationale:
The phosphate tag identifies NADPH as reducing power for synthetic reactions rather than a substrate for the electron transport chain.

The trap: NADH and FADH2 do feed the electron transport chain, even though all three cofactors carry reducing equivalents.

stem: During an enzyme-catalyzed redox reaction, a species written H− is transferred to NAD+. Which description is correct?
options: One proton and no electrons
One proton and one electron
One proton and two electrons
Two protons and two electrons
rationale:
A hydride is one proton plus two electrons. Its extra electron pair makes transfer of hydride a redox event.

The trap: one proton plus one electron is a neutral hydrogen atom, not hydride.

stem: A substrate loses two hydrogens while NAD+ is reduced. What is the expected immediate product pattern?
options: NADH2, with no proton released
NADH plus a leftover proton
NAD+ plus two hydrides
FADH2 plus a leftover proton
rationale:
NAD+ accepts one hydride, while the second hydrogen remains as H+, giving NADH + H+. NAD+ has room for only one hydride.

The trap: FAD can accept two hydrogens, but NAD+ cannot.

stem: A reaction removes two hydrogens from a substrate and transfers both intact to its oxidized carrier. Which carrier fits this physical arrangement?
options: Nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD+)
Nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate (NADP+)
Flavin adenine dinucleotide (FAD)
Coenzyme A (CoA)
rationale:
FAD can physically accept both hydrogens, becoming FADH2. NAD+ and NADP+ accept one hydride and leave one proton behind.

The trap: NAD+ is also a redox carrier, but its chemistry is not two intact hydrogens on the carrier.

stem: A saturated carbon chain is oxidized to introduce one carbon-carbon double bond. Which oxidized cofactor is reduced directly during this step?
options: Nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD+)
Nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate (NADP+)
Flavin adenine dinucleotide (FAD)
Ubiquinone (coenzyme Q)
rationale:
Oxidizing an alkane to an alkene removes two hydrogens and directly reduces FAD to FADH2 in the course oxidation-state framework.

The trap: most other oxidations on the chart use NAD+, but alkane to alkene is the named FAD pattern.

stem: An RNA polymerase reads a DNA strand 3′ to 5′. In which direction is the RNA product synthesized?
options: 5′ to 3′ only within exons
Either direction, based on promoter orientation
rationale:
DNA and RNA are synthesized 5′ to 3′, so the template is read 3′ to 5′.

The trap: promoter orientation determines which strand is used as the template, not the chemical direction in which RNA grows.

stem: A mutation removes histone H1 but leaves the core octamer intact. Which chromatin feature is most directly lost?
options: The two turns of DNA around the core
Linker-DNA association between nucleosomes
The positive charge of every core histone
The phosphodiester backbone of DNA
rationale:
Histone H1 binds the linker region of DNA; the core octamer is two copies each of the core histones around which DNA loops twice.

The trap: H1 is histone-associated but is not one of the eight core histones.

stem: A bacterial polymerase can extend DNA from a primer and remove a just-incorporated wrong base, but cannot remove RNA primers. Which enzyme is functioning?
options: DNA polymerase I
DNA polymerase III
DNA ligase
Primase
rationale:
DNA polymerase III performs most DNA synthesis and has 3′ to 5′ proofreading. Primer removal requires polymerase I's separate 5′ to 3′ exonuclease activity.

The trap: both polymerases proofread, but only polymerase I has the primer-removal snowplow function.

stem: After RNA primers are laid on lagging-strand fragments, which activity removes each primer in the direction described as a snowplow?
options: DNA polymerase I 5′→3′ exonuclease
DNA polymerase III 3′→5′ exonuclease
DNA ligase phosphodiester formation
Primase RNA polymerase activity
rationale:
DNA polymerase I's 5′ to 3′ exonuclease removes RNA primers, the snowplow function. Ligase seals the remaining nick after replacement DNA is present.

The trap: 3′ to 5′ exonuclease is proofreading, not primer removal.

stem: A karyotype contains 48 chromosomes because chromosomes 18 and 21 are each present in three copies. Which classification is correct?
options: Tetraploidy, because the total exceeds 46
Triploidy, because two chromosomes are duplicated
Aneuploidy, specifically double trisomy
Euploidy, because every chromosome is represented
rationale:
This is aneuploidy because 48 is not a multiple of the haploid set of 23. The two separately triplicated chromosomes make it a double trisomy.

The trap: tetraploidy means four complete haploid sets, which would total 92 chromosomes, not 48.

stem: A phenotypically normal parent carries a balanced reciprocal translocation. Why can that parent's child still have multiple malformations?
options: Balanced carriers always lose centromeres
Meiosis can produce unbalanced chromosome content
The parent must have an aneuploidy
Reciprocal exchanges always add a full haploid set
rationale:
A balanced carrier usually has the normal amount of genetic material, but meiosis can yield offspring with deletions and duplications, making them unbalanced.

The trap: normal appearance in a balanced carrier does not guarantee balanced gametes.

stem: An affected father directly transmits a condition to his son. Which inheritance categories are ruled out by that male-to-male transmission?
options: Autosomal dominant and autosomal recessive
X-linked and mitochondrial
Mitochondrial and autosomal recessive
X-linked and autosomal dominant
rationale:
Male-to-male transmission rules out X-linked and mitochondrial inheritance because fathers pass Y, not X, to sons and mitochondrial DNA is maternally transmitted.

The trap: male-to-male transmission is entirely compatible with autosomal inheritance.

stem: In a fully penetrant disorder, an affected man has an unaffected daughter. Which pattern becomes unlikely because an affected father should pass his mutant X to all daughters?
options: Autosomal dominant
Autosomal recessive
X-linked dominant
Mitochondrial inheritance
rationale:
In fully penetrant X-linked dominant inheritance, an affected father passes his mutant X chromosome to all female offspring. An unaffected daughter therefore argues against that pattern.

The trap: vertical transmission alone suggests dominance but does not distinguish autosomal from X-linked dominance.

stem: Two unaffected parents have an affected son and an affected daughter. The affected daughter's father is unaffected. Which inheritance pattern fits best?
options: Autosomal recessive
X-linked recessive
X-linked dominant
Mitochondrial
rationale:
Unaffected parents producing affected children suggests recessive inheritance, and an affected daughter with an unaffected father argues against X-linked recessive inheritance. Autosomal recessive best fits both sexes and the skipped generation.

The trap: a recessive-looking pedigree is not automatically X-linked; test whether an affected daughter's father could supply the required mutant X.

stem: All children of affected women are affected, whereas children of affected men are unaffected. Which pattern is illustrated?
options: Autosomal dominant
X-linked dominant
Homoplasmic mitochondrial
Autosomal recessive
rationale:
This is the key pattern for homoplasmic mitochondrial inheritance: affected mothers transmit to all children, while affected fathers do not transmit the condition.

The trap: vertical transmission can resemble dominance, but paternal nontransmission points to mitochondria.

stem: An inhibitor collapses the sodium gradient at the apical surface of intestinal enterocytes. Which absorption pattern best follows the course model?
options: Glucose and galactose uptake falls; fructose uptake can continue
Glucose uptake continues; galactose and fructose uptake falls
Fructose uptake falls; glucose and galactose uptake continue
All three monosaccharides require the same sodium-dependent entry
rationale:
Glucose and galactose use sodium-dependent uptake into enterocytes, whereas fructose is sodium independent. Removing the gradient therefore selectively disrupts glucose and galactose entry.

The trap: all three sugars reach portal blood after absorption, but only glucose and galactose share sodium-coupled apical entry.

stem: After milk feeding, a newborn develops jaundice, hepatomegaly, poor feeding, and urine positive for reducing substances but negative on a glucose-specific test. Which defect and accumulated metabolite best fit?
options: Galactokinase deficiency with isolated galactitol accumulation
GALT deficiency with galactose 1-phosphate accumulation
Aldolase B deficiency with fructose 1-phosphate accumulation
Lactase deficiency with circulating lactose accumulation
rationale:
The systemic neonatal illness plus a non-glucose reducing sugar indicates classic galactosemia from GALT deficiency, with galactose 1-phosphate accumulation and ATP depletion.

The trap: galactokinase deficiency can produce galactitol and cataracts, but it does not cause the severe liver disease of classic GALT deficiency.
sourceRef: L002 transcript 02:39–02:56; RR2 Galactosemia case and GALT section
